internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A 58-year-old man presents with crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm, lasting 45 minutes, with ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF on ECG. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
o: Left anterior descending artery
Left circumflex artery
Left main coronary artery
Posterior descending artery from the left circumflex
Right coronary artery
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: ST elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) classically indicates occlusion of the right coronary artery, which typically supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle in most individuals (right-dominant circulation).

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which cardiac biomarker rises earliest after acute myocardial infarction and is most useful for very early diagnosis (within 2-4 hours)?
o: Myoglobin
Troponin I
CK-MB
Lactate dehydrogenase
AST
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Myoglobin rises earliest (within 1-3 hours) after myocardial injury but lacks cardiac specificity; troponin, though highly specific, typically takes 3-6 hours to become detectable, making myoglobin more useful for very early exclusion when combined with other markers.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: High-sensitivity troponin remains the preferred biomarker for diagnosing myocardial infarction primarily because of which property?
o: Its extremely short half-life of under 1 hour
Complete absence from healthy individuals' serum
High cardiac specificity and sensitivity, remaining elevated for several days
Its exclusive elevation in unstable angina only
Its independence from renal clearance
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Troponin I and T are highly specific to cardiac myocyte injury and remain elevated for 7-14 days after infarction, providing both a sensitive diagnostic window and prognostic information.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A patient with an ST-elevation myocardial infarction presenting within 90 minutes to a hospital with catheterization facilities should receive which treatment as the preferred reperfusion strategy?
o: Thrombolytic therapy exclusively regardless of PCI availability
Coronary artery bypass grafting as first-line emergency treatment
Conservative medical management only
Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
Delayed elective angiography after 2 weeks
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy for STEMI when it can be performed promptly (within 90-120 minutes of first medical contact) by an experienced team, offering better outcomes than thrombolysis.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which class of drugs is contraindicated in the acute management of a patient with cocaine-induced chest pain due to risk of unopposed alpha-adrenergic coronary vasoconstriction?
o: Benzodiazepines
Nitrates
Aspirin
Non-selective beta-blockers
Calcium channel blockers
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Beta-blockers (especially non-selective agents) are avoided in cocaine-induced chest pain because blocking beta-2 mediated vasodilation leaves alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed, potentially worsening coronary spasm.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A patient with stable angina develops relief of chest pain within minutes of taking sublingual nitroglycerin. Which mechanism explains this therapeutic effect?
o: Direct positive inotropic effect on the myocardium
Venodilation reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand, along with coronary vasodilation
Reduction in heart rate via beta-receptor blockade
Inhibition of platelet aggregation
Direct anticoagulant effect
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle relaxation; venodilation reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand while also dilating epicardial coronary arteries, relieving ischemic pain.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which physical examination finding is most specific for severe aortic stenosis?
o: Wide pulse pressure with a collapsing pulse
Bounding pulses with a diastolic murmur at the left sternal border
Slow-rising, low-volume carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) with a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Pulsus paradoxus exceeding 10 mmHg
Water-hammer pulse
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Severe aortic stenosis classically produces a slow-rising, low-amplitude carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus) along with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotid arteries.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A collapsing (water-hammer) pulse with a wide pulse pressure is most characteristic of which valvular lesion?
o: Aortic regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Mitral stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis
Pulmonary stenosis
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Aortic regurgitation causes rapid diastolic runoff of blood back into the left ventricle, producing a widened pulse pressure and a collapsing, water-hammer quality pulse (Corrigan's pulse).

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position, accompanied by an opening snap, is characteristic of which valvular lesion?
o: Mitral stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Mitral stenosis classically produces a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, best heard with the bell in the left lateral position, often preceded by an opening snap from the stenotic mitral valve.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Atrial fibrillation is most strongly associated with which serious long-term complication if left inadequately anticoagulated?
o: Embolic stroke
Pulmonary embolism
Acute myocardial infarction directly
Aortic dissection
Constrictive pericarditis
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Atrial fibrillation predisposes to stasis of blood in the left atrial appendage, promoting thrombus formation that can embolize to the cerebral circulation, causing ischemic stroke.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: The CHA2DS2-VASc score is used clinically for which purpose in a patient with atrial fibrillation?
o: Estimating stroke risk to guide anticoagulation decisions
Estimating bleeding risk on anticoagulation
Diagnosing the underlying cause of atrial fibrillation
Determining the need for cardioversion timing
Grading the severity of associated valvular disease
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: The CHA2DS2-VASc score stratifies stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation based on clinical risk factors, guiding the decision on whether long-term anticoagulation is indicated.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A patient with atrial fibrillation of unknown duration requires cardioversion; which precaution is essential before the procedure unless it is an emergency?
o: Immediate cardioversion without any anticoagulation
Discontinuation of all antiarrhythmic drugs beforehand
Administration of thrombolytic therapy first
Insertion of a permanent pacemaker before cardioversion
Anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks prior, or transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial thrombus
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: In atrial fibrillation of unknown or prolonged duration, cardioversion carries a risk of dislodging an atrial thrombus; guidelines recommend either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or transesophageal echocardiography to exclude thrombus before elective cardioversion.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which ECG finding is characteristic of complete (third-degree) heart block?
o: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with independent atrial and ventricular rates
A progressively lengthening PR interval until a QRS is dropped
A constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves
A short PR interval with a delta wave
Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Complete heart block is characterized by total atrioventricular dissociation, where atrial and ventricular activity occur independently at their own rates, since no atrial impulses are conducted to the ventricles.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block is characterized by which ECG pattern?
o: A fixed, prolonged PR interval with intermittent dropped beats
Complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes
A short PR interval with a wide QRS
Progressive PR interval prolongation until a QRS complex is dropped
Absence of P waves altogether
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block shows progressively lengthening PR intervals until a P wave fails to conduct, after which the cycle resets, typically representing a benign block at the AV node level.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A wide-complex tachycardia in a patient with a history of myocardial infarction should be presumed to be which rhythm until proven otherwise?
o: Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy
Ventricular tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia
Atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: In a patient with structural heart disease (particularly prior infarction), a wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, as misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment (e.g., verapamil) can be fatal.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QT prolongation, is classically treated acutely with which agent?
o: Intravenous magnesium sulfate
Intravenous amiodarone as first-line
Oral quinidine
Intravenous verapamil
Intravenous digoxin
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment for torsades de pointes, regardless of serum magnesium level, as it stabilizes cardiac membrane excitability and can terminate the arrhythmia.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which class of antiarrhythmic drugs, including amiodarone, primarily works by blocking potassium channels and prolonging the action potential duration?
o: Class I antiarrhythmics
Class II antiarrhythmics
Class III antiarrhythmics
Class IV antiarrhythmics
Class V antiarrhythmics
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Class III antiarrhythmics (e.g., amiodarone, sotalol) block potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and the action potential duration, which helps terminate and prevent reentrant arrhythmias.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Amiodarone, a commonly used antiarrhythmic, is associated with which characteristic long-term adverse effect requiring periodic monitoring?
o: Acute renal failure exclusively
Hemolytic anemia exclusively
Peptic ulcer disease exclusively
Osteoporosis exclusively
Thyroid dysfunction and pulmonary fibrosis
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Amiodarone contains iodine and can cause both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, along with pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, and corneal microdeposits, necessitating periodic thyroid, liver, and pulmonary function monitoring.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A patient with decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema presents with severe dyspnea and bilateral crackles. Which initial pharmacological intervention provides the most rapid symptomatic relief?
o: Oral ACE inhibitor
Intravenous loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide)
Oral beta-blocker uptitration
Oral spironolactone
Intravenous digoxin as first-line
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Intravenous loop diuretics rapidly reduce preload and pulmonary congestion in acute decompensated heart failure, providing prompt symptomatic relief of dyspnea from pulmonary edema.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which class of heart failure medications has been shown to reduce mortality through neurohormonal blockade and is a cornerstone of chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction management?
o: Loop diuretics alone
Calcium channel blockers
Short-acting nitrates alone
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) and beta-blockers
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and more recently SGLT2 inhibitors and ARNI have all demonstrated mortality benefit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction through neurohormonal modulation.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a useful biomarker in the evaluation of a dyspneic patient primarily to help distinguish which conditions?
o: Bacterial versus viral pneumonia
Pulmonary embolism versus pneumothorax specifically
Asthma versus COPD specifically
Anemia versus polycythemia
Cardiac (heart failure) versus non-cardiac causes of dyspnea
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: BNP is released from ventricular myocardium in response to wall stress; elevated levels support a cardiac cause of dyspnea (heart failure), while normal levels make heart failure less likely, helping differentiate from primary pulmonary causes.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Constrictive pericarditis classically produces which physical sign due to impaired venous return during inspiration?
o: Pulsus paradoxus exceeding 10 mmHg as the defining feature
A collapsing water-hammer pulse
Wide, fixed splitting of the second heart sound
Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration)
Corrigan's sign
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Kussmaul's sign, a paradoxical increase in jugular venous pressure during inspiration, occurs in constrictive pericarditis because the rigid, non-compliant pericardium prevents the right heart from accommodating increased venous return.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Cardiac tamponade classically presents with which clinical triad (Beck's triad)?
o: Fever, cough, and pleuritic chest pain
Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration
Chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea
Hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds
Wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses, and flushed skin
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Beck's triad of hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled/distant heart sounds classically indicates cardiac tamponade, resulting from pericardial fluid compressing the heart and impairing diastolic filling.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Pulsus paradoxus, an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, is a classic finding in which condition?
o: Aortic stenosis
Cardiac tamponade
Mitral regurgitation
Complete heart block
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Pulsus paradoxus (a drop in systolic BP of more than 10 mmHg during inspiration) occurs in cardiac tamponade due to exaggerated ventricular interdependence within the constrained pericardial space.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy classically causes a systolic murmur that characteristically does which of the following with the Valsalva maneuver?
o: Decreases in intensity
Remains completely unchanged
Increases in intensity
Disappears entirely
Becomes a diastolic murmur instead
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, maneuvers that decrease venous return and left ventricular volume (like Valsalva or standing) worsen the dynamic outflow obstruction, increasing the murmur's intensity, unlike most other systolic murmurs.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a well-recognized cause of which serious event in young, otherwise healthy athletes?
o: Chronic stable angina only
Slowly progressive heart failure exclusively over decades
Sudden cardiac death
Isolated atrial fibrillation with no other risk
Infective endocarditis exclusively
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the leading causes of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, often due to ventricular arrhythmias triggered by the abnormal, disorganized myocardial architecture and outflow obstruction.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Infective endocarditis is most strongly suggested by which combination of clinical findings (modified Duke criteria)?
o: Isolated fever without any other findings
A single positive blood culture with a skin contaminant organism
Elevated white cell count alone
Presence of a innocent flow murmur alone
Persistently positive blood cultures with a typical organism and evidence of endocardial involvement (e.g., new valvular regurgitation) on echocardiography
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: The modified Duke criteria rely on major criteria including sustained bacteremia with a typical endocarditis organism and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation) to establish the diagnosis.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Janeway lesions, seen in infective endocarditis, are classically described as which type of finding?
o: Painless erythematous macules on the palms and soles
Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads
Splinter hemorrhages under the nails
Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers
Petechiae on the conjunctivae
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Janeway lesions are painless, erythematous or hemorrhagic macules typically found on the palms and soles in infective endocarditis, resulting from septic microemboli, distinguishing them from the painful Osler's nodes.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Osler's nodes in infective endocarditis are classically described as which type of lesion?
o: Painless macules on the palms and soles
Splinter hemorrhages of the nail bed
Roth spots on retinal examination
Clubbing of the fingers
Painful, tender nodules on the pulps of fingers and toes
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Osler's nodes are tender, painful, raised nodules on the finger and toe pads in infective endocarditis, thought to result from immune complex deposition, distinguishing them from the painless Janeway lesions.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Prophylactic antibiotics before dental procedures are recommended for patients with which condition to prevent infective endocarditis, per current major guidelines?
o: Any mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation
Isolated atrial septal defect (secundum type) without other lesions
Prosthetic heart valves or prior history of infective endocarditis
Well-controlled hypertension
Any innocent flow murmur
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Current guidelines restrict antibiotic prophylaxis to the highest-risk patients, including those with prosthetic heart valves, prior infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart diseases, and cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Deep vein thrombosis is a significant risk factor for which acute cardiopulmonary emergency?
o: Acute myocardial infarction directly
Aortic dissection
Cardiac tamponade
Pulmonary embolism
Constrictive pericarditis
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Deep vein thrombosis, particularly of the proximal lower limb veins, can embolize to the pulmonary circulation, causing acute pulmonary embolism, which can be life-threatening depending on clot burden.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: An S3 heart sound (third heart sound) in an adult is most classically associated with which condition?
o: Normal physiological finding in all healthy adults over 40
Severe aortic stenosis exclusively
Complete heart block exclusively
Constrictive pericarditis exclusively (rather than an S3-like knock)
Volume overload states such as heart failure
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: An S3 heart sound occurs due to rapid ventricular filling in early diastole and is a classic (though not universal) sign of volume overload states such as systolic heart failure, though it can be a normal finding in children and young adults.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: An S4 heart sound (fourth heart sound) is most classically associated with which underlying pathophysiology?
o: Volume overload of a normal ventricle
A stiff, non-compliant ventricle with atrial contraction against increased resistance
Complete absence of atrial contraction (as in atrial fibrillation)
Severe mitral regurgitation exclusively
Free wall rupture of the ventricle
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: An S4 sound results from atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff, non-compliant (hypertrophied or ischemic) ventricle, and is therefore absent in atrial fibrillation, where coordinated atrial contraction is lost.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Dressler's syndrome, occurring weeks after myocardial infarction, is best characterized as which type of process?
o: A recurrent myocardial infarction
A bacterial pericardial infection
A mechanical complication from papillary muscle rupture
A direct viral myocarditis unrelated to the prior infarction
An autoimmune-mediated pericarditis
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Dressler's syndrome is a delayed, autoimmune-mediated pericarditis (with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and pericardial effusion) occurring weeks to months after myocardial infarction, thought to result from an immune response against exposed myocardial antigens.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Which mechanical complication of myocardial infarction presents with a new loud holosystolic murmur and acute pulmonary edema due to rupture of a supporting structure of the mitral valve?
o: Free wall rupture with tamponade
Ventricular septal rupture
Papillary muscle rupture
Left ventricular aneurysm formation
Right ventricular infarction
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Papillary muscle rupture, most often complicating inferior MI (posteromedial papillary muscle, supplied by a single vessel), causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with a new murmur and sudden pulmonary edema.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A young patient presents with hypertension found to be significantly higher in the upper limbs than the lower limbs, with radiofemoral delay on examination. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Essential (primary) hypertension
Renal artery stenosis
Coarctation of the aorta
Pheochromocytoma
Primary hyperaldosteronism
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Coarctation of the aorta classically presents with hypertension in the upper extremities, weaker and delayed femoral pulses relative to the radial pulse (radiofemoral delay), and can be associated with notching of the ribs on chest X-ray from collateral vessels.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Secondary hypertension due to renal artery stenosis in a young woman is most commonly caused by which underlying pathology?
o: Atherosclerotic renal artery disease
Renal vein thrombosis
Polycystic kidney disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia
Diabetic nephropathy
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: In young women, fibromuscular dysplasia (causing a characteristic 'string of beads' appearance on angiography) is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis leading to secondary hypertension, in contrast to older patients where atherosclerosis predominates.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A fixed, widely split second heart sound that does not vary with respiration is a classic finding in which congenital heart defect?
o: Ventricular septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Atrial septal defect
Coarctation of the aorta
Tetralogy of Fallot
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Atrial septal defect causes equalized right and left atrial pressures with a fixed, widely split S2 that does not vary with the respiratory cycle, distinguishing it from normal physiological splitting.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: A continuous 'machinery' murmur heard throughout systole and diastole is classically associated with which congenital cardiac lesion?
o: Atrial septal defect
Ventricular septal defect
Pulmonary stenosis
Patent ductus arteriosus
Tricuspid atresia
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: A patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous, machinery-like murmur due to persistent flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery throughout the cardiac cycle, since aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure in both systole and diastole.

internal-medicine/cardiology.s: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of which four anatomical features?
o: Ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy
Atrial septal defect, mitral stenosis, aortic coarctation, and left ventricular hypertrophy
Patent ductus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, pulmonary atresia, and left ventricular hypertrophy
Ventricular septal defect, mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, and biventricular hypertrophy
Atrial septal defect, pulmonary atresia, transposition of great arteries, and right atrial enlargement
internal-medicine/cardiology.e: Tetralogy of Fallot comprises a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary (infundibular) stenosis, an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy secondary to the outflow obstruction, the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect presenting beyond infancy.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A patient with a long smoking history presents with progressive dyspnea, chronic cough, and pursed-lip breathing, with a barrel-shaped chest. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Acute bronchitis
Pulmonary embolism
Restrictive lung disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (emphysema-predominant)
Pneumothorax
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Emphysema-predominant COPD classically presents with progressive dyspnea, pursed-lip breathing (to prevent airway collapse), and a barrel-shaped chest from hyperinflation, typically in long-term smokers.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Spirometry findings of a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (below 0.7) with a reduced FEV1 are characteristic of which pattern of lung disease?
o: Restrictive lung disease
Normal lung function
Mixed pattern exclusively with no obstructive component
Pure diffusion defect
Obstructive lung disease
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio indicates airflow obstruction (as in COPD or asthma), since expiratory flow is disproportionately reduced relative to the total volume that can be exhaled.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Spirometry findings of a reduced FVC with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio are characteristic of which pattern of lung disease?
o: Restrictive lung disease
Obstructive lung disease
Normal variant with no pathology
Isolated small airway disease
Bronchiectasis exclusively
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, chest wall disorders) reduce total lung volumes proportionally, so FVC falls while the FEV1/FVC ratio remains normal or even increases.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A young patient presents with episodic wheeze, cough (worse at night), and chest tightness that improves with bronchodilator use. Spirometry shows reversible airflow obstruction. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Chronic bronchitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Bronchiectasis
Pneumoconiosis
Asthma
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Asthma is characterized by episodic, reversible airflow obstruction with symptoms often worse at night, classically demonstrating significant improvement in FEV1 after bronchodilator administration on spirometry.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Which inhaled medication class is considered first-line reliever (rescue) therapy for acute asthma symptoms?
o: Inhaled corticosteroids alone
Long-acting muscarinic antagonists
Short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol)
Leukotriene receptor antagonists
Long-acting beta-2 agonists alone without ICS
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol) provide rapid bronchodilation and are the first-line reliever therapy for acute asthma symptoms and exacerbations.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A patient in status asthmaticus presents with a silent chest on auscultation. What is the clinical significance of this finding?
o: It indicates the asthma attack has resolved completely
It indicates a normal, mild asthma exacerbation
It confirms a diagnosis of pneumothorax rather than asthma
It indicates the patient is hyperventilating excessively
It indicates severe, life-threatening airway obstruction with minimal air movement
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: A 'silent chest' in severe asthma indicates critically reduced air entry due to profound bronchoconstriction/obstruction, representing a life-threatening exacerbation requiring immediate aggressive treatment, not clinical improvement.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Chronic bronchitis is clinically defined as which of the following?
o: Any single episode of cough with sputum production lasting more than a week
Cough exclusively triggered by exercise
Cough associated with fever lasting 5 days
A productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years, after excluding other causes
Wheezing that resolves completely with bronchodilators
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Chronic bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis defined by a productive cough occurring on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, with other causes of chronic cough excluded.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency should be suspected in a patient presenting with emphysema under which clinical circumstance?
o: Emphysema in a 70-year-old with a 50-pack-year smoking history
Early-onset emphysema (before age 45) in a non-smoker or minimal smoker, often with panacinar distribution
Emphysema with a purely centriacinar distribution on imaging
Emphysema associated with occupational silica exposure
Emphysema occurring only in the upper lung zones
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency should be suspected in early-onset emphysema, particularly in non-smokers or with minimal smoking history, and characteristically produces panacinar (rather than centriacinar) emphysema, often more pronounced in the lower lung zones.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Bronchiectasis is characterized radiologically and pathologically by which finding?
o: Irreversible dilation of the bronchi with chronic inflammation and impaired mucus clearance
Diffuse alveolar consolidation with air bronchograms
Isolated pleural thickening without airway involvement
Reversible bronchial narrowing that fully resolves with bronchodilators
Isolated mediastinal lymphadenopathy
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Bronchiectasis involves permanent, abnormal dilation of the bronchi due to a cycle of infection, inflammation, and impaired mucociliary clearance, producing chronic cough with copious purulent sputum and recurrent infections.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Cystic fibrosis, a common cause of bronchiectasis in children, results from a defect in which gene/protein?
o: Dystrophin
Beta-globin
CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator)
Alpha-1 antitrypsin
Fibrillin-1
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Cystic fibrosis results from mutations in the CFTR gene, encoding a chloride channel; defective chloride transport leads to thick, viscous secretions affecting the lungs, pancreas, and other organs.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A community-acquired pneumonia severity assessment tool (CURB-65) includes which of the following parameters?
o: Only the patient's oxygen saturation
Only the chest X-ray findings
White blood cell count alone
C-reactive protein level alone
Confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and age 65 or older
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: CURB-65 scores confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60 mmHg), and age ≥65 to stratify pneumonia severity and guide site-of-care decisions.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae is classically associated with which extrapulmonary finding?
o: Massive pleural effusion in all cases
Lobar consolidation with rust-colored sputum as the hallmark
Cavitary lung lesions as a universal feature
Cold agglutinin-mediated hemolytic anemia
Empyema as the most common complication
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection can trigger production of IgM cold agglutinins, causing a mild hemolytic anemia, alongside its classic 'walking pneumonia' presentation with a dry cough and patchy, often bilateral, radiographic infiltrates.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A lung abscess is most classically associated with which risk factor related to airway protection?
o: Well-controlled type 2 diabetes without other comorbidities
Isolated seasonal allergic rhinitis
Chronic use of inhaled corticosteroids at standard doses
Aspiration in a patient with impaired consciousness or swallowing dysfunction
Mild intermittent asthma
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Lung abscesses classically arise following aspiration of oropharyngeal contents in patients with impaired consciousness, alcoholism, seizures, or swallowing dysfunction, introducing anaerobic and mixed oral flora into the lung parenchyma.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A pleural effusion is classified as an exudate (per Light's criteria) when which of the following is present?
o: Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio greater than 0.5, or pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio greater than 0.6
Pleural fluid protein less than 1 g/dL regardless of ratio
Pleural fluid glucose identical to serum glucose
Absence of any cells in the pleural fluid
Pleural fluid pH greater than 7.6
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Light's criteria classify pleural effusion as exudative if any one of: pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5, pleural/serum LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural LDH more than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH, is met.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A transudative pleural effusion is most commonly caused by which underlying condition?
o: Bacterial pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion)
Congestive heart failure
Pulmonary tuberculosis
Malignancy
Pulmonary embolism with infarction
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Congestive heart failure is the most common cause of transudative pleural effusion, resulting from increased hydrostatic pressure rather than increased capillary permeability or inflammation.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A sudden onset of unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea in a tall, thin young man, with absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side, suggests which diagnosis?
o: Acute myocardial infarction
Pulmonary embolism as the most likely cause
Community-acquired pneumonia
Pericarditis
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically occurs in tall, thin young men, often due to rupture of subpleural blebs, presenting with sudden pleuritic pain, dyspnea, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance on the affected side.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency requiring which immediate intervention?
o: Observation alone with serial chest X-rays
Oral analgesics and reassurance
Immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion
Elective outpatient follow-up in one week
Immediate intubation without any decompression
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Tension pneumothorax causes progressive intrapleural pressure buildup compromising venous return and cardiac output; it requires immediate needle decompression (typically at the second intercostal space, midclavicular line) followed by definitive chest tube placement.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Which occupational lung disease is characterized by nodular fibrosis predominantly in the upper lung zones, associated with coal mining?
o: Asbestosis
Silicosis exclusively unrelated to coal
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
Byssinosis
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis results from chronic coal dust inhalation, producing characteristic nodular opacities predominantly in the upper lung zones, which can progress to progressive massive fibrosis in advanced cases.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis classically presents with which auscultatory finding?
o: Fine, dry, bibasilar 'Velcro' crackles
Widespread expiratory wheeze
A pleural friction rub in all cases
Absent breath sounds bilaterally
Coarse crackles that clear with coughing
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis classically produces fine, dry, end-inspiratory crackles (often likened to the sound of Velcro being pulled apart) most prominent at the lung bases, reflecting the underlying fibrotic process.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Which imaging finding is characteristic of usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on high-resolution CT, associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
o: Subpleural, basal-predominant honeycombing with reticular opacities
Diffuse ground-glass opacities without honeycombing
Isolated hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal changes
Cavitary lesions in the upper lobes
A solitary well-circumscribed pulmonary nodule
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: The usual interstitial pneumonia pattern shows subpleural and basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, a hallmark high-resolution CT finding in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Sarcoidosis classically presents on chest imaging with which finding?
o: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
A solitary pulmonary nodule with spiculated margins
Massive unilateral pleural effusion
Diffuse miliary nodules exclusively
Isolated pneumothorax
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Sarcoidosis classically presents with bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on chest imaging, often with or without pulmonary parenchymal infiltrates, reflecting the underlying non-caseating granulomatous inflammation.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Non-caseating granulomas on lung biopsy are the characteristic histopathological finding in which disease?
o: Tuberculosis
Sarcoidosis
Histoplasmosis
Wegener's granulomatosis (GPA) exclusively
Lung abscess
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Sarcoidosis is defined histologically by non-caseating (non-necrotizing) granulomas, distinguishing it from tuberculosis and fungal infections, which typically show caseating necrosis within granulomas.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A patient with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis develops massive hemoptysis years later; a chest CT shows a fungus ball within an old cavity. Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Cryptococcus neoformans
Pneumocystis jirovecii
Histoplasma capsulatum
Aspergillus fumigatus (aspergilloma)
Blastomyces dermatitidis
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: An aspergilloma (fungus ball) forms when Aspergillus colonizes a pre-existing lung cavity (often from prior tuberculosis), and can cause life-threatening hemoptysis due to erosion of adjacent blood vessels.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A well's score or similar clinical prediction rule for pulmonary embolism incorporates which of the following clinical features?
o: Only the patient's age
Only the presence of a cough
Only a family history of any cardiovascular disease
Only the patient's blood pressure
Signs of deep vein thrombosis, tachycardia, immobilization/recent surgery, and prior VTE history
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: The Wells score for pulmonary embolism incorporates clinical findings such as signs of DVT, heart rate >100, immobilization or surgery in the past 4 weeks, prior VTE, hemoptysis, malignancy, and whether PE is the most likely diagnosis, to estimate pretest probability.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: The definitive diagnostic imaging test for confirming pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable patient is which of the following?
o: Plain chest X-ray alone
Abdominal ultrasound
Echocardiography alone without other imaging
Ventilation-perfusion scan as the universal first-line test regardless of renal function
CT pulmonary angiography
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: CT pulmonary angiography is the standard, widely available, definitive imaging modality for diagnosing pulmonary embolism in most patients, though V/Q scanning remains an alternative particularly when contrast is contraindicated (e.g., renal impairment).

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Obstructive sleep apnea is most strongly associated with which anthropometric/clinical risk factor?
o: Obesity with increased neck circumference
Being underweight with a low body mass index
Young age (under 20 years) as the primary risk factor
Female sex as the predominant risk factor
Regular aerobic exercise
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Obesity, particularly with increased neck circumference and upper airway soft tissue deposition, is the strongest risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, causing repeated upper airway collapse during sleep.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: The gold-standard diagnostic test for obstructive sleep apnea is which of the following?
o: Chest X-ray
Pulmonary function testing alone
Arterial blood gas analysis alone
Overnight pulse oximetry alone without other parameters
Polysomnography (overnight sleep study)
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Polysomnography, which records multiple physiological parameters overnight (airflow, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation, EEG), is the gold-standard test for diagnosing and quantifying the severity of obstructive sleep apnea.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the first-line treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea because it acts through which mechanism?
o: Directly stimulating the respiratory center in the brainstem
Reducing systemic blood pressure directly and independently of airway effects
Acting as a bronchodilator on the lower airways
Providing supplemental oxygen as its primary mechanism
Providing pneumatic splinting of the upper airway to prevent collapse during sleep
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: CPAP delivers continuous positive pressure that acts as a pneumatic splint, keeping the upper airway open during sleep and preventing the repetitive collapse characteristic of obstructive sleep apnea.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Type 1 (hypoxemic) respiratory failure is characterized by which arterial blood gas pattern?
o: Low PaO2 with markedly elevated PaCO2
Normal PaO2 with elevated PaCO2
Elevated PaO2 with low PaCO2
Low PaO2 with normal or low PaCO2
Normal values for both PaO2 and PaCO2
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Type 1 respiratory failure is defined by hypoxemia (low PaO2) with normal or low PaCO2, typically resulting from ventilation-perfusion mismatch or diffusion impairment, as seen in pneumonia or pulmonary edema.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure is characterized by which arterial blood gas pattern?
o: Low PaO2 with elevated PaCO2 (hypoventilation)
Normal PaO2 with normal PaCO2
Elevated PaO2 with elevated PaCO2
Low PaO2 with low PaCO2
Normal PaO2 with low PaCO2
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Type 2 respiratory failure involves alveolar hypoventilation, resulting in both hypoxemia and hypercapnia (elevated PaCO2), commonly seen in conditions like COPD exacerbation, opioid overdose, or neuromuscular respiratory failure.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is defined by which key diagnostic criterion regarding the PaO2/FiO2 ratio and chest imaging?
o: A PaO2/FiO2 ratio greater than 400 with a normal chest X-ray
Unilateral infiltrate with normal oxygenation
Isolated pleural effusion without parenchymal infiltrates
Bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging with a reduced PaO2/FiO2 ratio, in the absence of cardiac failure as the primary explanation
Elevated BNP with clear lung fields
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: ARDS is diagnosed using the Berlin definition, requiring bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on imaging, a reduced PaO2/FiO2 ratio (severity-graded), and exclusion of cardiogenic pulmonary edema/fluid overload as the sole explanation.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Lung cancer presenting with hoarseness of voice is most likely due to involvement of which structure?
o: Phrenic nerve
Vagus nerve at the level of the brainstem
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Sympathetic chain causing Horner's syndrome exclusively
Brachial plexus
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Hoarseness in lung cancer typically results from involvement (compression or invasion) of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, most often on the left side due to its longer intrathoracic course around the aortic arch.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor) can cause Horner's syndrome by involving which structure?
o: The recurrent laryngeal nerve exclusively
The sympathetic chain/stellate ganglion
The phrenic nerve exclusively
The vagus nerve at the neck
The brachial plexus lower trunk without sympathetic involvement
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: A Pancoast tumor at the lung apex can invade the sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion, producing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) alongside brachial plexus involvement causing arm pain and weakness.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Small cell lung carcinoma is most strongly associated with which paraneoplastic endocrine syndrome due to ectopic hormone secretion?
o: Primary hyperparathyroidism
Cushing's syndrome exclusively without any other paraneoplastic association
Carcinoid syndrome as the predominant association
Acromegaly
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Small cell lung carcinoma is classically associated with ectopic ADH secretion causing SIADH, as well as ectopic ACTH secretion (Cushing's syndrome) and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, reflecting its neuroendocrine origin.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is most strongly associated with which paraneoplastic syndrome due to ectopic hormone secretion?
o: SIADH as the predominant paraneoplastic finding
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome as the predominant finding
Hypercalcemia from ectopic PTH-related peptide secretion
Carcinoid syndrome as the predominant finding
Ectopic insulin secretion causing hypoglycemia
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung classically causes hypercalcemia through secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), which mimics PTH action on bone and kidney, distinguishing it from the SIADH/ACTH associations of small cell carcinoma.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: The 6-minute walk test in respiratory medicine is primarily used to assess which functional parameter?
o: Exercise tolerance and functional capacity, often with oxygen desaturation monitoring
Static lung volumes precisely
Airway hyperresponsiveness to methacholine
Diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide precisely
Maximum voluntary ventilation
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: The 6-minute walk test measures the distance a patient can walk in 6 minutes, providing a practical assessment of functional exercise capacity and often monitoring for exertional oxygen desaturation, useful in conditions like pulmonary fibrosis and COPD.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Which finding on arterial blood gas analysis would be expected in a patient hyperventilating due to acute anxiety (panic attack)?
o: Respiratory alkalosis with low PaCO2
Respiratory acidosis with high PaCO2
Metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate
Metabolic alkalosis with high bicarbonate
Normal arterial blood gas values in all cases of hyperventilation
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Hyperventilation causes excessive CO2 elimination, leading to a fall in PaCO2 and a resultant respiratory alkalosis (elevated pH), classically seen in acute anxiety/panic attacks.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: A patient with COPD exacerbation and chronic CO2 retention should have supplemental oxygen titrated carefully to avoid which potential complication?
o: Immediate cardiac arrest from any oxygen administration
Worsening hypercapnia from blunting of the hypoxic respiratory drive and altered V/Q matching
Acute pneumothorax directly caused by oxygen therapy
Hypoglycemia induced by oxygen supplementation
Sudden bronchospasm caused directly by oxygen
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: In chronic CO2 retainers, excessive oxygen supplementation can blunt hypoxic respiratory drive and worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatching, leading to progressive hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis; oxygen should be carefully titrated to a target saturation (typically 88-92%).

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: The most common causative organism of acute epiglottitis in unvaccinated children has historically been which pathogen?
o: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Respiratory syncytial virus
Parainfluenza virus
Haemophilus influenzae type b
Bordetella pertussis
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Haemophilus influenzae type b was historically the predominant cause of acute epiglottitis in children, though its incidence has dramatically declined with widespread Hib vaccination.

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.s: Pertussis (whooping cough), caused by Bordetella pertussis, classically presents in its paroxysmal stage with which characteristic feature?
o: A single dry cough lasting less than 3 days total
High fever as the dominant and defining symptom
A vesicular skin rash accompanying the cough
Paroxysms of severe coughing followed by an inspiratory 'whoop'
Immediate resolution of cough with a single dose of antibiotic
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.e: Pertussis classically progresses through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages; the paroxysmal stage features severe coughing fits followed by a characteristic high-pitched inspiratory whoop as the patient gasps for air.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: A patient with epigastric pain relieved by food, worse at night, is most likely to have an ulcer at which site?
o: Gastric ulcer
Duodenal ulcer
Esophageal ulcer
Jejunal ulcer
Cecal ulcer
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Duodenal ulcers classically present with pain that improves with food intake and recurs a few hours later, often waking the patient at night, unlike gastric ulcers where pain is often worsened by food.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Helicobacter pylori infection is most strongly associated with which two gastrointestinal conditions?
o: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease
Achalasia and esophageal varices
Celiac disease and irritable bowel syndrome
Peptic ulcer disease and gastric MALT lymphoma
Gallstone disease and acute pancreatitis
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: H. pylori is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease (both gastric and duodenal) and is strongly linked to gastric MALT lymphoma and adenocarcinoma through chronic inflammation.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: The urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori detection relies on which underlying principle?
o: Direct visualization of the organism via endoscopy
Serological detection of IgM antibodies exclusively
Stool culture for the organism
Bacterial urease activity converting labeled urea into detectable labeled CO2
Measurement of gastric pH alone
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: The urea breath test exploits H. pylori's urease enzyme, which hydrolyzes ingested labeled urea into ammonia and labeled CO2 that is then detected in the patient's exhaled breath, providing a non-invasive diagnostic method.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Standard first-line eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori typically includes which combination of drug classes?
o: A single antibiotic alone for 3 days
An antacid alone without antibiotics
A histamine H2 blocker alone
A proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics (triple therapy)
An antiemetic combined with a laxative
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Standard H. pylori eradication regimens combine a proton pump inhibitor with two antibiotics (commonly clarithromycin and amoxicillin, or metronidazole), given for 10-14 days, forming triple therapy.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) can lead to which premalignant metaplastic change in the distal esophagus if left untreated?
o: Squamous cell hyperplasia
Barrett's esophagus (columnar metaplasia)
Esophageal varices
Achalasia
Zenker's diverticulum
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Chronic acid reflux can cause the normal squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus to undergo metaplastic transformation into columnar epithelium (Barrett's esophagus), which carries an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Achalasia is characterized by which pathophysiological abnormality of the esophagus?
o: Excessive lower esophageal sphincter relaxation causing reflux
Failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation with loss of peristalsis due to degeneration of myenteric neurons
A structural stricture from chronic acid exposure
A hypermotile esophagus with excessive peristaltic contractions only
A congenital tracheoesophageal fistula
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Achalasia results from degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus neurons, causing failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and loss of normal esophageal peristalsis, producing dysphagia to both solids and liquids.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Barium swallow study in a patient with achalasia classically shows which characteristic radiographic finding?
o: A 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction with proximal esophageal dilation
A 'string sign' in the terminal ileum
An 'apple-core' lesion in the colon
A 'double bubble' sign
A 'Swiss cheese' pattern in the pancreas
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Achalasia produces the classic 'bird's beak' appearance on barium swallow, showing smooth, tapered narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter with significant dilation of the esophagus proximal to the obstruction.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which of the following is a key distinguishing histological feature of Crohn's disease compared to ulcerative colitis?
o: Inflammation limited strictly to the mucosa and submucosa
Transmural inflammation with skip lesions and non-caseating granulomas
Continuous involvement always starting from the rectum
Exclusive involvement of the colon with no small bowel disease possible
Presence of crypt abscesses as the defining and unique feature
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Crohn's disease characteristically causes transmural (full-thickness) inflammation with skip lesions (patchy involvement) and can show non-caseating granulomas, in contrast to ulcerative colitis's continuous, mucosa-limited inflammation.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Ulcerative colitis characteristically involves which portion of the gastrointestinal tract?
o: Any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus with skip lesions
Predominantly the terminal ileum with rectal sparing
Continuous inflammation starting from the rectum and extending proximally, limited to the colon
The esophagus and stomach exclusively
The small intestine exclusively, sparing the colon
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Ulcerative colitis characteristically begins in the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous fashion, confined to the colon, unlike Crohn's disease which can affect any part of the GI tract with skip lesions.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication most classically associated with which inflammatory bowel disease?
o: Crohn's disease exclusively
Celiac disease
Ulcerative colitis
Irritable bowel syndrome
Diverticulosis
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Toxic megacolon, characterized by severe colonic dilation with systemic toxicity, is a classic and life-threatening complication of severe ulcerative colitis (though it can rarely occur in Crohn's colitis as well).

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Celiac disease is caused by an immune-mediated reaction to which dietary component?
o: Lactose
Gluten (specifically gliadin)
Fructose
Casein
Purines
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Celiac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten (particularly the gliadin component) in genetically susceptible individuals (typically HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positive), causing villous atrophy in the small intestine.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: The characteristic small bowel biopsy finding in celiac disease is which of the following?
o: Non-caseating granulomas
Normal villous architecture with eosinophilic infiltration only
Whipple's disease-like PAS-positive macrophages
Complete absence of any inflammatory infiltrate
Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Celiac disease classically shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes on duodenal/jejunal biopsy, reflecting the immune-mediated damage to the small intestinal mucosa.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which serological antibody test is most commonly used for screening for celiac disease?
o: Anti-mitochondrial antibody
Anti-smooth muscle antibody
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)
Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody
Anti-centromere antibody
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA antibody is the primary serological screening test for celiac disease, given its high sensitivity and specificity, with total IgA level checked concurrently to exclude IgA deficiency.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Acute pancreatitis is most commonly caused by which two etiologies combined accounting for the majority of cases?
o: Viral infection and autoimmune disease
Trauma and medication use exclusively
Hypercalcemia and hypertriglyceridemia as the leading causes
Gallstones and alcohol use
Hereditary pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Gallstones (causing obstruction of the pancreatic duct) and chronic alcohol use together account for the vast majority of acute pancreatitis cases worldwide.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which laboratory finding is most useful for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
o: Serum lipase elevated more than 3 times the upper limit of normal
Elevated serum bilirubin alone
Elevated serum creatinine alone
Low serum amylase
Elevated serum ALT alone without other findings
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Serum lipase, more specific than amylase for pancreatic injury, elevated more than 3 times the upper limit of normal, combined with characteristic abdominal pain, supports the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Cullen's sign and Grey Turner's sign, indicating hemorrhagic pancreatitis, refer to bruising at which anatomical locations respectively?
o: The chest and the back
The palms and soles
The face and neck
The groin and thighs
Periumbilical region and the flanks
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Cullen's sign is periumbilical ecchymosis, while Grey Turner's sign is flank ecchymosis, both indicating retroperitoneal hemorrhage in severe (hemorrhagic) acute pancreatitis, resulting from tracking of blood along fascial planes.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Chronic pancreatitis characteristically causes malabsorption due to which mechanism?
o: Complete gastric outlet obstruction
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with reduced digestive enzyme secretion
Isolated bile acid deficiency without any enzyme deficiency
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth as the sole mechanism
Autoimmune destruction of intestinal villi
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Chronic pancreatitis progressively destroys pancreatic acinar tissue, reducing secretion of digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, protease), leading to fat malabsorption (steatorrhea) and other nutrient deficiencies.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which viral hepatitis is most commonly transmitted via the fecal-oral route and typically causes a self-limited acute illness without chronic infection?
o: Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis D
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B and C combined
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Hepatitis A is transmitted via the fecal-oral route (contaminated food/water) and characteristically causes an acute, self-limited illness without progression to chronic hepatitis, unlike hepatitis B and C.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Chronic hepatitis C infection is a major risk factor for which two serious long-term hepatic complications?
o: Acute fulminant hepatic failure exclusively
Gallstone disease exclusively
Primary biliary cholangitis exclusively
Wilson's disease
Cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Chronic hepatitis C infection, if untreated, can progress over years to decades to cirrhosis and significantly increases the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which hepatitis virus requires co-infection or superinfection with hepatitis B to cause disease, as it is a defective (satellite) virus?
o: Hepatitis A virus
Hepatitis C virus
Hepatitis E virus
Hepatitis G virus
Hepatitis D virus
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Hepatitis D virus is a defective RNA virus that requires the hepatitis B surface antigen for its assembly and infectivity, and therefore can only infect individuals who are also infected with hepatitis B.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Hepatitis E infection poses a particularly serious risk in which specific patient population?
o: Elderly men over age 70
Children under age 2
Patients with well-controlled diabetes
Pregnant women, in whom it can cause fulminant hepatic failure
Vegetarians
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Hepatitis E, though usually self-limited, carries a significantly increased risk of fulminant hepatic failure and mortality when acquired during pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which physical examination finding reflects portal hypertension in a patient with cirrhosis, resulting from dilated collateral veins around the umbilicus?
o: Spider angiomata
Palmar erythema
Dupuytren's contracture
Caput medusae
Gynecomastia
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Caput medusae refers to dilated, tortuous paraumbilical veins radiating from the umbilicus, resulting from portal hypertension causing recanalization of the umbilical vein and collateral flow through the abdominal wall.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Esophageal varices, a complication of portal hypertension, develop due to which underlying mechanism?
o: Portosystemic collateral formation via the left gastric (coronary) vein anastomosing with esophageal veins
Direct viral infection of esophageal veins
Isolated hepatic artery thrombosis
Primary esophageal malignancy
Chronic acid reflux alone without any vascular change
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Portal hypertension causes blood to seek alternative pathways to the systemic circulation, including via the left gastric vein anastomosing with esophageal venous plexuses, causing these vessels to become dilated and fragile (varices), prone to life-threatening bleeding.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Hepatic encephalopathy in a patient with cirrhosis is thought to result primarily from accumulation of which substance due to impaired hepatic clearance?
o: Bilirubin
Bile acids
Lactate
Ammonia
Urea
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Hepatic encephalopathy is primarily attributed to the accumulation of ammonia and other gut-derived neurotoxins that the cirrhotic liver fails to adequately clear, along with portosystemic shunting bypassing hepatic detoxification.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Lactulose is used in the management of hepatic encephalopathy primarily through which mechanism?
o: Directly binding and neutralizing ammonia in the bloodstream
Enhancing hepatic regeneration
Acidifying the colon to trap ammonia as ammonium ion and promoting its excretion via catharsis
Suppressing gut bacterial flora directly through an antibiotic effect as its primary action
Increasing hepatic blood flow
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Lactulose is metabolized by colonic bacteria to acidic byproducts that convert ammonia (NH3) to ammonium (NH4+), which is poorly absorbed and excreted; it also has a laxative effect that reduces ammonia-producing bacterial load and transit time.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in a cirrhotic patient with ascites is most commonly caused by which organism?
o: Staphylococcus aureus
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Clostridium difficile
Escherichia coli
Candida albicans
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, occurring in cirrhotic ascites without an obvious intra-abdominal source, is most commonly caused by translocation of enteric Gram-negative organisms, particularly Escherichia coli.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: A diagnostic paracentesis showing an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count above what threshold supports a diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
o: 10 cells/mm3
1000 cells/mm3 as the minimum required threshold
5000 cells/mm3
50 cells/mm3
250 cells/mm3
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: An ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or greater is the standard diagnostic threshold for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, prompting empiric antibiotic therapy.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Wilson's disease, an inherited disorder of copper metabolism, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: Hepatic dysfunction, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and Kayser-Fleischer rings
Isolated bronze skin pigmentation with diabetes as the sole presentation
Isolated pulmonary emphysema without hepatic disease
Recurrent pancreatitis as the primary and defining feature
Congenital hearing loss with liver disease
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Wilson's disease results from impaired biliary copper excretion (ATP7B gene mutation), causing copper accumulation in the liver (hepatitis/cirrhosis), brain (neuropsychiatric symptoms), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings).

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Hereditary hemochromatosis, a disorder of iron overload, classically presents with which combination of findings including a characteristic skin change?
o: Bronze skin pigmentation, diabetes mellitus, and cirrhosis (bronze diabetes)
Kayser-Fleischer rings with neuropsychiatric symptoms
Recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding as the primary feature
Congenital heart disease as the primary manifestation
Isolated hearing loss
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Hereditary hemochromatosis causes excessive iron deposition in tissues, classically producing the triad of bronze/grey skin pigmentation, diabetes mellitus (from pancreatic iron deposition), and cirrhosis, historically termed 'bronze diabetes.'

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Primary biliary cholangitis (formerly primary biliary cirrhosis) is most strongly associated with which serological marker?
o: Anti-dsDNA antibody
Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody
Anti-mitochondrial antibody
Anti-Smith antibody
Rheumatoid factor as the primary marker
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is present in the vast majority of patients with primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune disease causing progressive destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts, typically affecting middle-aged women.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Courvoisier's law states that a palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient is unlikely to be caused by which condition?
o: Pancreatic head carcinoma
Cholangiocarcinoma
Gallstones (cholelithiasis)
Ampullary carcinoma
Any malignant biliary obstruction
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Courvoisier's law states that a palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient suggests malignant obstruction (e.g., pancreatic head cancer) rather than gallstones, since chronic gallstone disease usually causes a fibrotic, non-distensible gallbladder.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain) is classically associated with which biliary condition?
o: Uncomplicated cholelithiasis
Acute ascending cholangitis
Acute pancreatitis
Acute appendicitis
Peptic ulcer perforation
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Charcot's triad of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain classically indicates acute ascending cholangitis, resulting from bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary tree, a medical emergency requiring urgent biliary decompression.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Reynolds' pentad, an extension of Charcot's triad with two additional findings, indicates which more severe condition?
o: Suppurative (severe) cholangitis with sepsis and altered mental status
Uncomplicated biliary colic
Chronic pancreatitis
Simple cholecystitis without cholangitis
Gallbladder polyps
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status to Charcot's triad, indicating severe suppurative cholangitis with sepsis, requiring urgent biliary drainage and aggressive supportive care.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Which of the following is the most common cause of acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults?
o: Hemorrhoids as the leading cause
Peptic ulcer disease (an upper GI source)
Diverticular disease
Meckel's diverticulum
Esophageal varices
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Diverticular disease of the colon is the most common cause of significant acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults, resulting from erosion of a vessel at the neck or dome of a diverticulum.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Meckel's diverticulum, a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct, most commonly presents in children with which symptom due to ectopic gastric mucosa?
o: Severe constipation
Painless rectal bleeding
Progressive dysphagia
Jaundice
Chronic cough
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Meckel's diverticulum often contains ectopic gastric mucosa that secretes acid, causing ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa and painless rectal bleeding, classically remembered by the rule of twos (2% of population, within 2 feet of ileocecal valve, etc.).

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, causing severe recurrent peptic ulcer disease, results from excessive secretion of which hormone by a pancreatic or duodenal tumor?
o: Insulin
Gastrin
Glucagon
Somatostatin
Vasoactive intestinal peptide
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), causing markedly elevated gastric acid secretion and severe, often refractory or atypically located peptic ulcers.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Irritable bowel syndrome is a diagnosis based primarily on which type of criteria, after exclusion of organic disease?
o: A specific diagnostic blood test
Characteristic findings on colonoscopy biopsy
A positive stool culture
Clinical symptom-based criteria (e.g., Rome criteria)
Elevated fecal calprotectin as a defining feature
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional gastrointestinal disorder diagnosed using symptom-based clinical criteria (such as the Rome IV criteria), after appropriate exclusion of organic pathology, since no specific diagnostic test exists.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Fecal calprotectin is a useful laboratory marker primarily for distinguishing which two categories of bowel disease?
o: Viral from bacterial gastroenteritis specifically
Colonic from small bowel malignancy specifically
Diverticulitis from diverticulosis specifically
Inflammatory bowel disease from functional (non-inflammatory) bowel disorders like IBS
Celiac disease from lactose intolerance specifically
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Fecal calprotectin, released by neutrophils in inflamed intestinal mucosa, is elevated in inflammatory bowel disease but typically normal in functional disorders like irritable bowel syndrome, helping guide the need for further invasive investigation.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: A Mallory-Weiss tear, causing upper gastrointestinal bleeding, classically results from which mechanism?
o: Chronic acid reflux causing a full-thickness esophageal tear
Variceal rupture from portal hypertension
Forceful vomiting/retching causing a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction
A congenital vascular malformation
Peptic ulcer perforation into the mediastinum
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Mallory-Weiss tears result from a sudden increase in intra-abdominal/intragastric pressure during forceful vomiting or retching, causing a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, presenting with hematemesis.

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.s: Boerhaave syndrome, a surgical emergency, refers to which condition?
o: A superficial mucosal tear limited to the gastroesophageal junction
Chronic peptic stricture of the esophagus
Esophageal varices without rupture
Full-thickness (transmural) esophageal rupture, typically from forceful vomiting
A benign esophageal web
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.e: Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness esophageal rupture, most often occurring after forceful vomiting, leading to mediastinitis and requiring emergency surgical intervention; it is more severe than the mucosal-only Mallory-Weiss tear.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Acute kidney injury is defined by which of the following changes in kidney function over a short time period?
o: A rapid rise in serum creatinine and/or reduction in urine output
A gradual decline in kidney function over more than 3 months
An isolated finding of proteinuria without any change in creatinine
A rise in blood urea nitrogen without any change in creatinine
An isolated electrolyte abnormality with normal creatinine
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Acute kidney injury is characterized by an abrupt (hours to days) decrease in kidney function, manifested as a rise in serum creatinine and/or a reduction in urine output, as defined by standard criteria such as KDIGO.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Pre-renal acute kidney injury results from which underlying mechanism?
o: Direct toxic injury to renal tubular cells
Obstruction of the urinary collecting system
Glomerulonephritis due to immune complex deposition
Interstitial nephritis from a drug reaction
Reduced renal perfusion (e.g., from hypovolemia or hypotension) without intrinsic kidney damage initially
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Pre-renal AKI results from decreased renal blood flow (e.g., dehydration, hemorrhage, heart failure) causing a functional decline in glomerular filtration rate, typically reversible with restoration of perfusion before intrinsic damage occurs.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Acute tubular necrosis, a common intrinsic cause of AKI, classically shows which finding on urine microscopy?
o: Red blood cell casts
White blood cell casts exclusively
Waxy casts exclusively
Hyaline casts exclusively with no other findings
Muddy brown granular casts
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Acute tubular necrosis classically shows muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy, reflecting sloughing of injured tubular epithelial cells, distinguishing it from the red cell casts of glomerulonephritis.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Red blood cell casts on urine microscopy are most indicative of which category of kidney disease?
o: Acute tubular necrosis
Lower urinary tract infection
Nephrolithiasis without glomerular involvement
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
Glomerulonephritis
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Red blood cell casts are highly specific for glomerular bleeding and are a hallmark finding in glomerulonephritis, distinguishing glomerular hematuria from lower urinary tract sources of bleeding.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by which combination of clinical and laboratory findings?
o: Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia
Hematuria, hypertension, and mild proteinuria (<1 g/day)
Isolated hematuria without proteinuria
Isolated glycosuria without proteinuria
Isolated hypertension without any urinary abnormality
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria (typically >3.5 g/day), resulting hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, and compensatory hepatic hyperlipidemia.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Minimal change disease, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, characteristically shows which finding on light microscopy?
o: Diffuse mesangial proliferation visible on light microscopy
Crescent formation in the majority of glomeruli
Membranous thickening of the capillary walls visible on light microscopy
Normal-appearing glomeruli, with foot process effacement visible only on electron microscopy
Nodular glomerulosclerosis
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Minimal change disease shows essentially normal glomeruli on light microscopy; the diagnostic abnormality (diffuse podocyte foot process effacement) is only visible on electron microscopy, and the condition is typically highly responsive to corticosteroids.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Nephritic syndrome is classically characterized by which combination of findings, distinguishing it from nephrotic syndrome?
o: Massive proteinuria exceeding 3.5 g/day as the dominant feature
Isolated hyperlipidemia without any urinary abnormality
Absence of hematuria with heavy proteinuria
Hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and mild-to-moderate proteinuria
Isolated edema without hematuria or hypertension
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Nephritic syndrome is characterized by an inflammatory glomerular process producing hematuria (often with red cell casts), hypertension, oliguria, and variable but generally less severe proteinuria than nephrotic syndrome.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis classically occurs how long after a preceding streptococcal throat or skin infection?
o: Immediately within 24 hours
1-3 weeks
6 months
1 year
Only after the infection has been present for over a year
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically develops 1-3 weeks after a group A streptococcal pharyngitis (or slightly longer after skin infection), reflecting the time needed for immune complex formation and deposition.
