internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) classically presents with which timing of hematuria relative to an upper respiratory infection?
o: Hematuria delayed by 2-3 weeks, similar to post-streptococcal GN
Hematuria occurring only months after the infection has resolved
No temporal relationship to respiratory infections at all
Synpharyngitic hematuria, occurring within 1-2 days of the infection
Hematuria that occurs exclusively during pregnancy
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: IgA nephropathy classically presents with gross hematuria occurring concurrently with (or within a day or two of) an upper respiratory tract infection ('synpharyngitic hematuria'), distinguishing it from the delayed onset of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease) classically presents with which combination of organ involvement?
o: Isolated skin rash without renal or pulmonary involvement
Isolated joint pain without any organ involvement
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage
Chronic diarrhea with isolated colonic involvement
Isolated hearing loss with renal involvement
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Goodpasture syndrome results from autoantibodies against the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, causing the combination of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Diabetic nephropathy classically shows which characteristic histological finding on kidney biopsy in advanced disease?
o: Crescents in the majority of glomeruli
Amyloid deposition as the primary and defining feature
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis)
Membranous thickening without any nodularity
Normal glomerular architecture throughout the disease course
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Diabetic nephropathy classically produces nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) in advanced disease, reflecting chronic hyperglycemia-induced mesangial matrix expansion.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: The earliest clinically detectable marker of diabetic nephropathy is which of the following?
o: Overt (macroscopic) proteinuria
A significant rise in serum creatinine
Microalbuminuria
Frank hematuria
Nephrotic-range proteinuria as the first detectable sign
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Microalbuminuria (a small but abnormal amount of albumin in the urine, below the threshold detected by standard urine dipstick) is the earliest clinically detectable marker of diabetic nephropathy, preceding overt proteinuria and GFR decline.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is most commonly caused by mutations in which gene?
o: CFTR
NPHS1
PKD1
COL4A5
WT1
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: The majority of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease cases result from mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1), with a smaller proportion from PKD2 mutations; the disease causes progressive cyst formation leading to renal failure.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with which important extrarenal vascular complication requiring screening?
o: Coronary artery aneurysms as the primary vascular risk
Intracranial (berry) aneurysms
Peripheral arterial aneurysms as the predominant finding
Aortic dissection as the primary extrarenal complication
Deep vein thrombosis as the characteristic vascular finding
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease carries an increased risk of intracranial (berry) aneurysms, which can rupture causing subarachnoid hemorrhage; screening is considered in patients with a family history of aneurysm or symptoms.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Which type of kidney stone is radiolucent (not visible) on plain abdominal X-ray, requiring CT for detection?
o: Calcium oxalate stones
Uric acid stones
Calcium phosphate stones
Struvite stones
Most mixed calcium stones
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray (since they lack calcium) but are well visualized on non-contrast CT, unlike calcium-containing stones which are typically radiopaque.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) kidney stones are most classically associated with which type of infection?
o: Escherichia coli urinary tract infection
Viral urinary tract infection
Urease-producing organisms such as Proteus mirabilis
Fungal urinary tract infection exclusively
Tuberculous infection of the urinary tract
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Struvite stones form in the presence of urease-producing bacteria (classically Proteus mirabilis), which hydrolyze urea to ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and promoting precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate, often forming large 'staghorn' calculi.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: The most common type of kidney stone overall is which of the following?
o: Calcium oxalate stones
Uric acid stones
Struvite stones
Cystine stones
Xanthine stones
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of kidney stone, accounting for the majority of cases, often associated with hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, or low urine volume.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Chronic kidney disease staging is primarily based on which laboratory parameter?
o: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
Serum sodium level
Serum potassium level alone
Urine specific gravity alone
Random blood glucose level
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Chronic kidney disease is staged (G1 through G5) based on estimated glomerular filtration rate, with staging further refined by the degree of albuminuria (A1-A3 categories) per KDIGO guidelines.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Renal osteodystrophy, a complication of chronic kidney disease, results primarily from disturbances in which two minerals/hormones?
o: Calcium-phosphate metabolism and secondary hyperparathyroidism
Sodium and potassium balance exclusively
Iron and vitamin B12 metabolism exclusively
Magnesium and zinc balance exclusively
Cortisol and aldosterone exclusively
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Chronic kidney disease impairs phosphate excretion and vitamin D activation, leading to hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism, which together drive the bone changes of renal osteodystrophy.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Erythropoietin deficiency in chronic kidney disease results in which hematological complication?
o: Microcytic hypochromic anemia as the primary type
Macrocytic megaloblastic anemia as the primary type
Normocytic normochromic anemia
Polycythemia
Hemolytic anemia as the primary mechanism
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Reduced renal production of erythropoietin in chronic kidney disease leads to inadequate stimulation of erythropoiesis, resulting in a normocytic, normochromic anemia, treatable with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Type 1 diabetes mellitus results primarily from which underlying pathophysiological process?
o: Peripheral insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency
Excessive glucagon secretion as the primary defect
A structural pancreatic tumor
Chronic pancreatitis as the primary underlying cause in most cases
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune-mediated destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency, typically presenting in childhood or young adulthood.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening complication predominantly of type 1 diabetes, is characterized by which triad of findings?
o: Hypoglycemia, alkalosis, and hyperkalemia as the defining triad
Normal glucose with severe acidosis alone
Hyperglycemia with respiratory alkalosis as the primary acid-base disturbance
Hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis
Hypoglycemia with ketosis and normal pH
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Diabetic ketoacidosis results from severe insulin deficiency causing hyperglycemia, uncontrolled lipolysis with ketone body production (ketosis), and resultant high anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Kussmaul breathing, seen in severe diabetic ketoacidosis, represents which physiological compensatory response?
o: A sign of primary respiratory failure unrelated to acid-base status
Deep, rapid respirations compensating for metabolic acidosis by increasing CO2 elimination
A compensatory response to metabolic alkalosis
An indication of pure hypoxemia without any acid-base disturbance
A sign of upper airway obstruction
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Kussmaul breathing consists of deep, labored, rapid respirations that serve as a compensatory mechanism for severe metabolic acidosis, increasing CO2 elimination to partially correct the low pH.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, occurring predominantly in type 2 diabetes, differs from diabetic ketoacidosis primarily by which feature?
o: Absence of significant ketosis and acidosis despite very high blood glucose levels
Presence of severe ketoacidosis as the defining feature
Occurrence exclusively in type 1 diabetic patients
Normal or low blood glucose levels
Rapid onset over a few hours as the defining feature
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is characterized by extreme hyperglycemia and profound dehydration/hyperosmolarity, typically without significant ketosis or acidosis, since residual endogenous insulin secretion in type 2 diabetes suppresses excessive lipolysis.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is used clinically to reflect which parameter of diabetes management?
o: Blood glucose level at the exact moment of testing
Renal function in diabetic patients
Presence of diabetic ketoacidosis
Insulin resistance measured directly
Average blood glucose control over the preceding 2-3 months
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: HbA1c reflects the percentage of hemoglobin that has become glycated over the lifespan of red blood cells (approximately 120 days), providing an integrated measure of average blood glucose control over the preceding 2-3 months.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Graves' disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, is caused by which underlying immunological mechanism?
o: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells
A benign thyroid adenoma secreting excess hormone autonomously as the primary cause
Iodine deficiency
Autoantibodies (TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies) that activate the TSH receptor
Pituitary tumor secreting excess TSH
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Graves' disease results from TSH receptor-stimulating autoantibodies that mimic TSH action, causing continuous stimulation of thyroid hormone production and diffuse thyroid gland enlargement.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Exophthalmos (proptosis) is a characteristic extrathyroidal finding specifically associated with which cause of hyperthyroidism?
o: Toxic multinodular goiter
Graves' disease
Toxic adenoma
Subacute (De Quervain's) thyroiditis
Iatrogenic thyroid hormone overreplacement
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Exophthalmos results from autoimmune-mediated inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition in the retro-orbital tissues, a finding specific to Graves' disease (Graves' ophthalmopathy) among the causes of hyperthyroidism.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, is characterized by which serological finding?
o: Anti-TSH receptor stimulating antibodies
Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies
Anti-dsDNA antibodies
Anti-centromere antibodies
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition characterized by anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, causing progressive lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of the thyroid gland leading to hypothyroidism.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Myxedema coma, a severe and life-threatening manifestation of hypothyroidism, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: Hyperthermia, tachycardia, and agitation
Normal temperature with isolated confusion
Hypertension with tachyarrhythmia as the predominant finding
Isolated skin rash without any systemic findings
Hypothermia, altered mental status, and bradycardia
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Myxedema coma represents decompensated severe hypothyroidism, presenting with hypothermia, depressed mental status (ranging from lethargy to coma), bradycardia, and hypoventilation, requiring urgent thyroid hormone replacement and supportive care.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Primary hyperparathyroidism is most commonly caused by which underlying pathology?
o: Parathyroid carcinoma as the most common cause
Chronic kidney disease as the primary cause of primary hyperparathyroidism
Vitamin D deficiency as the primary cause
A solitary parathyroid adenoma
Hypocalcemia-driven parathyroid hyperplasia as the most common cause
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: A solitary parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, causing autonomous excess PTH secretion, hypercalcemia, and hypophosphatemia.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: The classic mnemonic for symptomatic hypercalcemia in primary hyperparathyroidism includes which set of findings?
o: Fever, rash, and joint pain
Tremor, weight loss, and heat intolerance
Bones, stones, groans, and psychiatric overtones
Weight gain, cold intolerance, and constipation
Polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia as the exclusive triad
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: The mnemonic 'bones, stones, groans, and psychiatric overtones' captures the classic manifestations of hypercalcemia: bone pain/fractures, kidney stones, abdominal pain/constipation, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Cushing's syndrome resulting from a pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH is specifically termed which of the following?
o: Ectopic ACTH syndrome
Cushing's disease
Primary adrenal Cushing's syndrome
Iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome
Nelson's syndrome
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Cushing's disease specifically refers to Cushing's syndrome caused by a pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH, which is the most common endogenous cause of Cushing's syndrome, distinct from other causes (adrenal tumor, ectopic ACTH, exogenous steroids).

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Which clinical features are characteristic of Cushing's syndrome due to cortisol excess?
o: Weight loss, hyperpigmentation, and hypotension
Hypoglycemia and bradycardia as the primary features
Central obesity, moon face, purple striae, and proximal muscle weakness
Hyperthermia and diarrhea as the defining features
Hypocalcemia and tetany
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Cushing's syndrome classically presents with central obesity, a rounded 'moon' face, purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, and often hypertension and hyperglycemia, reflecting the catabolic and metabolic effects of cortisol excess.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) classically presents with which characteristic skin finding, distinguishing it from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
o: Hyperpigmentation, due to elevated ACTH/MSH precursor levels
Pallor without any pigmentary change
Jaundice as the primary skin finding
Vitiligo as the universal and defining skin change
Cyanosis as the primary skin change
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) causes compensatory pituitary overproduction of ACTH (and co-secreted MSH), leading to characteristic hyperpigmentation of skin and mucous membranes, a feature absent in secondary adrenal insufficiency (low ACTH).

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: An adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency) is a medical emergency treated urgently with which intervention?
o: Intravenous hydrocortisone and aggressive fluid resuscitation
Oral prednisone only, with no urgency
Insulin administration as the first priority
Immediate surgical adrenalectomy
Beta-blocker therapy as the primary treatment
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Adrenal crisis requires urgent treatment with intravenous stress-dose hydrocortisone and aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation to correct hypotension and electrolyte disturbances, as delay can be rapidly fatal.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla, classically presents with which paroxysmal symptom triad?
o: Chronic diarrhea, weight gain, and bradycardia
Episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis (sweating)
Persistent hypotension with bradycardia
Chronic constipation and cold intolerance
Isolated skin hyperpigmentation without cardiovascular symptoms
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Pheochromocytoma classically causes paroxysmal episodes of severe headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating, associated with markedly elevated blood pressure due to episodic catecholamine release.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: The diagnostic biochemical test of choice for suspected pheochromocytoma is measurement of which substance?
o: Serum cortisol
Plasma or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines
Serum aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Serum calcium
Serum TSH
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are the most sensitive biochemical tests for diagnosing pheochromocytoma, reflecting metabolites of the excess catecholamines produced by the tumor.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Diabetes insipidus, characterized by polyuria and polydipsia with dilute urine, results from a deficiency or resistance to which hormone?
o: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin)
Aldosterone
Cortisol
Growth hormone
Parathyroid hormone
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: Diabetes insipidus results from either inadequate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (central DI) or renal resistance to its action (nephrogenic DI), leading to the excretion of large volumes of dilute urine despite normal or elevated plasma osmolality.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: The water deprivation test is used clinically to help distinguish which two conditions presenting with polyuria?
o: Type 1 from type 2 diabetes mellitus
Nephrotic from nephritic syndrome
Acute from chronic kidney disease
Hyperthyroidism from hypothyroidism
Diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: The water deprivation test assesses the ability to concentrate urine when water intake is withheld; failure to concentrate urine appropriately (with correction after desmopressin administration) supports a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus rather than primary polydipsia.

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.s: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) classically causes which electrolyte disturbance?
o: Hyponatremia with concentrated urine despite low serum osmolality
Hypernatremia with dilute urine
Hyperkalemia as the primary electrolyte finding
Hypercalcemia as the primary electrolyte finding
Hypophosphatemia as the primary electrolyte finding
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.e: SIADH causes excessive water retention due to inappropriate ADH secretion, resulting in dilutional hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine relative to the low serum osmolality.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A patient presents with sudden onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking, symptoms resolving completely within 45 minutes. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Completed ischemic stroke
Hemorrhagic stroke
Todd's paralysis following a seizure
Migraine with aura
Transient ischemic attack
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: A transient ischemic attack is defined by focal neurological symptoms resulting from transient cerebral ischemia that resolve completely (classically within an hour), without evidence of permanent infarction, and requires urgent evaluation given the high subsequent stroke risk.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: The most important initial investigation in a patient presenting with acute stroke symptoms, before administering thrombolysis, is which of the following?
o: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging as the mandatory first test
Lumbar puncture
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
Non-contrast CT scan of the head to exclude hemorrhage
Echocardiography
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: A non-contrast CT scan of the head is essential before considering thrombolytic therapy to exclude intracranial hemorrhage, since thrombolysis is contraindicated and dangerous in hemorrhagic stroke.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase) for acute ischemic stroke is most effective and indicated when administered within which time window from symptom onset?
o: Within 24 hours in all cases without exception
Within 7 days
Within 4.5 hours
Only after 24 hours to allow for stabilization
There is no time window; it can be given at any time
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Intravenous alteplase for acute ischemic stroke is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients, as earlier treatment is associated with better outcomes and the risk of hemorrhagic transformation increases with delay.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A lesion of the middle cerebral artery territory affecting the dominant (usually left) hemisphere characteristically produces which language deficit alongside contralateral weakness?
o: Isolated dysarthria without language comprehension deficit
Complete mutism with normal comprehension
Isolated apraxia without any language deficit
Anosognosia as the primary deficit
Aphasia
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Middle cerebral artery strokes affecting the dominant hemisphere characteristically cause aphasia (expressive, receptive, or global depending on the specific area involved) alongside contralateral face and arm-predominant weakness.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A lesion of the anterior cerebral artery territory characteristically produces contralateral weakness that is most pronounced in which body part?
o: The lower limb
The face
The upper limb
Equal weakness of face, arm, and leg
Isolated facial weakness with normal limb strength
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, corresponding to the leg motor and sensory cortex, so ACA infarcts characteristically cause leg-predominant contralateral weakness.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A lacunar stroke, typically resulting from small vessel disease in patients with hypertension and diabetes, classically presents with which type of clinical syndrome?
o: Global aphasia with hemianopia
Isolated cortical blindness
Locked-in syndrome exclusively
Complete hemiplegia with cortical sensory loss and neglect
Pure motor or pure sensory stroke without cortical signs (e.g., no aphasia or neglect)
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Lacunar strokes result from occlusion of small penetrating arteries and classically produce pure motor or pure sensory syndromes without cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, visual field defects), since they spare the cerebral cortex.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A subarachnoid hemorrhage classically presents with which characteristic symptom description?
o: Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache, often described as the worst headache of the patient's life
A gradually progressive headache developing over several weeks
A headache relieved completely by over-the-counter analgesics within minutes
Chronic daily headache without other symptoms
A headache exclusively triggered by exertion with no other features
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Subarachnoid hemorrhage classically presents with a sudden-onset, severe 'thunderclap' headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds, often described by patients as the worst headache of their life, frequently from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: The most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is which of the following?
o: Arteriovenous malformation as the most common cause
Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage extending into the subarachnoid space
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm
Amyloid angiopathy as the most common cause
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm, most commonly located at branch points of the circle of Willis, is the most common cause of spontaneous (non-traumatic) subarachnoid hemorrhage.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Which investigation is most appropriate as the initial test for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, and what follow-up test is performed if this initial test is negative but suspicion remains high?
o: MRI brain initially; CT angiography if negative
Lumbar puncture initially; CT head only if positive
Carotid Doppler ultrasound initially; MRI if negative
EEG initially; CT head only if abnormal
Non-contrast CT head initially; lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT is negative
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Non-contrast CT head is highly sensitive for subarachnoid hemorrhage especially within the first 6-24 hours; if CT is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia (from breakdown of red blood cells) is performed.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: An epidural (extradural) hematoma classically results from injury to which vessel, often associated with a temporal bone fracture?
o: Bridging cerebral veins
Superior sagittal sinus
Internal carotid artery
Middle meningeal artery
Anterior communicating artery
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Epidural hematomas classically result from rupture of the middle meningeal artery, often following a temporal bone fracture, producing a rapidly expanding lens (biconvex)-shaped hematoma on CT with a classic 'lucid interval.'

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A subdural hematoma classically results from injury to which type of vessel, particularly in elderly or alcoholic patients with brain atrophy?
o: Middle meningeal artery
Basilar artery
Anterior cerebral artery
Bridging veins
Posterior communicating artery
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Subdural hematomas result from tearing of bridging veins that traverse the subdural space, particularly vulnerable in elderly or alcoholic patients with brain atrophy, producing a crescent-shaped hematoma on CT.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in which brain structure?
o: Substantia nigra pars compacta
Cerebellum
Hippocampus
Caudate nucleus exclusively without substantia nigra involvement
Frontal cortex
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Parkinson's disease results from progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to depletion of striatal dopamine and the classic motor features of the disease.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: The classic clinical triad of Parkinson's disease includes bradykinesia, resting tremor, and which additional feature?
o: Ataxia
Chorea
Dystonia as the third classic feature
Myoclonus as the third classic feature
Rigidity
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: The classic triad of Parkinson's disease consists of bradykinesia, resting (pill-rolling) tremor, and cogwheel rigidity, often with postural instability as a fourth cardinal feature in later stages.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Levodopa, the mainstay treatment for Parkinson's disease, is typically co-administered with carbidopa for which reason?
o: To inhibit peripheral decarboxylation of levodopa, reducing peripheral side effects and increasing central availability
To directly stimulate dopamine receptors in the brain
To prevent hepatotoxicity from levodopa
To enhance renal clearance of levodopa
To treat the tremor component specifically while levodopa treats rigidity
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Carbidopa is a peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the blood-brain barrier; it prevents peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, reducing peripheral side effects (nausea, hypotension) and allowing more levodopa to reach the brain.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Alzheimer's disease is pathologically characterized by which two hallmark microscopic findings in the brain?
o: Amyloid (senile) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles
Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra
Demyelinating plaques in the white matter
Negri bodies in neurons
Non-caseating granulomas
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Alzheimer's disease is characterized histopathologically by extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, along with cortical atrophy.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Multiple sclerosis is characterized pathologically by which underlying process affecting the central nervous system?
o: Demyelination of central nervous system white matter with relative axonal sparing
Progressive neuronal loss in the substantia nigra
Peripheral nerve demyelination exclusively
Vascular occlusion causing infarction
Amyloid deposition in cerebral vessels
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, causing discrete plaques of demyelination disseminated in space and time, classically affecting the optic nerves, periventricular white matter, brainstem, and spinal cord.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Which diagnostic finding on cerebrospinal fluid analysis supports a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
o: Oligoclonal bands not present in matched serum
Markedly elevated protein exceeding 500 mg/dL
Neutrophilic pleocytosis
Low glucose (hypoglycorrhachia)
Positive bacterial culture
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: The presence of oligoclonal IgG bands in the cerebrospinal fluid that are not present in the serum supports intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, a supportive finding in the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Guillain-Barré syndrome is classically characterized by which pattern of weakness and its typical antecedent history?
o: Descending paralysis beginning with the cranial nerves and no antecedent illness
Purely sensory symptoms without any motor weakness
Asymmetric, patchy weakness affecting only one limb
Weakness confined exclusively to the facial muscles
Ascending, symmetric flaccid paralysis, often preceded by a gastrointestinal or respiratory infection (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni)
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Guillain-Barré syndrome classically presents with rapidly progressive, ascending, symmetric flaccid paralysis and areflexia, frequently preceded by an infectious illness such as Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis, reflecting a post-infectious autoimmune mechanism.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis in Guillain-Barré syndrome classically shows which finding, termed albuminocytological dissociation?
o: Elevated cell count with normal protein
Elevated protein with normal cell count
Low glucose with elevated protein
Elevated cell count and elevated protein together
Normal protein and normal cell count
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Albuminocytological dissociation, characteristic of Guillain-Barré syndrome, refers to markedly elevated CSF protein with a normal or only mildly elevated white cell count, reflecting inflammation of the nerve roots without significant meningeal cellular response.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Myasthenia gravis results from autoantibodies directed against which target at the neuromuscular junction?
o: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Acetylcholinesterase enzyme
Sodium channels on the muscle membrane
Motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior horn
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease caused by antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, reducing effective neuromuscular transmission and causing fatigable muscle weakness.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: A key clinical feature distinguishing myasthenia gravis from other causes of weakness is which pattern of symptom fluctuation?
o: Weakness that is constant and unchanging throughout the day
Weakness that improves progressively with repeated muscle use
Weakness confined exclusively to the lower limbs
Weakness that is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day
Fatigability, with weakness worsening with repeated use and improving with rest
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Myasthenia gravis characteristically causes fatigable weakness that worsens with sustained or repeated activity and improves with rest, classically affecting ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, often a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with small cell lung cancer, results from antibodies against which target?
o: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Acetylcholinesterase
Myelin basic protein
Muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) exclusively
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, impairing acetylcholine release; unlike myasthenia gravis, strength characteristically improves with repeated muscle activity.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by which classic clinical presentation?
o: Sudden, severe, brief episodes of unilateral facial pain triggered by light touch or chewing
A constant, dull, bilateral facial ache lasting for weeks
Progressive facial weakness without any pain
Pain that is always accompanied by facial rash
Chronic headache unrelated to facial sensation
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Trigeminal neuralgia produces sudden, severe, brief, electric shock-like unilateral facial pain, often triggered by innocuous stimuli such as light touch, chewing, or talking, within the distribution of the trigeminal nerve.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Bell's palsy is characterized by acute unilateral facial weakness affecting which distribution?
o: Only the lower face, sparing the forehead (upper motor neuron pattern)
Bilateral facial weakness equally
Isolated weakness of eye closure only, with the rest of the face spared
Weakness confined to the tongue only
Both the upper and lower face on the affected side (lower motor neuron pattern)
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Bell's palsy causes a lower motor neuron pattern of facial weakness, affecting both the upper face (forehead, unable to raise eyebrow) and lower face on the involved side, distinguishing it from upper motor neuron (central) facial weakness which spares the forehead.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Status epilepticus is defined as continuous seizure activity or repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness lasting for at least how long?
o: 5 minutes
30 seconds
1 hour
24 hours
10 seconds
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Modern operational definitions classify status epilepticus as continuous seizure activity lasting 5 minutes or more, or recurrent seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them, prompting urgent treatment given the risk of neuronal injury with prolonged seizures.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: The first-line pharmacological treatment for actively convulsing status epilepticus is which class of medication?
o: Oral phenytoin
Benzodiazepines (e.g., intravenous lorazepam or diazepam)
Intramuscular antipsychotics
Intravenous mannitol
Oral valproate
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Benzodiazepines, particularly intravenous lorazepam, are the first-line agents for terminating active status epilepticus due to their rapid onset of action via potentiation of GABAergic inhibition.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically causes symmetric polyarthritis with a predilection for which joints, sparing the distal interphalangeal joints?
o: Distal interphalangeal joints predominantly
The lumbar spine predominantly
The sacroiliac joints predominantly
Metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints
The first carpometacarpal joint predominantly
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Rheumatoid arthritis classically causes symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis affecting the small joints of the hands, particularly the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, while sparing the distal interphalangeal joints (more typical of osteoarthritis).

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Morning stiffness lasting more than one hour is a characteristic clinical feature helping distinguish which type of arthritis from osteoarthritis?
o: Osteoarthritis itself
Gout during an acute attack exclusively
Septic arthritis exclusively
Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis
Traumatic joint injury
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Prolonged morning stiffness (typically over an hour) improving with activity is characteristic of inflammatory arthritides like rheumatoid arthritis, in contrast to osteoarthritis where stiffness is usually brief (under 30 minutes) and worsens with activity.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Ankylosing spondylitis characteristically causes inflammatory back pain and is strongly associated with which HLA allele?
o: HLA-DR4
HLA-DQ2
HLA-B8
HLA-Cw6
HLA-B27
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Ankylosing spondylitis, a seronegative spondyloarthropathy causing progressive sacroiliitis and spinal fusion, is strongly associated with HLA-B27, present in the majority of affected patients.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Gout results from deposition of which crystal type within joints, causing acute inflammatory arthritis?
o: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals
Calcium oxalate crystals
Cholesterol crystals
Monosodium urate crystals
Hydroxyapatite crystals exclusively
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Gout results from deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and periarticular tissues, triggering an acute inflammatory response, classically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra).

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid in gout classically shows crystals with which optical property?
o: Rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent crystals
Crystals with no birefringence at all
Round, non-crystalline debris only
Star-shaped crystals with variable birefringence
Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Monosodium urate crystals in gout appear needle-shaped and exhibit strong negative birefringence under polarized light microscopy, distinguishing them from the rhomboid, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals of pseudogout.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease) classically shows which crystal finding on synovial fluid analysis?
o: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals
No crystals detected on any analysis
Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals
Cholesterol crystals with a notched appearance
Amorphous debris without any defined crystal shape
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals, which appear rhomboid-shaped with weak positive birefringence under polarized light, in contrast to the needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals of gout.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Septic arthritis is most commonly caused by which organism in a previously healthy young sexually active adult?
o: Staphylococcus aureus as the most common organism in this specific population
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Escherichia coli
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: In young, sexually active adults, disseminated gonococcal infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a common cause of septic arthritis, often accompanied by a migratory polyarthralgia and characteristic skin lesions before localizing to one or a few joints.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Septic arthritis is most commonly caused by which organism in the general adult population overall (excluding the gonococcal-risk group)?
o: Staphylococcus aureus
Neisseria gonorrhoeae as the most common organism overall
Salmonella species as the most common organism overall
Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the most common organism overall
Candida albicans as the most common organism overall
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism of septic arthritis in the general adult population, requiring urgent joint aspiration, antibiotic therapy, and often surgical drainage to prevent joint destruction.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is characterized pathologically by excessive deposition of which substance in the skin and internal organs?
o: Amyloid protein
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals
Collagen (fibrosis)
Urate crystals
Immunoglobulin light chains
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Systemic sclerosis is characterized by excessive collagen deposition (fibrosis) in the skin and internal organs (lungs, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, heart), driven by immune activation, vascular injury, and fibroblast dysfunction.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Polymyalgia rheumatica classically presents in elderly patients with which combination of clinical findings?
o: Symmetric proximal muscle pain and stiffness (shoulders and hips) with markedly elevated ESR
Distal small joint symmetric arthritis with normal inflammatory markers
Isolated muscle weakness without any pain or stiffness
A vesicular skin rash with joint pain
Unilateral limb weakness with normal inflammatory markers
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Polymyalgia rheumatica presents in older adults with symmetric aching and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdle muscles, accompanied by markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), and is closely associated with giant cell arteritis.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Wernicke's encephalopathy, resulting from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency classically in chronic alcoholics, presents with which clinical triad?
o: Fever, neck stiffness, and photophobia
Resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia
Ascending paralysis with areflexia
Confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia
Hemiparesis with aphasia
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Wernicke's encephalopathy classically presents with the triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia (often nystagmus or sixth nerve palsy), resulting from thiamine deficiency and requiring urgent thiamine replacement to prevent progression to Korsakoff syndrome.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, affecting the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, results from deficiency of which vitamin?
o: Vitamin B1 (thiamine)
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
Vitamin D
Vitamin E
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration, affecting the dorsal columns (loss of vibration/proprioception) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spasticity), often alongside peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anemia.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated neuropsychiatric involvement and other systemic manifestations are most closely monitored using which complement-related laboratory trend during disease flares?
o: Rising complement levels correlating with disease flares
Falling complement levels (C3/C4) correlating with increased disease activity
Complement levels that remain entirely unrelated to disease activity
Elevated complement as a diagnostic requirement for SLE
Absence of any correlation between complement and any lupus manifestation
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Complement levels (C3 and C4) typically fall during active lupus flares due to consumption via immune complex-mediated activation, making serial complement measurement useful for monitoring disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis.

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.s: Sjögren's syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy, classically presents with which combination of symptoms?
o: Dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia)
Recurrent joint swelling with a butterfly facial rash as the defining feature
Progressive muscle weakness with a heliotrope rash
Raynaud's phenomenon with skin thickening as the defining feature
Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with uveitis
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.e: Sjögren's syndrome is characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, classically causing dry eyes and dry mouth due to reduced lacrimal and salivary gland secretion, and can occur primarily or secondary to other autoimmune diseases.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Which phase of wound healing is characterized by neutrophil and macrophage infiltration to clear debris and bacteria, typically occurring in the first few days after injury?
o: Proliferative phase
Remodeling phase
Inflammatory phase
Hemostasis phase exclusively without any cellular infiltration
Maturation phase occurring within hours
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The inflammatory phase of wound healing, occurring in the first 2-5 days, is characterized by neutrophil and then macrophage infiltration to clear debris, bacteria, and damaged tissue, setting the stage for subsequent repair.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The proliferative phase of wound healing is characterized primarily by which process?
o: Platelet aggregation and clot formation
Neutrophil-mediated debris clearance as the primary event
Fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, and angiogenesis forming granulation tissue
Scar maturation and collagen cross-linking as the primary event
Epithelial cell apoptosis
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The proliferative phase (roughly days 3-21) is dominated by fibroblast proliferation, collagen (initially type III) synthesis, and angiogenesis, forming granulation tissue that fills the wound defect.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Wound healing by primary intention, as opposed to secondary intention, refers to which type of wound closure?
o: Healing of a wound left open to close by granulation and contraction
Healing exclusively of infected wounds
Direct apposition of clean wound edges (e.g., a surgical incision closed with sutures)
Healing that always requires a skin graft
Healing that occurs without any inflammatory phase
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Primary intention healing occurs when clean wound edges are directly approximated (e.g., a sutured surgical incision), resulting in minimal scarring and faster healing compared to secondary intention, where a wound is left open to heal via granulation, contraction, and epithelialization.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Which vitamin deficiency is most classically associated with impaired collagen synthesis and poor wound healing?
o: Vitamin B12
Vitamin D
Vitamin K
Vitamin C
Vitamin A (though it plays a supportive role, vitamin C deficiency is the classic association)
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes required for collagen cross-linking; its deficiency (scurvy) classically causes impaired wound healing and fragile blood vessels.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A surgical site infection classified as 'superficial incisional' involves which tissue layer?
o: Fascia and muscle layers
Organ or body cavity space
Bone exclusively
Skin and subcutaneous tissue only
Only the deep muscle layer without skin involvement
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Superficial incisional surgical site infections are limited to the skin and subcutaneous tissue at the incision site, distinguished from deep incisional (fascia/muscle) and organ/space infections by standard CDC/NHSN surveillance definitions.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification system is used primarily for which purpose before surgery?
o: Assessing a patient's preoperative systemic health and estimating anesthetic/surgical risk
Determining the exact surgical technique to be used
Calculating postoperative pain medication dosing precisely
Classifying the type of anesthesia agent required
Determining hospital billing codes exclusively
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The ASA classification (I-VI) stratifies patients by their preoperative systemic health status, helping anesthesiologists and surgeons estimate perioperative risk and plan appropriate anesthetic management.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Which preoperative fasting guideline is generally recommended for clear liquids before elective surgery under general anesthesia?
o: At least 24 hours
No fasting required for clear liquids
At least 12 hours
At least 2 hours
At least 48 hours
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Modern preoperative fasting guidelines typically allow clear liquids up to 2 hours before elective surgery, while solid food generally requires a longer fasting period (commonly 6-8 hours), balancing aspiration risk against patient comfort and hydration.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis in surgical patients typically includes which combination of measures?
o: Complete bed rest without any other intervention
Aspirin alone in all surgical patients regardless of risk
Mechanical methods (e.g., compression stockings/intermittent pneumatic compression) plus pharmacological prophylaxis (e.g., low molecular weight heparin) based on risk
Prophylactic antibiotics alone
No prophylaxis needed for any elective surgery
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: VTE prophylaxis is tailored to patient risk and typically combines mechanical methods (compression devices) with pharmacological agents (e.g., low molecular weight heparin) for at-risk surgical patients, reducing postoperative thromboembolic complications.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Malignant hyperthermia, a rare but life-threatening anesthetic complication, is triggered by which class of anesthetic agents?
o: Local anesthetics exclusively
Intravenous propofol exclusively
Volatile inhalational anesthetics and succinylcholine
Nitrous oxide exclusively
Opioid analgesics exclusively
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., halothane, sevoflurane) and the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine in genetically susceptible individuals, causing a hypermetabolic crisis with severe hyperthermia and muscle rigidity.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Dantrolene is the specific treatment for which perioperative emergency?
o: Anaphylaxis
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity
Tension pneumothorax
Malignant hyperthermia
Postoperative hemorrhage
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Dantrolene acts by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle, directly counteracting the pathophysiology of malignant hyperthermia, and is the definitive specific treatment.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Postoperative fever occurring on postoperative day 1 is most commonly attributed to which cause, following the classic 'five W's' mnemonic?
o: Water (urinary tract infection)
Wound (surgical site infection)
Walking (deep vein thrombosis)
Wind (atelectasis)
Wonder drugs (drug fever)
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Early postoperative fever (within the first 24-48 hours) is most commonly attributed to atelectasis ('wind'), following the classic mnemonic progression of postoperative fever causes over time (wind, water, wound, walking, wonder drugs).

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Postoperative ileus, characterized by transient impairment of bowel motility after abdominal surgery, typically resolves within which time frame in uncomplicated cases?
o: 2-3 hours
2-3 days
2-3 weeks
2-3 months
It never resolves without surgical reintervention
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Uncomplicated postoperative ileus typically resolves within 2-3 days as bowel motility gradually returns, first in the small intestine, then stomach, then colon; prolonged ileus beyond this warrants investigation for complications.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Anastomotic leak following bowel surgery classically presents with which combination of clinical findings?
o: Isolated mild constipation without any systemic signs
Fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain, and signs of peritonitis or sepsis
Painless abdominal distension without fever
Isolated skin rash at the incision site
Bradycardia and hypothermia as the primary findings
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Anastomotic leak typically presents with systemic signs of sepsis (fever, tachycardia) along with localized or generalized abdominal pain and peritonitis, often several days after surgery, requiring prompt imaging and often reoperation.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Surgical drains are used postoperatively primarily for which purpose?
o: Providing nutritional support directly
Delivering intravenous medications
Monitoring blood pressure continuously
Removing accumulated fluid, blood, or air from a surgical site to prevent collection and infection
Replacing the need for wound dressing changes
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Surgical drains evacuate blood, serous fluid, pus, or air from a surgical site, preventing fluid collections (hematoma, seroma, abscess) that could impair healing or promote infection.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A surgical 'time out' performed immediately before incision is primarily intended to prevent which type of error?
o: Anesthetic drug dosing errors exclusively
Postoperative wound infection exclusively
Wrong-site, wrong-procedure, or wrong-patient surgery
Errors in postoperative pain management exclusively
Billing and coding errors
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The surgical 'time out,' part of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, is a final verification step performed before incision to confirm correct patient identity, surgical site, and procedure, preventing catastrophic wrong-site or wrong-patient errors.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Hypovolemic shock in a trauma or surgical patient is characterized by which hemodynamic pattern?
o: Increased cardiac output with decreased systemic vascular resistance
Normal cardiac output with markedly elevated blood pressure
Decreased cardiac output, decreased blood pressure, and increased systemic vascular resistance (compensatory tachycardia)
Increased blood pressure with bradycardia as the primary finding
Elevated central venous pressure as the primary early finding
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Hypovolemic shock results from reduced circulating blood volume, causing decreased cardiac output and blood pressure, with compensatory tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction (increased systemic vascular resistance) to maintain perfusion to vital organs.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: In the initial assessment of a trauma patient, the 'ABCDE' primary survey approach prioritizes which sequence of assessment?
o: Exposure, Disability, Circulation, Breathing, Airway
Circulation, Airway, Breathing, Disability, Exposure
Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
Disability, Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Exposure
Breathing, Airway, Circulation, Exposure, Disability
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The ABCDE primary survey (Airway with cervical spine protection, Breathing, Circulation with hemorrhage control, Disability/neurological status, Exposure) prioritizes assessment and management of the most immediately life-threatening problems first.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Class III hemorrhagic shock, per the Advanced Trauma Life Support classification, corresponds to approximately what percentage of blood volume loss?
o: Less than 15%
Greater than 40% as the defining lower limit
Exactly 50% precisely
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: ATLS classifies hemorrhagic shock into four classes based on estimated blood loss; Class III corresponds to approximately 30-40% blood volume loss, typically presenting with marked tachycardia, hypotension, and altered mental status.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The 'lethal triad' in severely injured trauma patients, associated with worsening outcomes, consists of which three factors?
o: Hyperglycemia, hypertension, and tachycardia
Fever, leukocytosis, and hypoalbuminemia
Hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, and alkalosis
Hypothermia, coagulopathy, and metabolic acidosis
Hypoxia, hypercapnia, and bradycardia
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The lethal triad of hypothermia, coagulopathy, and metabolic acidosis creates a self-perpetuating cycle in severely injured trauma patients that significantly worsens outcomes, guiding the damage control resuscitation approach.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Damage control surgery in a severely injured, physiologically unstable trauma patient prioritizes which surgical approach?
o: Complete definitive repair of all injuries in a single prolonged operation
Immediate discharge with outpatient follow-up
Non-operative management exclusively regardless of injury severity
Delaying all surgical intervention until the patient is fully stable
Rapid control of hemorrhage and contamination, deferring definitive repair to a later staged operation
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Damage control surgery prioritizes rapid, abbreviated control of life-threatening hemorrhage and contamination in unstable patients, followed by ICU resuscitation and correction of the lethal triad before a planned, staged definitive repair.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A patient develops signs of compartment syndrome after a lower limb fracture, including severe pain out of proportion to injury and pain with passive stretch. What is the definitive emergency treatment?
o: Elevation of the limb alone
Emergency fasciotomy
Application of a tight compressive bandage
Oral analgesics alone with observation
Delayed surgical intervention after 48 hours of observation
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Compartment syndrome requires emergency fasciotomy to relieve elevated intracompartmental pressure and prevent irreversible muscle and nerve ischemia, as delayed treatment risks permanent functional loss or limb loss.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The six 'P's' classically used to describe the clinical features of acute limb ischemia include pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, poikilothermia, and which additional feature?
o: Polyuria
Pyrexia
Pruritus
Paralysis
Polydipsia
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The six P's of acute limb ischemia are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, poikilothermia (temperature change), and paralysis, with paralysis representing a late and ominous sign indicating severe, potentially irreversible ischemia.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis for clean-contaminated procedures is generally most effective when administered at which time relative to incision?
o: Immediately after wound closure
24 hours before surgery
Only if signs of infection develop postoperatively
At the time of suture removal
Within 60 minutes before skin incision
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis is most effective when administered within 60 minutes before skin incision (or within 120 minutes for certain antibiotics like vancomycin), ensuring adequate tissue concentration at the time of the surgical incision.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A surgical wound classified as 'clean-contaminated' typically involves which type of procedure?
o: Controlled entry into the respiratory, alimentary, or genitourinary tract without significant spillage
A procedure with no entry into any hollow viscus and no break in sterile technique
A traumatic wound with retained devitalized tissue
A procedure involving established infection or pus at the operative site
A procedure performed entirely outside the operating room
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Clean-contaminated wounds involve controlled entry into a colonized hollow viscus (respiratory, alimentary, or genitourinary tract) under elective, controlled conditions without significant spillage, carrying an intermediate infection risk between clean and contaminated wounds.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Which type of suture material is classified as absorbable and commonly used for deep tissue closure that does not require removal?
o: Silk
Nylon
Polyglactin (Vicryl)
Polypropylene (Prolene)
Stainless steel wire
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Polyglactin (Vicryl) is a synthetic absorbable suture commonly used for deep tissue and fascial closure, gradually degrading via hydrolysis, unlike non-absorbable materials such as silk, nylon, and polypropylene used for skin or where permanent strength is needed.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A keloid scar differs from a hypertrophic scar primarily by which characteristic?
o: Keloid scars always regress spontaneously within weeks
Hypertrophic scars extend beyond the wound margins while keloids do not
Keloids occur only on the face
Hypertrophic scars are more common in darker-skinned individuals than keloids
Keloid tissue extends beyond the original wound margins, while hypertrophic scars remain confined to the wound boundary
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Keloid scars are characterized by excessive collagen deposition that extends beyond the original wound margins and does not regress, whereas hypertrophic scars remain within the wound boundary and often improve over time.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A patient develops a seroma at a surgical site several days postoperatively. Which management approach is typically appropriate for a small, asymptomatic seroma?
o: Immediate surgical re-exploration in all cases
Systemic antibiotics as the primary treatment regardless of infection signs
Observation, as many small seromas resolve spontaneously
Urgent CT-guided drainage in every case regardless of size
Amputation of the affected limb
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Small, asymptomatic seromas often resorb spontaneously with observation; aspiration or drainage is reserved for larger, symptomatic, or infected collections.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency characterized by which key pathological process?
o: Rapidly progressive infection and necrosis along fascial planes with systemic toxicity
A slowly progressive, localized skin abscess without systemic symptoms
A purely viral skin infection with no bacterial component
An allergic skin reaction without any infective process
A benign inflammatory skin condition
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening soft tissue infection spreading along fascial planes, causing tissue necrosis and severe systemic toxicity, requiring emergency surgical debridement alongside antibiotics.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The presence of crepitus and pain out of proportion to visible findings on physical examination of a wound raises concern for which serious diagnosis?
o: A simple superficial abrasion
A benign lipoma
Necrotizing fasciitis or gas gangrene
Uncomplicated cellulitis without deeper involvement
A sebaceous cyst
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Crepitus (from gas-forming organisms) combined with pain disproportionate to examination findings are red-flag signs for necrotizing soft tissue infection or gas gangrene, requiring urgent surgical exploration.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Which nutritional marker is commonly used preoperatively to help assess a patient's nutritional status and predict wound healing/surgical risk?
o: Serum sodium
Serum potassium
Serum calcium
Random blood glucose alone
Serum albumin
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Serum albumin, though affected by factors beyond nutrition, is a commonly used marker of nutritional status preoperatively, with hypoalbuminemia associated with increased risk of poor wound healing and postoperative complications.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Total parenteral nutrition is indicated in which clinical scenario?
o: A patient who can tolerate a normal oral diet without difficulty
A patient with a non-functioning gastrointestinal tract who cannot tolerate enteral feeding for a prolonged period
A patient requiring only short-term (24-hour) fasting before a minor procedure
As routine first-line nutrition for all postoperative patients regardless of gut function
A patient with mild, self-limited nausea only
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Total parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients with a non-functional or inaccessible gastrointestinal tract who require nutritional support for a prolonged period, since enteral feeding is generally preferred whenever the gut is functional (‘if the gut works, use it’).

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Refeeding syndrome, a potentially dangerous complication of nutritional repletion in severely malnourished patients, is characterized by which electrolyte disturbance?
o: Severe hypophosphatemia, along with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
Severe hyperkalemia as the primary and defining abnormality
Isolated hypercalcemia
Isolated hypernatremia
Isolated hyperphosphatemia
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Refeeding syndrome results from a sudden shift from catabolism to anabolism upon reintroducing nutrition, causing intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, leading to severe hypophosphatemia as the hallmark finding, with cardiac and neurological complications.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The Glasgow Coma Scale, commonly used in trauma assessment, evaluates which three components?
o: Pulse, blood pressure, and respiratory rate
Temperature, oxygen saturation, and heart rate
Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
Pupil size, reflexes, and skin color
Blood glucose, hemoglobin, and white cell count
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The Glasgow Coma Scale assesses eye opening, verbal response, and motor response, each scored separately and summed to give a total score (3-15) reflecting the level of consciousness, widely used in trauma and neurological assessment.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A surgical patient develops a sudden drop in oxygen saturation and dyspnea on postoperative day 5, with risk factors including recent immobilization and pelvic surgery. Which diagnosis should be urgently considered?
o: Simple atelectasis as the most likely and only consideration
Acute asthma exacerbation as the most likely diagnosis
Anxiety-related hyperventilation as the primary consideration
Chronic bronchitis exacerbation
Pulmonary embolism
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Postoperative immobilization and pelvic/major surgery are significant risk factors for venous thromboembolism; a sudden drop in oxygen saturation with dyspnea in this context should prompt urgent evaluation for pulmonary embolism.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols aim to improve postoperative outcomes primarily through which general approach?
o: Prolonging bed rest and fasting to allow maximal recovery time
Using only a single specific intervention such as early mobilization, without other components
Delaying oral intake for at least a week after abdominal surgery
A multimodal, evidence-based perioperative care pathway minimizing surgical stress and promoting early recovery
Eliminating the need for any pain management protocol
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: ERAS protocols employ a bundle of evidence-based perioperative interventions (optimized pain control, early mobilization, early oral intake, minimizing fasting and drains) to reduce surgical stress response and accelerate recovery, shortening hospital stay.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: A patient on long-term warfarin requires an elective surgical procedure. Which perioperative strategy is generally used to manage anticoagulation risk?
o: Continuing full-dose warfarin without any interruption regardless of bleeding risk
Stopping all anticoagulation permanently after any surgery
Doubling the warfarin dose immediately before surgery
Switching to aspirin alone as a direct substitute in all cases
Bridging therapy with a short-acting anticoagulant (e.g., low molecular weight heparin) while warfarin is held, based on thromboembolic risk
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Perioperative anticoagulation management often involves temporarily holding warfarin and using bridging anticoagulation (e.g., LMWH) in patients at high thromboembolic risk, balancing bleeding risk during surgery against thrombosis risk from anticoagulant interruption.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Which phase of wound healing occurs first, immediately after injury, and is characterized by platelet aggregation and clot formation?
o: Inflammatory phase
Hemostasis phase
Proliferative phase
Remodeling phase
Epithelialization phase occurring before any clotting
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Hemostasis is the first phase of wound healing, occurring within minutes of injury, involving vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation, and activation of the coagulation cascade to form a fibrin clot before the inflammatory phase begins.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) prevention bundles typically include which key measure during insertion?
o: Insertion without any skin antisepsis to save time in emergencies
Routine insertion in the femoral vein as the preferred site to reduce infection
Maximal sterile barrier precautions and chlorhexidine skin antisepsis
Leaving the dressing unchanged for the duration of catheter use
Avoiding hand hygiene to reduce procedure time
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Central line insertion bundles reduce CLABSI rates through measures including hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions (cap, mask, sterile gown/gloves, full body drape), chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, optimal site selection (avoiding femoral when possible), and daily review of line necessity.

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist is structured around which three time points during an operation?
o: Admission, discharge, and follow-up only
Sign in (before anesthesia), time out (before incision), and sign out (before leaving the operating room)
Preoperative consultation, surgery, and postoperative ward round only
Anesthesia induction, wound closure, and hospital discharge only
Consent, billing, and discharge planning
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has three phases: sign in (before induction of anesthesia, confirming patient identity, site, and consent), time out (before skin incision, confirming the team and procedure), and sign out (before the patient leaves the operating room, confirming counts and specimens).

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.s: Neurogenic shock, resulting from spinal cord injury and loss of sympathetic tone, is classically distinguished from hypovolemic shock by which hemodynamic finding?
o: Marked tachycardia and cool, clammy extremities identical to hypovolemic shock
Elevated blood pressure with bradycardia
Normal blood pressure with marked tachycardia
Hypertension and warm extremities with tachycardia
Hypotension with bradycardia (rather than the compensatory tachycardia seen in hypovolemic shock)
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.e: Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic vascular tone after spinal cord injury, causing hypotension with paradoxical bradycardia (rather than the compensatory tachycardia of hypovolemic shock) and warm extremities from vasodilation.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A patient presents with progressive dysphagia, first to solids and then to liquids, along with significant weight loss. Which diagnosis is most concerning and should be excluded first?
o: Achalasia as the most likely diagnosis in this presentation
Gastroesophageal reflux disease alone
Esophageal carcinoma
Esophageal candidiasis
Diffuse esophageal spasm
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids, especially with weight loss in an older patient, is a red-flag presentation for esophageal carcinoma and requires urgent endoscopic evaluation to exclude malignancy.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus is most strongly associated with which risk factors?
o: Chronic alcohol use and smoking
Chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease as the predominant risk factor
Obesity as the predominant risk factor
Barrett's esophagus as the predominant risk factor
Achalasia as the predominant and most significant risk factor
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus (more common in the proximal/mid esophagus) is strongly associated with chronic alcohol use and smoking, while adenocarcinoma (distal esophagus) is more strongly linked to GERD and Barrett's esophagus.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Esophageal adenocarcinoma is most strongly associated with which precursor condition?
o: Chronic alcohol use as the predominant association
Barrett's esophagus
Achalasia as the predominant association
Plummer-Vinson syndrome as the predominant association
Esophageal diverticula as the predominant association
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Esophageal adenocarcinoma typically arises in the setting of Barrett's esophagus, a metaplastic complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, and is increasingly common in Western populations.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Zenker's diverticulum, a pharyngoesophageal pouch, classically presents with which symptom due to trapped food and secretions?
o: Severe odynophagia as the primary symptom
Regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis
Hematemesis as the primary presenting symptom
Acute abdominal pain
Isolated hoarseness without any swallowing symptoms
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Zenker's diverticulum results from a posterior pharyngoesophageal wall outpouching above the cricopharyngeus muscle, causing food to become trapped and later regurgitated, along with characteristic halitosis from stagnant food debris.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Peptic ulcer perforation classically presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and which characteristic finding on erect chest X-ray?
o: Air-fluid levels in the small bowel as the defining finding
Free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum)
A normal chest X-ray in the majority of cases
Bilateral pleural effusions as the primary finding
Diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Perforated peptic ulcer allows gas to escape into the peritoneal cavity, classically visible as free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest or abdominal X-ray, a key diagnostic sign of gastrointestinal perforation.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Gastric outlet obstruction, a complication of chronic peptic ulcer disease, classically presents with which symptom?
o: Bilious vomiting as the defining feature
Painless jaundice as the primary symptom
Non-bilious vomiting of previously ingested food
Bloody diarrhea
Sudden onset of severe chest pain radiating to the back
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Gastric outlet obstruction, from scarring/edema near the pylorus in chronic peptic ulcer disease, causes non-bilious vomiting of undigested, often previously eaten food, since the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct entry point.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Which electrolyte and acid-base disturbance is classically seen with prolonged vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction or pyloric stenosis?
o: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis as the primary disturbance
Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis
Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
Normal acid-base status despite vomiting
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium through vomiting classically produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, a hallmark finding in conditions like pyloric stenosis or gastric outlet obstruction.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents in which age group and with which characteristic finding on physical examination?
o: Adults, with a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa
Newborns within the first 24 hours of life, with bilious vomiting
Adolescents, with a palpable mass in the left upper quadrant
Elderly patients, with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder
Infants around 2-8 weeks of age, with a palpable 'olive-shaped' mass in the epigastrium
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically presents at 2-8 weeks of age with projectile non-bilious vomiting and a palpable, firm, mobile 'olive-shaped' mass representing the hypertrophied pylorus, often in the epigastric/right upper quadrant region.
