general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: The classic surgical treatment for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is which procedure?
o: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
Total gastrectomy
Billroth II gastrojejunostomy
Nissen fundoplication
Whipple procedure
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, involving a longitudinal incision through the hypertrophied pyloric muscle without entering the mucosa, is the definitive surgical treatment for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A 6-month-old infant presents with episodic abdominal pain, drawing up of the legs, vomiting, and passage of 'red currant jelly' stool. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Hirschsprung's disease
Intussusception
Meckel's diverticulum bleeding as the most likely cause
Necrotizing enterocolitis
Malrotation with volvulus
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Intussusception, most common in infants 6 months to 2 years, classically presents with episodic colicky abdominal pain, drawing up of the legs, vomiting, and the characteristic 'red currant jelly' stool from mucosal ischemia and sloughing.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: The first-line diagnostic and often therapeutic intervention for intussusception in a stable infant is which of the following?
o: Immediate exploratory laparotomy in all cases regardless of stability
Observation alone without any intervention
Oral rehydration therapy alone
Colonoscopy as the first-line intervention
Air or contrast enema reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: In a hemodynamically stable infant without signs of perforation or peritonitis, air or contrast enema reduction under radiological guidance is both diagnostic and often therapeutic for intussusception, avoiding the need for surgery in most cases.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Hirschsprung's disease results from which underlying pathological abnormality of the colon?
o: Excessive ganglion cell proliferation in the colon
A structural stricture from acquired inflammation
An acquired autoimmune destruction of colonic ganglia
Congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the distal colon/rectum
A vascular malformation of the colon
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of neural crest cell migration during development, causing congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel (most commonly the rectosigmoid), leading to a functional obstruction due to failure of that segment to relax.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A newborn with Hirschsprung's disease classically presents with which finding in the first 48 hours of life?
o: Early, excessive passage of loose, watery stool
Bilious vomiting on the first feed as the presenting symptom
A palpable abdominal mass at birth
Jaundice as the primary presenting sign
Failure to pass meconium
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Failure to pass meconium within the first 24-48 hours of life is a classic presenting feature of Hirschsprung's disease, reflecting the functional obstruction caused by the aganglionic segment.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Acute appendicitis classically presents with pain that migrates from which initial location to which final location?
o: Periumbilical region to the right iliac fossa (McBurney's point)
Right iliac fossa to the epigastrium
Left iliac fossa to the suprapubic region
Epigastrium to the left upper quadrant
Suprapubic region to the periumbilical area
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Classic acute appendicitis presents with initial vague periumbilical pain (visceral, referred pain from midgut structures) that later localizes to the right iliac fossa (McBurney's point) as the inflamed appendix irritates the adjacent parietal peritoneum.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Rovsing's sign, a clinical finding supportive of acute appendicitis, refers to which examination finding?
o: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip
Pain on extension of the right hip while lying on the left side
Pain in the right iliac fossa elicited by palpation of the left iliac fossa
Rebound tenderness at McBurney's point only
Guarding limited to the epigastric region
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Rovsing's sign is positive when palpation of the left iliac fossa produces pain referred to the right iliac fossa, supporting peritoneal irritation from an inflamed appendix.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: The psoas sign, supportive of acute appendicitis (particularly with a retrocecal appendix), is elicited by which maneuver?
o: Pain on flexion of the right knee only
Pain on deep palpation of the left upper quadrant
Pain on coughing localized to the epigastrium
Pain on percussion of the costovertebral angle
Pain on passive extension of the right hip
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: The psoas sign is elicited by passive extension of the hip (or active hip flexion against resistance) with the patient lying on their side, causing pain due to irritation of the psoas muscle by an inflamed, often retrocecal, appendix.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Small bowel obstruction is most commonly caused by which etiology in a patient with a prior history of abdominal surgery?
o: Hernia as the most common cause in post-surgical patients
Malignancy as the most common cause in post-surgical patients
Adhesions
Intussusception as the most common cause in adults
Volvulus as the most common cause in post-surgical patients
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Postoperative adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in patients with a history of prior abdominal surgery, resulting from fibrous bands that can kink or compress bowel loops.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A large bowel obstruction is most commonly caused by which etiology in an elderly patient population?
o: Adhesions as the most common cause of large bowel obstruction
Volvulus as the most common overall cause
Diverticular stricture as the most common overall cause
Colorectal carcinoma
Intussusception as the most common cause
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Colorectal carcinoma is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in elderly patients, followed by diverticular disease and volvulus, in contrast to small bowel obstruction where adhesions predominate.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Sigmoid volvulus classically presents with which finding on plain abdominal X-ray?
o: Multiple air-fluid levels in the small bowel exclusively
A 'double bubble' sign
Free air under the diaphragm as the primary finding
Calcified gallstones visible in the right upper quadrant
A markedly dilated loop of colon with a 'coffee bean' sign
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Sigmoid volvulus classically produces a massively dilated sigmoid colon loop with a characteristic 'coffee bean' appearance on plain abdominal X-ray, resulting from torsion of a redundant sigmoid colon around its mesenteric axis.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Ischemic colitis, resulting from inadequate blood flow to the colon, most classically affects which vascular watershed area?
o: The rectum, due to its dual blood supply
The splenic flexure
The cecum, due to its dual blood supply
The transverse colon uniformly throughout its length
The entire colon uniformly with no particular predilection
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: The splenic flexure is a classic watershed area between the superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery territories, making it particularly vulnerable to ischemia during periods of reduced perfusion.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Diverticulitis most commonly affects which segment of the colon in Western populations?
o: Cecum
Sigmoid colon
Ascending colon
Transverse colon
Rectum
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: In Western populations, diverticulosis and its complication diverticulitis most commonly affect the sigmoid colon, likely related to higher intraluminal pressures in this segment.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A colovesical fistula, a recognized complication of diverticulitis, classically presents with which symptom?
o: Painless hematuria as the primary and defining symptom
Pneumaturia (air in the urine)
Isolated flank pain without urinary symptoms
Bilateral lower limb edema
Acute urinary retention as the primary symptom
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: A colovesical fistula, connecting the colon to the bladder (often from diverticulitis), classically causes pneumaturia and fecaluria due to passage of colonic gas and fecal material into the urinary tract.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Familial adenomatous polyposis, a hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome, results from mutation in which gene?
o: BRCA1 gene
TP53 gene as the primary causative gene
MLH1 gene as the primary causative gene in FAP specifically
RET proto-oncogene
APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline mutations in the APC tumor suppressor gene, causing hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomatous polyps with near-universal progression to colorectal cancer if untreated (typically by prophylactic colectomy).

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) results from germline mutations in which type of gene?
o: The APC tumor suppressor gene
DNA mismatch repair genes (e.g., MLH1, MSH2)
The BRCA1/BRCA2 genes
The RET proto-oncogene
The KRAS oncogene
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Lynch syndrome results from germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), leading to microsatellite instability and a significantly increased risk of colorectal and other cancers without the polyposis seen in FAP.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A sliding hiatal hernia, the most common type, is characterized by which anatomical finding?
o: The gastroesophageal junction remains in normal position while the fundus herniates alongside the esophagus
Complete herniation of the stomach into the thorax with organoaxial volvulus
Herniation of the transverse colon into the thorax only
The gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach slide upward through the diaphragmatic hiatus into the thorax
A congenital absence of the diaphragm with no true hernia sac
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: In a sliding (type I) hiatal hernia, the gastroesophageal junction and proximal stomach migrate upward through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax, accounting for over 90% of hiatal hernias and often associated with GERD.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A paraesophageal (rolling) hiatal hernia is distinguished from a sliding hernia by which feature?
o: The gastroesophageal junction always migrates into the thorax while the fundus stays fixed
It occurs exclusively in infants
The gastroesophageal junction remains in its normal position while the gastric fundus herniates alongside the esophagus
It never requires surgical repair regardless of symptoms
It is caused by esophageal carcinoma in the majority of cases
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: In a paraesophageal hernia, the gastroesophageal junction remains anchored in its normal location while the gastric fundus rolls up alongside the esophagus through the hiatus, carrying a risk of gastric volvulus and strangulation.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Boerhaave syndrome refers to which clinical entity?
o: Spontaneous transmural esophageal rupture, classically following forceful vomiting
A benign esophageal motility disorder with normal peristalsis
A superficial mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction
A congenital esophageal web
Chronic reflux-induced esophageal stricture
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Boerhaave syndrome is a spontaneous, full-thickness (transmural) rupture of the esophagus, classically occurring after forceful vomiting and causing severe chest pain, mediastinitis, and a surgical emergency requiring urgent repair.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A Mallory-Weiss tear, unlike Boerhaave syndrome, involves which type of esophageal injury?
o: A full-thickness transmural rupture of the esophageal wall
A mucosal and submucosal (non-transmural) longitudinal tear near the gastroesophageal junction
A chronic stricture from long-standing acid reflux
A congenital duplication cyst of the esophagus
Malignant infiltration of the esophageal wall
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a superficial mucosal and submucosal longitudinal laceration near the gastroesophageal junction, typically from forceful retching or vomiting, usually managed conservatively as it does not involve the full esophageal wall thickness (unlike Boerhaave syndrome).

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Achalasia, a primary esophageal motility disorder, is characterized by which pathophysiological findings on manometry and barium swallow?
o: Failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis, producing a 'bird's beak' appearance on barium swallow
Excessive lower esophageal sphincter relaxation causing severe reflux
Normal peristalsis with an isolated distal stricture from malignancy
Diffuse esophageal spasm with a 'corkscrew' appearance as the defining finding
Complete absence of the lower esophageal sphincter
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the esophageal myenteric plexus, causing failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis, producing the classic tapering 'bird's beak' appearance on barium swallow.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding presenting with hematemesis and melena is best initially evaluated and often treated with which procedure?
o: Colonoscopy as the first-line investigation
Upper GI endoscopy
Barium swallow as the first-line investigation
Diagnostic laparotomy as the first-line investigation
Abdominal ultrasound as the first-line investigation
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Upper GI endoscopy is the first-line investigation for suspected upper gastrointestinal bleeding, allowing identification of the bleeding source and often simultaneous therapeutic intervention (e.g., injection, clipping, banding).

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Bleeding esophageal varices, a complication of portal hypertension, are classically treated acutely with which combination of measures?
o: Immediate esophagectomy as first-line management
Oral proton pump inhibitors alone without any endoscopic intervention
Endoscopic band ligation, vasoactive drugs (e.g., octreotide), and prophylactic antibiotics
Observation alone, since variceal bleeds always resolve spontaneously
High-dose oral iron supplementation as the primary treatment
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Acute variceal hemorrhage is managed with endoscopic band ligation, vasoactive drugs (octreotide or terlipressin) to reduce portal pressure, and prophylactic antibiotics (reducing the risk of infection and rebleeding), with balloon tamponade or TIPS reserved for refractory bleeding.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Gastric adenocarcinoma with diffuse infiltration causing a rigid, thickened stomach wall is classically termed which of the following?
o: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Linitis plastica
Menetrier's disease
Barrett's esophagus
Curling's ulcer
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Linitis plastica refers to diffuse infiltrative gastric adenocarcinoma (often signet ring cell type) causing thickening and rigidity of the stomach wall, giving a characteristic 'leather bottle' appearance, and carrying a poor prognosis.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A left supraclavicular lymph node enlarged due to metastatic gastric cancer is classically known by which eponym?
o: Sister Mary Joseph nodule
Krukenberg tumor
Blumer's shelf
Troisier's sign as the name of the node itself
Virchow's node
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Virchow's node refers to a palpable, enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node resulting from metastatic spread of intra-abdominal malignancy, classically gastric cancer, via the thoracic duct.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Bilateral ovarian metastases from a primary gastric (signet ring cell) adenocarcinoma are termed which of the following?
o: Krukenberg tumors
Virchow's nodes
Sister Mary Joseph nodules
Meigs syndrome
Trousseau's sign
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic ovarian tumors, classically bilateral, originating from a primary signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma most commonly of gastric origin, spreading via transcoelomic or lymphatic routes.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Helicobacter pylori infection is a major risk factor for which combination of upper gastrointestinal conditions?
o: Achalasia and diffuse esophageal spasm exclusively
Boerhaave syndrome exclusively
Congenital pyloric stenosis exclusively
Esophageal varices exclusively
Peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma, and MALT lymphoma
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Helicobacter pylori infection is strongly associated with peptic ulcer disease (particularly duodenal ulcers), and is classified as a class I carcinogen for gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphoma.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Meckel's diverticulum, the most common congenital anomaly of the small intestine, results from incomplete obliteration of which embryological structure?
o: The urachus
The processus vaginalis
The ductus arteriosus
The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
The foramen ovale
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Meckel's diverticulum results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, classically following the 'rule of twos': found in about 2% of the population, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, and often presenting before age 2.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Crohn's disease affecting the gastrointestinal tract is characterized by which pattern of involvement, distinguishing it from ulcerative colitis?
o: Transmural, skip-lesion involvement that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus
Continuous, mucosal-only inflammation limited strictly to the colon and rectum
Exclusive involvement of the esophagus with sparing of the intestines
A pattern identical to ulcerative colitis in all respects
Involvement limited strictly to the appendix
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Crohn's disease characteristically causes transmural inflammation with skip lesions (areas of normal bowel between diseased segments) that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, in contrast to ulcerative colitis, which causes continuous, mucosal-only inflammation limited to the colon and rectum.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Toxic megacolon, a life-threatening complication most associated with severe ulcerative colitis, is characterized by which finding on abdominal imaging?
o: A normal-caliber colon with systemic toxicity
Isolated small bowel dilation with a normal colon
Diffuse free air without any colonic dilation
Calcification of the colonic wall
Marked colonic dilation (often greater than 6 cm) with signs of systemic toxicity
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Toxic megacolon is characterized by non-obstructive colonic dilation (typically greater than 6 cm) accompanied by systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis), carrying a high risk of perforation and requiring urgent medical and often surgical management.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: A chronic anal fissure, causing severe pain with defecation, most commonly occurs at which location on the anal canal?
o: The anterior midline exclusively in all patients
The right lateral position exclusively
The posterior midline
The left lateral position exclusively
Circumferentially involving the entire anal canal
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Anal fissures most commonly occur in the posterior midline, an area of relatively poor blood supply, making healing difficult and predisposing to chronicity; fissures in atypical locations should raise suspicion for underlying conditions like Crohn's disease.

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.s: Internal hemorrhoids are classified by degree based on which clinical feature?
o: Their exact size in millimeters measured endoscopically
The extent of prolapse through the anal canal on straining or defecation
Whether they are painful or painless exclusively
Their histological grade on biopsy
The number of hemorrhoidal columns present
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.e: Internal hemorrhoids are graded (I-IV) based on the degree of prolapse: grade I does not prolapse, grade II prolapses with straining but reduces spontaneously, grade III requires manual reduction, and grade IV is irreducible.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Biliary colic, from a gallstone transiently obstructing the cystic duct, classically presents with pain in which location, often triggered by fatty food?
o: Right upper quadrant, sometimes radiating to the right shoulder or scapula
Left upper quadrant radiating to the left shoulder
Suprapubic region radiating to the back
Periumbilical region radiating to the groin
Left lower quadrant radiating to the flank
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Biliary colic classically causes right upper quadrant pain, often triggered by fatty meals (which stimulate cholecystokinin-mediated gallbladder contraction), sometimes radiating to the right shoulder or scapula via referred phrenic nerve pathways.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Acute cholecystitis is most commonly caused by which underlying process?
o: A primary bacterial infection without any obstruction
Direct viral infection of the gallbladder
Autoimmune destruction of the gallbladder wall
Malignant infiltration of the gallbladder
Obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone, causing gallbladder inflammation
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Acute cholecystitis most commonly results from cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone, causing gallbladder distension, wall inflammation, and secondary bacterial infection, distinguishing it from simple biliary colic where obstruction is transient.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Murphy's sign, used to support a clinical diagnosis of acute cholecystitis, is elicited by which examination technique?
o: Pain on percussion of the costovertebral angle
Inspiratory arrest on palpation of the right subcostal region due to pain
Pain on deep palpation of the left iliac fossa
Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa
Pain on passive extension of the hip
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Murphy's sign is positive when the examiner's fingers palpate the right subcostal area while the patient inspires deeply, causing an inspiratory pause due to pain as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto the examining hand.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: The imaging modality of choice for initial evaluation of suspected acute cholecystitis or gallstones is which of the following?
o: CT scan of the abdomen as the first-line test
MRI of the abdomen as the first-line test
Abdominal ultrasound
Plain abdominal X-ray
Nuclear hepatobiliary (HIDA) scan as the first-line test
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Abdominal ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality for suspected gallstones or acute cholecystitis due to its high sensitivity for detecting gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid, along with wide availability and lack of radiation.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: A HIDA (hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid) scan is useful in confirming acute cholecystitis when it demonstrates which finding?
o: Normal, prompt filling of the gallbladder
Direct visualization of gallstones
Non-visualization of the gallbladder due to cystic duct obstruction
Enhanced liver parenchymal uptake only
Absence of any tracer excretion into the bowel
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: A HIDA scan demonstrates non-visualization of the gallbladder (due to cystic duct obstruction preventing tracer entry) in acute cholecystitis, while a functioning gallbladder that fills normally makes acute cholecystitis unlikely.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Choledocholithiasis, the presence of stones within the common bile duct, is best confirmed by which imaging investigation when ultrasound is inconclusive?
o: Plain abdominal X-ray
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
Barium swallow
Chest CT scan
Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic artery
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: MRCP provides detailed, non-invasive imaging of the biliary tree and is highly sensitive for detecting common bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis) when transabdominal ultrasound findings are inconclusive.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is primarily useful for which combination of purposes in biliary disease?
o: Diagnosis only, with no therapeutic capability
Exclusively for diagnosing gallbladder polyps
Both diagnosis and therapeutic intervention (e.g., stone extraction, stent placement) for biliary and pancreatic duct pathology
Exclusively for staging liver malignancy
Assessment of liver synthetic function
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: ERCP combines endoscopic and fluoroscopic techniques to both visualize the biliary and pancreatic ducts and perform therapeutic interventions such as sphincterotomy, stone extraction, and stent placement, making it both diagnostic and therapeutic.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: The most feared complication of ERCP, occurring in a notable minority of patients, is which of the following?
o: Post-ERCP pancreatitis
Immediate cardiac arrest as the most common complication
Permanent blindness
Acute renal failure as the most common complication
Complete biliary obstruction as a direct procedural complication in most cases
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the most common and clinically significant complication of the procedure, resulting from mechanical or chemical irritation of the pancreatic duct/ampulla during cannulation and instrumentation.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Gallstone ileus, a rare cause of mechanical bowel obstruction, results from which pathological process?
o: Direct extension of gallbladder cancer into the bowel
A gallstone passing normally through the biliary tree without any fistula
An unrelated adhesive band causing obstruction
Volvulus of the sigmoid colon coincidentally associated with gallstones
A gallstone eroding through a cholecystoenteric fistula and obstructing the bowel lumen, often at the ileocecal valve
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Gallstone ileus occurs when a large gallstone erodes through a cholecystoenteric (often cholecystoduodenal) fistula into the bowel lumen and becomes impacted, most commonly at the narrow ileocecal valve, causing mechanical small bowel obstruction.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Which imaging finding is classically associated with gallstone ileus on plain abdominal X-ray?
o: Isolated free air under the diaphragm without any bowel dilation
A normal abdominal X-ray in the vast majority of cases
Pneumobilia (air in the biliary tree) with signs of small bowel obstruction
Isolated colonic dilation without small bowel involvement
Calcified gallstones visible in the appendix
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Rigler's triad for gallstone ileus includes pneumobilia (from the abnormal cholecystoenteric fistula allowing air into the biliary tree), small bowel obstruction, and an ectopic gallstone, though all three are not always visible.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Cholangiocarcinoma arising at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts is specifically termed which of the following?
o: Courvoisier tumor
Krukenberg tumor
Whipple tumor
Klatskin tumor
Virchow tumor
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: A Klatskin tumor refers specifically to cholangiocarcinoma arising at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts (the hilar region), the most common location for this malignancy.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Primary sclerosing cholangitis, a chronic cholestatic liver disease, is most strongly associated with which underlying condition?
o: Ulcerative colitis
Crohn's disease as the predominant association
Celiac disease as the predominant association
Chronic pancreatitis as the predominant association
Diabetes mellitus as the predominant association
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Primary sclerosing cholangitis has a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis, and is characterized by progressive fibrosing inflammation of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, with an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Acute pancreatitis severity is often assessed using scoring systems such as Ranson's criteria or APACHE II, primarily to help predict which outcome?
o: The exact underlying cause of pancreatitis
The need for antibiotic therapy specifically
Disease severity and risk of complications/mortality
The patient's blood type
The precise duration of hospital stay in days
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Severity scoring systems for acute pancreatitis (Ranson's criteria, APACHE II, BISAP) use clinical and laboratory parameters to stratify patients by risk of severe disease, organ failure, and mortality, guiding the intensity of monitoring and management.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: A pancreatic pseudocyst, a recognized complication of acute or chronic pancreatitis, is best characterized as which type of collection?
o: A true cyst lined by epithelium
An encapsulated collection of pancreatic fluid lacking a true epithelial lining
A solid malignant tumor of the pancreas
An abscess with a confirmed bacterial infection at diagnosis by definition
A congenital pancreatic anomaly present from birth
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid and debris surrounded by a fibrous or granulation tissue wall lacking a true epithelial lining, typically developing 4 or more weeks after an episode of pancreatitis.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma arising in the head of the pancreas classically presents with which symptom due to compression of the common bile duct?
o: Acute severe abdominal pain radiating to the back as the presenting symptom in most cases
Massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage as the initial presentation
Sudden onset of diabetic ketoacidosis as the presenting feature
Painless obstructive jaundice
Isolated diarrhea without any other symptoms
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Pancreatic head tumors classically compress the distal common bile duct as it passes through the pancreatic head, causing painless progressive obstructive jaundice, often the earliest presenting symptom, sometimes accompanied by Courvoisier's sign.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: The Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) is the standard surgical treatment for resectable tumors located in which part of the pancreas?
o: The tail of the pancreas exclusively
The body of the pancreas exclusively
The entire pancreas requiring total pancreatectomy in all resectable cases
The uncinate process exclusively as an isolated procedure without duodenal resection
The head of the pancreas
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: The Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy), removing the pancreatic head, duodenum, distal common bile duct, gallbladder, and part of the stomach, is the standard surgical approach for resectable tumors of the pancreatic head.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Trousseau's sign of malignancy, associated with pancreatic cancer, refers to which clinical finding?
o: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder
Hyperpigmentation of the skin
A palpable abdominal mass in the epigastrium in all cases
Bilateral lower limb edema
Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Trousseau's sign of malignancy refers to migratory (recurrent, in different locations) superficial thrombophlebitis, classically associated with occult visceral malignancy, particularly pancreatic adenocarcinoma, due to a hypercoagulable paraneoplastic state.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Portal hypertension leading to splenomegaly and hypersplenism can result in which hematological abnormality?
o: Pancytopenia (or isolated thrombocytopenia) from increased splenic sequestration and destruction of blood cells
Polycythemia as the primary hematological finding
Isolated eosinophilia as the primary finding
Isolated lymphocytosis without any cytopenia
Isolated basophilia
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Hypersplenism from portal hypertension-related splenomegaly causes increased sequestration and destruction of blood cells within the enlarged spleen, commonly resulting in thrombocytopenia and sometimes pancytopenia.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: A hepatic hydatid cyst (Echinococcus granulosus infection) requires cautious surgical management primarily to avoid which serious complication?
o: Direct malignant transformation of the cyst during surgery
Immediate massive hemorrhage unrelated to cyst content spillage
Complete resistance to any medical therapy requiring surgery in all cases
Spillage of cyst contents causing anaphylaxis or peritoneal seeding
Spontaneous cyst rupture being entirely harmless
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Surgical management of hepatic hydatid cysts requires careful technique to avoid spillage of the highly antigenic cyst fluid and scolices, which can cause severe anaphylactic reactions or secondary peritoneal hydatid seeding.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: A liver abscess in a patient from an endemic area with recent dysentery is most likely caused by which organism if amoebic in origin?
o: Echinococcus granulosus
Entamoeba histolytica
Fasciola hepatica
Ascaris lumbricoides
Schistosoma mansoni
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Amoebic liver abscess, classically presenting as a single large abscess in the right lobe with 'anchovy paste' pus, results from hematogenous spread of Entamoeba histolytica from the colon following amoebic dysentery.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: The Couinaud classification divides the liver into how many functionally independent segments, each with its own vascular inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage?
o: Four
Six
Ten
Two (right and left lobes only)
Eight
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: The Couinaud classification divides the liver into eight functionally independent segments, each with its own portal pedicle (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct) and hepatic venous drainage, allowing anatomically based liver resections.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Hepatocellular carcinoma is most strongly associated with which combination of underlying risk factors?
o: Chronic hepatitis B or C infection and cirrhosis of any cause
Cholelithiasis alone as the predominant risk factor
Primary sclerosing cholangitis as the predominant risk factor
Acute viral hepatitis A infection as the predominant risk factor
Isolated obesity without any other liver disease
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Hepatocellular carcinoma is most strongly associated with chronic hepatitis B and C infection and cirrhosis from any cause (including alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease), which create a background of chronic liver injury and regeneration predisposing to malignant transformation.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Which serum tumor marker is most useful for surveillance and diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma?
o: CA 19-9 as the primary marker for hepatocellular carcinoma
CA-125 as the primary marker for hepatocellular carcinoma
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) as the primary marker for hepatocellular carcinoma
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the most widely used serum tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance and diagnosis, though it lacks perfect sensitivity and specificity and is used alongside imaging.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Blunt hepatic trauma is graded using the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) liver injury scale, primarily based on which imaging findings?
o: The patient's serum liver enzyme levels alone
The extent of hepatic laceration and hematoma seen on contrast-enhanced CT
The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score
The mechanism of injury alone without any imaging correlation
The presence of gallstones on ultrasound
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: The AAST liver injury grading scale (I-VI) is based on the extent and depth of hepatic laceration and the size/location of associated hematoma as seen on contrast-enhanced CT, guiding decisions between non-operative management and surgical intervention.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Portal hypertension is most commonly caused by which underlying condition in adults?
o: Cirrhosis of the liver
Portal vein thrombosis as the most common cause in adults
Budd-Chiari syndrome as the most common cause in adults
Schistosomiasis as the most common cause in adults worldwide
Congenital hepatic fibrosis as the most common cause in adults
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Cirrhosis (from any cause, most commonly chronic viral hepatitis or alcohol) is the most common cause of portal hypertension in adults, resulting from increased intrahepatic resistance to portal blood flow.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is primarily used to manage which complication of portal hypertension?
o: Refractory variceal bleeding or refractory ascites
Hepatocellular carcinoma directly, as a curative treatment
Acute cholecystitis in cirrhotic patients
Cholangitis as the primary indication
Gallstone disease in cirrhotic patients
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: TIPS creates a shunt between the portal and hepatic venous systems, reducing portal pressure, and is primarily used for refractory variceal hemorrhage or refractory ascites not controlled by medical management.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: The Child-Pugh score is used to assess the severity of liver cirrhosis based on which parameters?
o: Blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate only
Serum creatinine and urine output only
Bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy
White blood cell count and C-reactive protein only
Body mass index and waist circumference only
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: The Child-Pugh score assesses cirrhosis severity using five parameters (serum bilirubin, serum albumin, INR/prothrombin time, presence and severity of ascites, and presence and severity of hepatic encephalopathy), classifying patients into classes A, B, or C with prognostic and surgical risk implications.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, a complication of cirrhotic ascites, is diagnosed by which finding on ascitic fluid analysis?
o: An ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or greater
A completely sterile ascitic fluid culture with no cellular response
An ascitic fluid protein level above 3.5 g/dL as the diagnostic criterion
A serum-ascites albumin gradient below 1.1 g/dL as the diagnostic criterion
The presence of malignant cells on cytology
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or greater, typically in the setting of cirrhotic ascites without an evident intra-abdominal surgical source of infection.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Hepatorenal syndrome, a serious complication of advanced cirrhosis and portal hypertension, is characterized by which pathophysiology?
o: Primary intrinsic glomerular disease directly caused by cirrhosis
Renal failure due to direct toxic injury from bilirubin
Functional renal failure due to severe splanchnic and systemic vasodilation with renal vasoconstriction, in the absence of intrinsic kidney disease
Obstructive uropathy from hepatic compression of the ureters
Acute tubular necrosis from a nephrotoxic antibiotic used to treat cirrhosis
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional (not structural) form of renal failure in advanced cirrhosis, resulting from splanchnic and systemic arterial vasodilation triggering compensatory renal vasoconstriction and reduced renal perfusion, occurring in the absence of intrinsic renal pathology.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Biliary atresia, a cause of neonatal cholestasis, requires timely diagnosis because definitive surgical treatment (the Kasai procedure) is most effective when performed before which approximate age?
o: 12 months of age
5 years of age
Age is not a factor in surgical outcome for biliary atresia
8 weeks of age
18 years of age, as it is typically diagnosed and treated in adulthood
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Biliary atresia requires early diagnosis, as the Kasai portoenterostomy achieves the best outcomes when performed before approximately 8 weeks of age; delayed diagnosis and surgery beyond this window is associated with progressive liver fibrosis and worse outcomes.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Charcot's triad, suggestive of acute cholangitis, consists of which three clinical findings?
o: Fever, hypotension, and altered mental status
Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice
Abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea
Jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable gallbladder
Hematemesis, melena, and abdominal pain
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Charcot's triad (fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice) is classically associated with acute cholangitis, resulting from biliary obstruction (often by a common bile duct stone) combined with infection of the biliary tree.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Reynold's pentad, indicating a more severe, suppurative form of cholangitis, adds which two features to Charcot's triad?
o: Jaundice and weight loss (already part of the triad in a modified form)
Hematemesis and melena
Diarrhea and abdominal distension
Hypotension and altered mental status
Hematuria and flank pain
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Reynold's pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status to Charcot's triad (fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice), indicating severe suppurative cholangitis with septic shock, requiring urgent biliary decompression.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: A porcelain gallbladder, characterized by extensive calcification of the gallbladder wall, is clinically significant primarily because of its association with which condition?
o: A guaranteed benign course requiring no further management
An increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma
Acute cholecystitis exclusively, with no chronic implications
Biliary atresia in adults
Pancreatitis as its most common complication
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: A porcelain gallbladder, from chronic inflammation leading to wall calcification, has historically been associated with an increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma, and prophylactic cholecystectomy is generally recommended, particularly with irregular or incomplete calcification patterns.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Acute pancreatitis in most populations is most commonly caused by which two etiologies?
o: Gallstones and chronic alcohol use
Viral infection and autoimmune disease
Trauma and medication use exclusively
Hypercalcemia and hypertriglyceridemia as the two leading causes worldwide
Pancreatic divisum and annular pancreas as the two leading causes
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Gallstones and chronic alcohol use together account for the large majority of acute pancreatitis cases, with other causes (hypertriglyceridemia, medications, ERCP, trauma, hypercalcemia) being comparatively less common.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Pancreatic necrosis, a severe complication of acute pancreatitis, is most reliably identified using which imaging modality?
o: Plain abdominal X-ray as the most reliable modality
Abdominal ultrasound as the most reliable modality for necrosis specifically
Upper GI endoscopy
Chest X-ray
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Contrast-enhanced CT scan is the most reliable imaging modality for identifying pancreatic necrosis, demonstrating areas of non-enhancing pancreatic parenchyma, typically best assessed 72-96 hours after symptom onset.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Chronic pancreatitis, resulting from repeated episodes of pancreatic inflammation (classically from long-term alcohol use), is characterized by which combination of clinical features?
o: Acute abdominal pain only, with normal pancreatic function between episodes
Painless jaundice as the dominant and defining feature
Isolated diabetes mellitus without any pain or malabsorption
Complete resolution of symptoms after a single episode without any long-term sequelae
Chronic abdominal pain, exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea), and endocrine insufficiency (diabetes)
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Chronic pancreatitis causes progressive, irreversible pancreatic damage leading to chronic abdominal pain, exocrine insufficiency (malabsorption and steatorrhea from inadequate digestive enzyme production), and eventually endocrine insufficiency (diabetes mellitus from islet cell destruction).

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Pancreatic divisum, the most common congenital pancreatic ductal anomaly, results from which developmental abnormality?
o: Complete agenesis of the pancreas
Duplication of the entire pancreas
Ectopic pancreatic tissue within the stomach wall
Failure of fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts during embryological development
Annular pancreas encircling the duodenum
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Pancreatic divisum results from failure of fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts during development, causing most pancreatic exocrine secretion to drain through the smaller minor papilla, which can predispose to recurrent pancreatitis in some individuals.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Whipple's triad, used to support a diagnosis of insulinoma, includes hypoglycemic symptoms, a documented low blood glucose during symptoms, and which third criterion?
o: A palpable abdominal mass on examination
Elevated serum amylase during the episode
Jaundice occurring simultaneously with the hypoglycemic episode
Elevated blood pressure during the episode
Relief of symptoms with administration of glucose
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Whipple's triad for insulinoma consists of symptoms of hypoglycemia, a documented low plasma glucose concurrent with symptoms, and relief of symptoms upon administration of glucose, supporting a diagnosis of an insulin-secreting tumor.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, such as insulinomas and gastrinomas, most commonly arise from which cell population within the pancreas?
o: Acinar (exocrine) cells
Ductal epithelial cells as the predominant cell of origin
Pancreatic stellate cells
Adipocytes within the pancreatic stroma
Islet cells of Langerhans
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from the islet cells of Langerhans (the endocrine component of the pancreas), and are classified by their hormone secretion (e.g., insulinoma, gastrinoma, glucagonoma), distinguishing them from the more common exocrine (ductal) adenocarcinomas.

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.s: Acute cholangitis, once diagnosed, is managed with intravenous antibiotics and which definitive intervention to relieve biliary obstruction?
o: Observation alone with antibiotics, deferring any drainage procedure indefinitely
Urgent biliary decompression, most commonly via ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction or stent placement
Immediate liver transplantation as the first-line treatment
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid alone without any drainage procedure
Total pancreatectomy as the definitive treatment
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.e: Acute cholangitis requires prompt intravenous antibiotics together with urgent biliary decompression, most commonly achieved endoscopically via ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction or stent placement, particularly in patients with severe or non-responding disease.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A palpable breast lump that is hard, irregular, fixed to underlying tissue, and associated with skin dimpling is most concerning for which diagnosis?
o: Fibroadenoma
Fibrocystic change
Breast carcinoma
A simple breast cyst
Fat necrosis following minor trauma
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: A hard, irregular, fixed mass with skin dimpling (from involvement of Cooper's ligaments) is a classic clinical presentation of breast carcinoma, warranting urgent triple assessment (clinical exam, imaging, and biopsy).

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: The 'triple assessment' approach to a breast lump includes which three components?
o: Blood tests, urinalysis, and chest X-ray
Family history, genetic testing, and physical examination only
Clinical examination, imaging (mammography/ultrasound), and pathological (needle biopsy) assessment
Mammography alone repeated three times
Ultrasound, MRI, and PET scan
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Triple assessment combines clinical examination, imaging (mammography and/or ultrasound depending on age), and pathological sampling (fine needle aspiration or core needle biopsy) to comprehensively evaluate a breast lump and minimize diagnostic error.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A fibroadenoma, the most common benign breast tumor in young women, is classically described on examination as which type of mass?
o: A hard, fixed, irregular mass with skin tethering
A fluctuant, tender, erythematous mass with fever
A mass with bloody nipple discharge as a universal feature
A smooth, mobile, well-circumscribed, rubbery mass ('breast mouse')
A mass that rapidly ulcerates through the skin
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Fibroadenomas are classically smooth, well-circumscribed, mobile, and rubbery on palpation, often called a 'breast mouse' due to their mobility, typically occurring in women under 30 years old.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Which breast imaging modality is generally preferred as the initial investigation for a palpable lump in a woman under 35 years of age?
o: Mammography as the first-line test regardless of age
MRI as the first-line test
CT scan of the chest
Ultrasound
PET-CT scan
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Ultrasound is preferred as the initial imaging modality in younger women (typically under 35) because of denser breast tissue that limits mammographic sensitivity, and ultrasound avoids radiation exposure.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Paget's disease of the nipple is a clinical presentation of breast cancer characterized by which finding?
o: A rapidly growing painless mass in the axilla only
Bilateral, symmetric breast enlargement
Isolated nipple retraction without any skin change
Eczematous, scaly, or ulcerated changes of the nipple-areolar complex
A cystic mass with clear fluid on aspiration
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Paget's disease of the nipple presents with eczema-like, scaly, or ulcerated changes of the nipple and areola, resulting from malignant cells extending along the mammary ducts to the nipple epidermis, often associated with an underlying ductal carcinoma.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Inflammatory breast cancer classically presents with which clinical appearance, often mistaken for mastitis?
o: Diffuse erythema, warmth, and skin edema with a 'peau d'orange' (orange peel) appearance
A single small, painless, mobile nodule
A clear, watery nipple discharge without any skin change
Isolated axillary lymphadenopathy without any breast finding
A slowly growing mass over several years with no skin change
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Inflammatory breast cancer presents with rapid onset of diffuse erythema, warmth, and skin edema producing a characteristic 'peau d'orange' appearance from dermal lymphatic invasion by tumor cells, often misdiagnosed initially as infectious mastitis.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: The most important prognostic factor for axillary lymph node involvement in breast cancer staging is best assessed initially by which procedure in a clinically node-negative patient?
o: Sentinel lymph node biopsy
Complete axillary lymph node dissection as the first step in all patients
Fine needle aspiration of all axillary nodes regardless of imaging findings
PET-CT scan alone without any tissue sampling
Clinical palpation alone without any biopsy
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Sentinel lymph node biopsy, identifying and sampling the first draining lymph node(s), is the standard initial staging procedure for the clinically node-negative axilla, avoiding the morbidity of complete axillary dissection when the sentinel node is negative.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is typically treated with which class of adjuvant hormonal therapy?
o: Trastuzumab as the primary hormonal treatment
Cytotoxic chemotherapy exclusively without any hormonal therapy
Tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors
Insulin therapy
Radioactive iodine therapy
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers benefit from adjuvant hormonal therapy, using selective estrogen receptor modulators like tamoxifen (particularly in premenopausal women) or aromatase inhibitors (particularly in postmenopausal women).

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: HER2/neu overexpression in breast cancer is clinically significant because it allows for targeted therapy with which agent?
o: Tamoxifen as the targeted therapy for HER2-positive disease
Anastrozole as the targeted therapy for HER2-positive disease
Letrozole as the targeted therapy for HER2-positive disease
Raloxifene as the targeted therapy for HER2-positive disease
Trastuzumab
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting the HER2/neu receptor, which is overexpressed in approximately 15-20% of breast cancers, significantly improving outcomes when added to treatment for HER2-positive disease.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A solitary thyroid nodule found to be 'cold' on radioactive iodine uptake scan carries which clinical significance regarding malignancy risk?
o: No malignancy risk whatsoever, as cold nodules are always benign
A lower risk of malignancy compared to hot nodules
A higher relative risk of malignancy compared to a 'hot' (functioning) nodule
Certainty of malignancy requiring immediate total thyroidectomy without biopsy
The same malignancy risk as a hot nodule
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: A 'cold' thyroid nodule (not taking up radioactive iodine, implying non-functioning tissue) carries a comparatively higher risk of malignancy than a 'hot' (hyperfunctioning) nodule, though most cold nodules are still ultimately benign; fine needle aspiration remains the key diagnostic step.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common type of thyroid cancer, is characterized histologically by which finding?
o: Amyloid deposition within the tumor stroma
Sheets of small round blue cells with rosette formation
Hurthle cell change as the defining feature
Extensive vascular invasion as a universal and defining feature
Psammoma bodies and 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Papillary thyroid carcinoma classically shows characteristic nuclear features including 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei (clear, empty-appearing nuclei) and often contains psammoma bodies (concentric calcifications), and generally carries an excellent prognosis.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from which cell type within the thyroid gland?
o: Follicular epithelial cells
Thyroid stromal fibroblasts
Parafollicular C cells
Hurthle cells specifically as the cell of origin
Squamous epithelial remnants
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from the parafollicular (C) cells, which secrete calcitonin; it can occur sporadically or as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) syndromes.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) is associated with mutations in which proto-oncogene?
o: APC gene
BRCA1 gene
RET proto-oncogene
MEN1 gene as the causative gene in MEN2 specifically
TP53 gene
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: MEN2 syndromes (2A and 2B) result from germline mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, predisposing to medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and (in MEN2A) primary hyperparathyroidism.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is characterized clinically by which feature that distinguishes it from other thyroid cancer subtypes?
o: Slow, indolent growth over decades with excellent prognosis
Exclusive occurrence in children
Complete curability with radioactive iodine alone
Association with excellent long-term survival exceeding 90% at 10 years
Rapid growth and aggressive local invasion with poor prognosis
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is one of the most aggressive human malignancies, characterized by rapid growth, extensive local invasion, and a very poor prognosis, typically affecting older patients.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A patient develops hoarseness of voice following thyroidectomy. Which structure was most likely injured during the surgery?
o: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve as the primary cause of hoarseness
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Vagus nerve at the level of the jugular foramen
Hypoglossal nerve
Phrenic nerve
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve, which runs in close proximity to the thyroid gland and inferior thyroid artery, is at risk during thyroidectomy; its injury causes vocal cord paralysis and resultant hoarseness.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Postoperative hypocalcemia following total thyroidectomy most commonly results from which surgical complication?
o: Inadvertent removal or devascularization of the parathyroid glands
Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Excessive blood loss during surgery
Injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Postoperative wound infection
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: The parathyroid glands, located adjacent to or within the thyroid gland, can be inadvertently removed or have their blood supply compromised during thyroidectomy, leading to postoperative hypoparathyroidism and resultant hypocalcemia.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Tetany, a manifestation of postoperative hypocalcemia, can be elicited on examination by which classic clinical sign involving facial nerve tapping?
o: Trousseau's sign as the sign elicited by facial nerve tapping specifically
Homan's sign
Babinski sign
Kernig's sign
Chvostek's sign
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Chvostek's sign is elicited by tapping over the facial nerve near the angle of the jaw, causing twitching of the facial muscles in the presence of hypocalcemia-induced neuromuscular irritability; Trousseau's sign uses blood pressure cuff-induced ischemia to elicit carpal spasm.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A parathyroid adenoma causing primary hyperparathyroidism is most definitively treated with which intervention in a symptomatic patient?
o: Lifelong bisphosphonate therapy alone as definitive treatment
Calcitonin therapy alone as definitive treatment
Surgical parathyroidectomy
Radioactive iodine therapy
Cinacalcet therapy alone as the preferred first-line definitive treatment over surgery
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Surgical removal of the parathyroid adenoma (parathyroidectomy) is the definitive curative treatment for symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, resolving the hypercalcemia and its associated complications.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Which two genes, when mutated in germline form, confer the highest hereditary risk of breast (and ovarian) cancer?
o: APC and MLH1
BRCA1 and BRCA2
RET and MEN1
TP53 and RB1 as the primary hereditary breast cancer genes
KRAS and BRAF
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Germline mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes confer a substantially elevated lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer, and their carriers are often offered enhanced screening or risk-reducing surgery.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Breast cancer staging using the TNM system incorporates which three primary components?
o: Tumor grade, patient age, and menopausal status
Estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 status only
Tumor size/extent, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis
Family history, genetic testing result, and tumor location only
Patient performance status, comorbidities, and tumor markers only
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: The TNM staging system for breast cancer (and most solid tumors) is based on Tumor size/local extent, regional lymph Node involvement, and presence of distant Metastasis, combined to determine an overall stage that guides prognosis and treatment.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A modified radical mastectomy differs from a radical (Halsted) mastectomy primarily by which feature?
o: It removes only the tumor with a margin of normal tissue, preserving the entire breast
It preserves the pectoralis major muscle while removing the breast tissue and axillary lymph nodes
It involves removal of both breasts simultaneously in all cases
It does not involve any axillary lymph node assessment
It is performed exclusively for benign breast disease
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: A modified radical mastectomy removes the breast tissue, overlying skin, nipple-areolar complex, and axillary lymph nodes while preserving the pectoralis major (and often minor) muscle, unlike the historical radical mastectomy which also removed the pectoral muscles.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Lymphedema of the arm is a recognized long-term complication following which breast cancer treatment procedure?
o: Sentinel lymph node biopsy alone in the vast majority of cases
Lumpectomy without any axillary surgery
Tamoxifen therapy alone
Axillary lymph node dissection
Mammographic screening alone
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Axillary lymph node dissection, by disrupting lymphatic drainage of the arm, carries a significant risk of chronic lymphedema, a risk considerably lower with the more limited sentinel lymph node biopsy approach.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Acute mastitis, most common in breastfeeding women, is most commonly caused by which organism?
o: Escherichia coli as the most common causative organism
Neisseria gonorrhoeae as the most common causative organism
Staphylococcus aureus
Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the most common causative organism
Candida albicans as the most common causative organism
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Acute mastitis in lactating women is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, typically entering through a cracked or fissured nipple, and is managed with continued breastfeeding/milk drainage plus appropriate antibiotics.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Fat necrosis of the breast, which can mimic carcinoma clinically and radiologically, is most commonly associated with which preceding event?
o: Pregnancy without any trauma
Chronic Staphylococcus aureus infection
Trauma to the breast (including prior surgery)
Long-term oral contraceptive use
Excessive caffeine intake
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Fat necrosis of the breast typically follows trauma (including surgical trauma, such as prior biopsy or reduction mammoplasty), causing a firm, sometimes irregular mass that can mimic carcinoma clinically and on imaging, requiring biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A phyllodes tumor of the breast is best characterized as which type of lesion?
o: An exclusively malignant epithelial carcinoma
A purely benign, slow-growing cyst that never recurs
An inflammatory condition rather than a true neoplasm
A fibroepithelial tumor that can be benign, borderline, or malignant, and tends to grow rapidly
A vascular malformation of the breast
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial neoplasms that can range from benign to borderline to malignant, characteristically growing rapidly and sometimes reaching a large size; wide local excision is generally preferred over enucleation due to recurrence risk.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Gynecomastia, the benign enlargement of male breast tissue, is most commonly caused by which underlying mechanism?
o: An imbalance favoring estrogen relative to androgen effect on breast tissue
Direct malignant transformation of ductal epithelium
Chronic bacterial infection of the breast
Excessive androgen effect relative to estrogen
A hereditary BRCA2 mutation in the vast majority of cases
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Gynecomastia results from a relative imbalance favoring estrogenic over androgenic stimulation of breast tissue, occurring physiologically in neonates, puberty, and old age, or pathologically due to medications, liver disease, hypogonadism, or certain tumors.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Male breast cancer, though rare, is most strongly associated with which risk factor among the following?
o: Physical exercise as a risk-increasing factor
Low body mass index as the predominant risk factor
Early onset of puberty as the predominant risk factor
BRCA2 mutation
Vegetarian diet as the predominant risk factor
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: BRCA2 mutations (more than BRCA1) confer a notably increased risk of male breast cancer compared to the general male population, along with other risk factors such as Klinefelter syndrome and conditions causing hyperestrogenism.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is distinguished from invasive ductal carcinoma by which key histological feature?
o: Malignant cells have already spread to distant organs
The tumor cells are entirely benign despite the name
It always presents with a palpable, hard mass rather than being detected on imaging
Malignant cells are confined within the ductal basement membrane without invasion into surrounding stroma
It is defined by the presence of axillary lymph node metastasis
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Ductal carcinoma in situ is a non-invasive breast malignancy in which abnormal cells are confined within the mammary duct system by an intact basement membrane, without invasion into surrounding stroma, distinguishing it from invasive ductal carcinoma.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A unilateral, spontaneous, blood-stained nipple discharge is most commonly caused by which benign lesion?
o: Fibroadenoma as the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge
Simple breast cyst as the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge
Intraductal papilloma
Lipoma of the breast
Sebaceous cyst of the areola
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Intraductal papilloma, a benign proliferation within a lactiferous duct, is the most common cause of unilateral, spontaneous, blood-stained nipple discharge, though malignancy must still be excluded in the workup.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Thyroid function is typically assessed initially using which blood test?
o: Serum calcium as the first-line thyroid function test
Serum calcitonin as the first-line thyroid function test
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate as the first-line thyroid function test
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Random blood glucose as the first-line thyroid function test
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: TSH is the most sensitive initial screening test for thyroid dysfunction, reflecting the pituitary feedback response to circulating thyroid hormone levels, with free T4/T3 measured to further characterize abnormal results.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Graves' disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, results from which underlying immunological mechanism?
o: Autoantibodies that destroy thyroid follicular cells, causing hypothyroidism
A benign autonomously functioning thyroid adenoma
Autoantibodies (TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies) that stimulate the thyroid gland
Malignant transformation of thyroid follicular cells
Iodine deficiency as the primary underlying mechanism
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Graves' disease is an autoimmune condition caused by TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies that activate the TSH receptor, leading to diffuse thyroid hyperplasia and excessive thyroid hormone production, often accompanied by ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxedema.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A toxic multinodular goiter causing hyperthyroidism differs from Graves' disease in that it typically results from which process?
o: Autoimmune TSH receptor antibody stimulation identical to Graves' disease
Autonomous hormone secretion from one or more hyperfunctioning thyroid nodules, independent of TSH receptor antibodies
Complete destruction of the thyroid gland
A single dominant malignant nodule in the majority of cases
Iodine-131 therapy as the underlying cause
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Toxic multinodular goiter results from autonomous, TSH-independent hormone secretion by one or more hyperfunctioning nodules within a longstanding multinodular goiter, distinguishing it pathophysiologically from the autoimmune mechanism of Graves' disease.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Thyroid storm, a life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis, is characterized by which combination of features?
o: Hypothermia, bradycardia, and coma as the classic presentation
A completely asymptomatic presentation detected only on routine blood work
Severe hyperthermia, tachycardia, and altered mental status, often precipitated by an acute stressor (e.g., infection or surgery)
Isolated skin findings without any cardiovascular or neurological involvement
Normal vital signs with isolated laboratory abnormalities
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Thyroid storm is a severe, life-threatening form of thyrotoxicosis presenting with high fever, marked tachycardia (often with arrhythmia), and altered mental status, frequently triggered by an acute stressor such as infection, surgery, or trauma in a patient with underlying uncontrolled hyperthyroidism.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis classically presents with which combination of features following a viral illness?
o: A painless, non-tender goiter with permanent hypothyroidism from onset
Rapidly progressive, painless thyroid enlargement suggestive of malignancy
Isolated hypocalcemia without any thyroid enlargement
Sudden onset of severe hypertension as the presenting feature
A painful, tender thyroid gland with transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, often following a viral upper respiratory illness, presents with a painful, tender thyroid gland and a self-limited course of transient hyperthyroidism (from follicular disruption releasing stored hormone), often followed by a hypothyroid phase before recovery.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, is characterized by which immunological finding?
o: Elevated TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies as the defining finding
Absence of any detectable autoantibodies
Elevated anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies
Elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies
Elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland and elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, leading to progressive thyroid destruction and hypothyroidism.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A thyroglossal duct cyst, a congenital midline neck mass, is classically distinguished from other neck masses by which clinical feature?
o: It moves upward with swallowing and with protrusion of the tongue
It is located exclusively in the lateral neck, along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid
It is present only in adults over 60 years of age
It transilluminates brightly, unlike any other neck mass
It is always associated with hyperthyroidism
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: A thyroglossal duct cyst arises from remnants of the thyroglossal duct along the path of thyroid gland descent, classically presenting as a midline neck mass that moves upward with swallowing and with tongue protrusion, due to its attachment to the hyoid bone and duct tract.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A branchial cleft cyst, a congenital neck mass typically presenting in older children or young adults, is classically located in which region?
o: The lateral neck, along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
The midline neck, at or below the level of the hyoid bone
Exclusively within the thyroid gland parenchyma
The posterior triangle of the neck exclusively
The floor of the mouth exclusively
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Branchial cleft cysts, arising from incomplete obliteration of the branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus during development, classically present as a lateral neck mass along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, in contrast to the midline location of thyroglossal duct cysts.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Secondary hyperparathyroidism, commonly seen in patients with chronic kidney disease, results from which underlying process?
o: A primary autonomous parathyroid adenoma independent of renal function
Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands
Malignant infiltration of all four parathyroid glands
Excessive vitamin D intake causing hypercalcemia
Compensatory parathyroid hormone overproduction in response to chronic hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism develops as a compensatory response to chronic hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia (from reduced renal phosphate excretion and impaired vitamin D activation) in chronic kidney disease, driving persistent parathyroid hormone hypersecretion.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: A pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor typically arising from the adrenal medulla, classically presents with which symptom triad?
o: Chronic constipation, weight gain, and cold intolerance
Painless jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable abdominal mass
Episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis (sweating), often with paroxysmal hypertension
Polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss
Bone pain, kidney stones, and abdominal pain
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Pheochromocytoma classically presents with the triad of episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis, often accompanied by paroxysmal (or sustained) hypertension, resulting from excessive catecholamine secretion by the tumor.

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.s: Prior to surgical resection of a pheochromocytoma, which class of medication must be started first to prevent an intraoperative hypertensive crisis?
o: Alpha-adrenergic blockers (e.g., phenoxybenzamine), started before any beta-blocker
Beta-adrenergic blockers, started before any alpha-blocker
Thiazide diuretics as the first agent used
ACE inhibitors as the first agent used
Calcium supplementation as the first preoperative measure
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.e: Alpha-adrenergic blockade (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) must be established first and adequately achieved before adding a beta-blocker in pheochromocytoma preoperative preparation, since beta-blockade alone (or first) can cause unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and a hypertensive crisis.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) classically causes lower urinary tract symptoms due to which mechanism?
o: Malignant infiltration of the bladder wall
Bladder outlet obstruction from enlargement of the transitional zone of the prostate
Autoimmune destruction of detrusor muscle
Direct compression of the ureters at the pelvic brim
Chronic bacterial infection of the prostate in all cases
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: BPH results from hyperplasia of the transitional zone of the prostate, which surrounds the urethra, leading to bladder outlet obstruction and resultant lower urinary tract symptoms (hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, incomplete emptying).

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Acute urinary retention is initially managed by which immediate intervention?
o: Immediate open prostatectomy
High-dose diuretics to force urine output
Observation alone without any drainage
Emergency dialysis
Urethral (or suprapubic if urethral fails) catheterization to decompress the bladder
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Acute urinary retention requires prompt bladder decompression via urethral catheterization; if urethral catheterization is unsuccessful (e.g., due to stricture), suprapubic catheterization is performed.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A patient with a renal colic presents with severe, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin. Which imaging modality is preferred for initial evaluation of suspected ureteric stones?
o: Barium enema
Upper GI endoscopy
Plain chest X-ray alone
Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (CT KUB)
MRI of the brain
