general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (CT KUB) is the imaging modality of choice for suspected urolithiasis, offering high sensitivity and specificity for detecting stones of any composition, including radiolucent ones missed on plain X-ray.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A ureteric stone measuring 4 mm in the distal ureter, in a patient with well-controlled pain and no signs of infection or obstruction-related renal impairment, is generally managed by which initial approach?
o: Immediate open surgical removal
Emergency nephrectomy
Permanent nephrostomy tube placement
Conservative management with analgesia, hydration, and alpha-blockers to facilitate spontaneous passage
Immediate hemodialysis
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Small ureteric stones (typically under 5-6 mm), especially in the distal ureter, have a high likelihood of spontaneous passage and are managed conservatively with analgesia, hydration, and medical expulsive therapy (e.g., alpha-blockers like tamsulosin).

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A ureteric stone causing complete obstruction with fever and signs of sepsis (an infected obstructed system) constitutes which type of emergency?
o: A condition that can be safely managed as an outpatient with oral antibiotics alone
A condition requiring only observation without any intervention
A urological emergency requiring urgent decompression (e.g., ureteric stent or nephrostomy) alongside antibiotics
An indication for immediate nephrectomy in all cases
A contraindication to any antibiotic therapy
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: An infected, obstructed urinary system (pyonephrosis) is a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage via ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, combined with systemic antibiotics, to prevent urosepsis and renal damage.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Testicular torsion, a urological emergency, is characterized by which key clinical feature requiring immediate surgical exploration?
o: Gradual onset of painless testicular swelling over several months
Sudden onset of severe testicular pain with a high-riding, horizontally oriented testis and absent cremasteric reflex
Bilateral, symmetric testicular enlargement without pain
Testicular pain relieved by elevation of the scrotum (positive Prehn's sign)
Fever as the dominant and earliest presenting symptom in most cases
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Testicular torsion presents with sudden severe testicular pain, a high-riding or horizontally lying testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex; it is a surgical emergency since testicular viability declines rapidly with delayed detorsion (ideally within 6 hours).

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Testicular torsion is best distinguished clinically from epididymo-orchitis in part by which examination finding?
o: Both conditions always present identically with no distinguishing features
Prehn's sign: pain relief with testicular elevation suggests epididymitis, while torsion pain is typically not relieved (or worsened)
Epididymo-orchitis always presents with a completely painless testis
Torsion is always bilateral while epididymitis is always unilateral
Fever is present in 100% of torsion cases and never in epididymitis
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Prehn's sign (relief of pain with testicular elevation) is classically associated with epididymo-orchitis, whereas pain in testicular torsion is typically unrelieved or worsened by elevation, though this sign is not entirely reliable and urgent doppler ultrasound or surgical exploration should not be delayed.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A hydrocele is best described as which type of scrotal swelling?
o: A solid, non-transilluminating testicular mass
A collection of blood within the scrotum following trauma
A dilated, tortuous collection of veins within the pampiniform plexus
An abnormal communication between the peritoneal cavity and scrotum containing bowel
A collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis that transilluminates on examination
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis, classically transilluminating with a torch due to its fluid content, distinguishing it from solid masses.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A varicocele, a dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus, is classically described on examination as having which characteristic feel?
o: A 'bag of worms' texture, more prominent on standing and reducing on lying down
A hard, fixed, non-reducible mass
A fluctuant, transilluminating swelling
A pulsatile mass synchronous with the arterial pulse
A tender, erythematous, warm swelling with fever
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: A varicocele is classically described as feeling like a 'bag of worms' due to the dilated, tortuous veins of the pampiniform plexus; it becomes more prominent when standing (increased venous pressure) and reduces or disappears when lying down.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A sudden onset, left-sided varicocele in an older man should raise clinical suspicion for which underlying pathology?
o: Left renal cell carcinoma obstructing the left testicular (gonadal) vein
A completely benign, isolated finding requiring no further investigation regardless of age or laterality
Bilateral idiopathic varicocele as the most likely explanation
Testicular torsion as the most likely explanation
A normal anatomical variant seen exclusively on the right side
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: A new-onset varicocele, particularly left-sided and in an older patient, or one that does not reduce when lying flat, raises concern for renal cell carcinoma obstructing the left testicular vein (which drains into the left renal vein), warranting further imaging.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Painless gross hematuria in an older adult patient should prompt urgent investigation to exclude which diagnosis?
o: Simple viral cystitis as the most likely and sole explanation
Benign prostatic hyperplasia as the definitive and only diagnosis without further workup
A normal, clinically insignificant finding requiring no investigation
Acute pyelonephritis as the most likely and sole cause requiring no cystoscopy
Bladder cancer (urothelial carcinoma)
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Painless gross hematuria, especially in older adults, is a red flag symptom requiring urgent evaluation (cystoscopy and upper tract imaging) to exclude bladder cancer or other urothelial malignancy, even though benign causes are also possible.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Cigarette smoking is a major recognized risk factor for which urological malignancy?
o: Bladder (urothelial) carcinoma
Testicular seminoma as the malignancy most strongly linked to smoking
Benign prostatic hyperplasia as a malignancy resulting from smoking
Wilms tumor in adults as the predominant smoking-related urological cancer
Renal cystic disease as a malignant process caused by smoking
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Cigarette smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for urothelial (bladder) carcinoma, related to carcinogen exposure from tobacco metabolites excreted in urine, roughly doubling to quadrupling the risk compared to non-smokers.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Peripheral arterial disease of the lower limb classically presents with which symptom on exertion?
o: Constant, severe pain unrelated to activity that is worse at rest and improves with walking
Painless swelling of the limb without any exertional component
Isolated numbness without any associated pain
Fever and warmth of the limb suggesting infection rather than vascular disease
Intermittent claudication: cramping pain in the calf (or other muscle group) that occurs with walking and resolves with rest
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Intermittent claudication, the hallmark symptom of peripheral arterial disease, is exertional muscle pain (commonly calf pain) caused by inadequate blood flow to meet metabolic demand during activity, characteristically relieved by rest.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Critical limb ischemia, a severe manifestation of peripheral arterial disease, is characterized by which combination of features?
o: Mild claudication only, occurring after walking more than one kilometer
Painless, well-perfused skin with normal pulses
Rest pain, non-healing ulcers, and/or gangrene due to severely compromised blood flow
Isolated varicose veins without any arterial compromise
Symptoms that occur exclusively at night and resolve completely with elevation of the limb
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Critical limb ischemia represents severe arterial insufficiency manifesting as rest pain, non-healing ischemic ulcers, and/or gangrene, indicating a high risk of limb loss without revascularization.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is a non-invasive test used to assess peripheral arterial disease. A value below which threshold is generally considered diagnostic of significant arterial disease?
o: Below 0.9
Above 1.4 as the diagnostic threshold for significant disease
Exactly 1.0 as the diagnostic cutoff for disease
Below 2.0 as the threshold used clinically
The ABI is not used in the diagnosis of peripheral arterial disease
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: An ankle-brachial index below 0.9 is generally considered indicative of peripheral arterial disease, with lower values correlating with more severe disease; values above 1.4 suggest non-compressible, calcified vessels rather than normal circulation.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is generally defined as an aortic diameter exceeding which measurement?
o: 1 cm as the diagnostic threshold
10 cm as the diagnostic threshold
The normal diameter regardless of size, since aneurysm is defined by symptoms alone
6 cm as the threshold that defines any aneurysm regardless of baseline aortic size
3 cm
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is typically defined as a focal dilation of the aorta exceeding 3 cm in diameter (or more than 1.5 times the expected normal diameter), with elective surgical repair generally considered once the diameter reaches approximately 5.5 cm due to rupture risk.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm classically presents with which triad of clinical features?
o: Severe abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass
Painless abdominal distension with normal blood pressure
Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
Isolated lower limb swelling without any abdominal symptoms
Chest pain radiating to the jaw with normal blood pressure
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: The classic triad of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm includes sudden severe abdominal and/or back pain, hypotension (from hemorrhage), and a pulsatile abdominal mass, representing a surgical emergency requiring immediate intervention.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Varicose veins most commonly result from which underlying pathophysiological process?
o: Arterial insufficiency causing reduced blood flow to the superficial venous system
Complete arterial occlusion of the lower limb
An isolated congenital absence of the deep venous system in all cases
Incompetence of venous valves leading to venous reflux and dilation of superficial veins
Bacterial infection of the venous wall
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Varicose veins result from valvular incompetence in the superficial venous system (often involving the great or small saphenous veins), causing venous reflux, increased venous pressure, and progressive dilation and tortuosity of the affected veins.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is most reliably diagnosed using which initial imaging investigation?
o: Plain X-ray of the limb
Arteriography as the first-line test
Chest CT scan as the first-line test for limb DVT
Compression (duplex) ultrasound of the affected limb
MRI of the brain
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Compression (duplex) ultrasound is the first-line, non-invasive imaging investigation for suspected deep vein thrombosis, assessing for non-compressibility of the vein (indicating thrombus) along with Doppler flow assessment.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: The Wells score is a clinical prediction tool used to assess the pretest probability of which condition?
o: Deep vein thrombosis (and, in a modified form, pulmonary embolism)
Acute appendicitis as the primary condition it assesses
Acute cholecystitis as the primary condition it assesses
Testicular torsion as the primary condition it assesses
Peptic ulcer perforation as the primary condition it assesses
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: The Wells score is a validated clinical prediction rule used to stratify pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis (and a modified version for pulmonary embolism), guiding the need for further investigation such as D-dimer testing or ultrasound.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Standard initial anticoagulation treatment for an acute, uncomplicated deep vein thrombosis typically involves which class of medication?
o: Aspirin alone as the standard first-line anticoagulant for DVT
Low molecular weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant
Thrombolytic therapy as first-line treatment for all uncomplicated DVT
Immediate surgical thrombectomy for all uncomplicated DVT
Vitamin K supplementation to promote clot formation
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Acute uncomplicated DVT is typically treated with anticoagulation using low molecular weight heparin (often bridging to or alongside warfarin) or a direct oral anticoagulant, to prevent clot propagation and embolization while the body's natural fibrinolytic processes resolve the thrombus.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Renal cell carcinoma classically presents with which triad of symptoms, though this complete triad is now relatively uncommon at diagnosis?
o: Dysuria, frequency, and urgency
Fever, weight loss, and night sweats as the classic triad
Polyuria, polydipsia, and glycosuria
Jaundice, pruritus, and pale stools
Hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: The classic triad of renal cell carcinoma is hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass, though this complete triad is now uncommon at presentation since many tumors are detected incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common renal malignancy of childhood, classically presents with which clinical finding?
o: Painless gross hematuria as the most common presenting feature
Chronic diarrhea as the most common presenting feature
Bilateral leg edema as the most common presenting feature
An asymptomatic, palpable abdominal mass discovered by a caregiver or on examination
Recurrent urinary tract infections as the most common presenting feature
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Wilms tumor most commonly presents as an asymptomatic abdominal mass noticed incidentally by a parent or caregiver during bathing or dressing, typically in children under 5 years of age.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Bladder cancer is staged based on depth of invasion, with a key distinction between which two categories that determines management approach?
o: Non-muscle-invasive versus muscle-invasive disease
Papillary versus flat morphology exclusively, regardless of depth
Unifocal versus multifocal tumors exclusively
Presence versus absence of hematuria
Male versus female sex of the patient
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Bladder cancer staging distinguishes non-muscle-invasive (superficial) disease, typically managed with transurethral resection and intravesical therapy, from muscle-invasive disease, which usually requires radical cystectomy or chemoradiation given the higher risk of metastasis.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is used as a screening tool for prostate cancer, but its specificity is limited because it can also be elevated in which benign conditions?
o: Testicular torsion and epididymitis
Bladder cancer exclusively, with no other benign causes
Renal cell carcinoma exclusively
Erectile dysfunction alone
Benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: PSA lacks perfect specificity for prostate cancer, as it can also be elevated by benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, urinary retention, and recent prostatic manipulation (including digital rectal examination or catheterization), necessitating correlation with other clinical findings.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: The Gleason grading system for prostate cancer is based on which histological feature?
o: The tumor's size on digital rectal examination alone
The absolute PSA value at diagnosis
The architectural pattern of glandular differentiation seen on biopsy
The patient's age at diagnosis
The presence or absence of bone metastases
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: The Gleason grading system scores prostate cancer based on the architectural pattern of glandular differentiation in the two most predominant areas of the tumor on biopsy, with higher scores indicating more poorly differentiated, aggressive disease.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Posterior urethral valves, a congenital cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants, can lead to which long-term complication if undiagnosed?
o: Isolated undescended testis with no urinary tract involvement
Precocious puberty as the primary long-term complication
Bilateral hydronephrosis and progressive renal impairment
Hypospadias as a direct consequence of the valves
Testicular torsion as the primary long-term complication
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Posterior urethral valves cause bladder outlet obstruction in male infants, leading to back-pressure changes including bilateral hydronephrosis, bladder wall hypertrophy, and progressive renal impairment if not diagnosed and treated promptly.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Vesicoureteral reflux, the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and kidney, is clinically significant primarily because of its association with which complication?
o: Bladder cancer as the primary long-term risk
Testicular torsion as the primary associated complication
Erectile dysfunction later in life as the primary concern
Renal cell carcinoma as the primary long-term risk
Recurrent urinary tract infections and risk of renal scarring (reflux nephropathy)
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Vesicoureteral reflux predisposes to recurrent urinary tract infections and ascending pyelonephritis, which can result in renal scarring (reflux nephropathy) over time, particularly if not identified and managed in childhood.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Acute epididymitis in a sexually active young man is most commonly caused by which group of organisms?
o: Escherichia coli as the predominant cause in this age group
Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the predominant cause in this age group
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Candida species as the predominant cause in this age group
Treponema pallidum as the predominant cause of epididymitis
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: In sexually active young men, acute epididymitis is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted organisms, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, whereas in older men it is more often due to urinary pathogens such as Escherichia coli.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Fournier's gangrene, a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineal and genital region, is best managed by which primary intervention?
o: Oral antibiotics alone on an outpatient basis
Observation alone, since it typically resolves spontaneously
Topical antifungal cream as the primary treatment
Urgent, extensive surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Delayed surgery only after complete resolution of infection with antibiotics
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Fournier's gangrene is a surgical emergency requiring urgent, aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue combined with broad-spectrum antibiotics and hemodynamic support, given its rapid progression and high mortality if treatment is delayed.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Priapism, a prolonged and often painful penile erection unrelated to sexual stimulation, requires urgent management primarily to prevent which complication?
o: Bladder rupture as the primary risk of untreated priapism
Testicular torsion as a direct consequence of priapism
Ischemic damage to the corpus cavernosum and subsequent erectile dysfunction
Renal failure as the primary risk of untreated priapism
Urethral stricture as the immediate primary risk
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism, if not promptly treated, leads to progressive ischemic damage and fibrosis of the corpus cavernosum smooth muscle, resulting in permanent erectile dysfunction, making urgent decompression a priority.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Phimosis refers to which condition of the foreskin?
o: Inability to reduce a retracted foreskin back over the glans, causing distal swelling
Complete absence of the foreskin from birth
Chronic inflammation of the glans penis without any foreskin involvement
Inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis
A congenital urethral abnormality unrelated to the foreskin
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Phimosis is the inability to retract the foreskin proximally over the glans penis, which can be physiological in young children or pathological (from scarring or infection) in older individuals; it is distinguished from paraphimosis, where a retracted foreskin cannot be reduced back.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Paraphimosis is considered a urological emergency because of which risk if left untreated?
o: Progression to malignant transformation of the glans penis
Venous congestion and edema of the glans progressing to ischemia and necrosis
Ascending urinary tract infection as the primary risk
Immediate development of erectile dysfunction unrelated to any vascular compromise
Spontaneous resolution without any intervention needed in all cases
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Paraphimosis, where a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans, causes a constricting band that leads to venous congestion, progressive edema, and if untreated, arterial compromise resulting in ischemia and necrosis of the glans, requiring urgent reduction.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis), if left uncorrected, is associated with an increased risk of which long-term complication?
o: Erectile dysfunction as the primary long-term risk
Renal cell carcinoma as the primary long-term risk
Infertility and testicular malignancy
Bladder cancer as the primary long-term risk
Priapism as the primary long-term risk
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Undescended testis carries an increased long-term risk of infertility (from impaired spermatogenesis at higher intra-abdominal temperature) and testicular malignancy, particularly seminoma, making early surgical correction (orchidopexy) important.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: A transient ischemic attack in a patient found to have significant carotid artery stenosis on duplex ultrasound is most appropriately managed by considering which intervention, in addition to medical therapy, for high-grade stenosis?
o: Carotid endarterectomy (or carotid artery stenting in selected patients)
Immediate coronary artery bypass grafting regardless of coronary status
Observation alone regardless of the degree of stenosis
Anticoagulation with warfarin as the definitive treatment instead of any surgical intervention
Amputation of the affected limb
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Symptomatic patients with high-grade carotid artery stenosis (typically greater than 70%) are considered for carotid endarterectomy or carotid artery stenting, in addition to optimal medical therapy, to reduce the risk of subsequent stroke.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Subclavian steal syndrome results from significant stenosis or occlusion of the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of which vessel, causing retrograde flow and symptoms with arm exercise?
o: The common carotid artery as the vessel involved in retrograde flow
The brachial artery as the vessel involved in retrograde flow
The axillary artery as the vessel involved in retrograde flow
The internal thoracic (mammary) artery as the vessel involved in retrograde flow
The vertebral artery
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Subclavian steal syndrome occurs when proximal subclavian artery stenosis causes retrograde ('stolen') blood flow down the ipsilateral vertebral artery to supply the arm during exercise, potentially causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency symptoms such as dizziness or syncope.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease), a segmental inflammatory vasculitis affecting small and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities, is most strongly associated with which risk factor?
o: Diabetes mellitus as the predominant and defining risk factor
Hypertension as the predominant and defining risk factor
Tobacco use
Hyperlipidemia as the predominant and defining risk factor
Advanced age as the predominant risk factor, typically affecting patients over 70
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Buerger's disease is strongly and almost exclusively associated with tobacco use, typically affecting young male smokers, and disease progression is closely tied to continued smoking, with cessation being the cornerstone of management.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Raynaud's phenomenon, characterized by episodic vasospasm of the digital arteries in response to cold or stress, classically causes which sequence of color changes in the affected digits?
o: Red, then white, then blue as the classic sequence
Blue, then red, then white as the classic sequence
Only a single, isolated color change without any sequence
White (pallor), then blue (cyanosis), then red (reactive hyperemia)
Yellow discoloration progressing to black necrosis in nearly all cases
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Raynaud's phenomenon classically produces a triphasic color change: initial pallor (white) from vasospasm and reduced blood flow, followed by cyanosis (blue) from deoxygenation, and finally erythema (red) from reactive hyperemia upon rewarming.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: An arteriovenous fistula, the preferred long-term vascular access for hemodialysis, is created by which surgical technique?
o: Insertion of a synthetic graft between two veins only, without any arterial connection
Placement of a tunneled central venous catheter
Percutaneous needle puncture of the radial artery for temporary access
Ligation of the great saphenous vein
Direct surgical anastomosis between a native artery and vein, most commonly in the forearm
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: An arteriovenous fistula is created by directly anastomosing a native artery to a vein (commonly the radial artery to the cephalic vein at the wrist), allowing the vein to arterialize and dilate over several weeks, providing durable, high-flow access preferred over grafts or catheters for long-term hemodialysis.

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.s: Chronic venous insufficiency, often resulting from valvular incompetence in the deep or superficial venous system, classically leads to venous ulcers located in which characteristic area?
o: The plantar surface of the foot, over pressure points
The dorsum of the foot exclusively
The lateral malleolus exclusively, sparing the medial side
The medial malleolus (gaiter area) of the lower leg
The anterior shin over the tibia exclusively
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.e: Venous ulcers classically occur over the medial malleolus (the 'gaiter area'), resulting from chronic venous hypertension and valvular incompetence causing skin changes (hyperpigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis) and eventual ulceration, in contrast to arterial ulcers which more often occur distally over pressure points.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Naegele's rule for estimating the expected date of delivery is calculated by which method from the first day of the last menstrual period?
o: Add 14 days and subtract 1 month
Subtract 7 days and add 9 months
Add 7 days, subtract 3 months, and add 1 year
Add 40 days exactly with no adjustment for months or years
Add 3 months and subtract 7 days
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Naegele's rule estimates the expected date of delivery by adding 7 days to the first day of the last menstrual period, subtracting 3 months, and adding 1 year, assuming a regular 28-day cycle.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: The first fetal heart sounds are typically detectable by handheld Doppler at approximately which gestational age?
o: 10-12 weeks
2-4 weeks
20-24 weeks only
36-38 weeks only
28-30 weeks only
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Fetal heart tones can typically first be detected using a handheld Doppler device at approximately 10-12 weeks of gestation, whereas a standard fetoscope may not detect them until closer to 18-20 weeks.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Quickening, the maternal perception of fetal movement, is typically first noticed by a primigravida at approximately which gestational age?
o: 8-10 weeks
28-30 weeks
18-20 weeks
36-38 weeks
6-8 weeks
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Quickening is typically first perceived by a primigravida at around 18-20 weeks of gestation, while multigravidas may notice it slightly earlier, around 16-18 weeks, due to prior recognition of the sensation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Symphysis-fundal height measurement in centimeters, from around 20 to 34 weeks of gestation, is generally expected to correspond approximately to which parameter?
o: The gestational age in weeks
Twice the gestational age in weeks
Half the gestational age in weeks
The maternal weight in kilograms
The estimated fetal weight in hundreds of grams
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Between approximately 20 and 34 weeks of gestation, the symphysis-fundal height in centimeters approximately correlates with the gestational age in weeks, providing a simple clinical screening tool for fetal growth, though it has recognized limitations.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: The oral glucose tolerance test for screening gestational diabetes mellitus is typically performed at which gestational age in average-risk women?
o: 6-8 weeks
36-38 weeks
24-28 weeks
First trimester (before 12 weeks) exclusively
Only after delivery, as a postpartum screening test
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Universal screening for gestational diabetes mellitus with an oral glucose tolerance test is typically performed at 24-28 weeks of gestation in average-risk women, when insulin resistance from placental hormones is most pronounced.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Folic acid supplementation is recommended periconceptionally and in early pregnancy primarily to reduce the risk of which fetal anomaly?
o: Congenital heart disease as the primary target anomaly
Neural tube defects
Down syndrome as the primary target anomaly
Cleft lip and palate as the primary target anomaly
Limb reduction defects as the primary target anomaly
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Periconceptional folic acid supplementation significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects (such as spina bifida and anencephaly), which result from failure of neural tube closure in early embryonic development.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Which antenatal screening test uses maternal serum markers (such as PAPP-A and free beta-hCG) combined with nuchal translucency measurement in the first trimester to assess risk for chromosomal abnormalities?
o: The oral glucose tolerance test
Combined first-trimester screening
The quadruple test performed in the second trimester
Amniocentesis as a first-trimester screening test
Chorionic villus sampling as a screening (rather than diagnostic) test
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Combined first-trimester screening integrates maternal age, nuchal translucency ultrasound measurement, and serum biochemical markers (PAPP-A and free beta-hCG) to estimate the risk of chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Chorionic villus sampling, an invasive prenatal diagnostic test, is typically performed at which gestational age range, offering an advantage over amniocentesis?
o: 24-28 weeks, similar timing to glucose screening
36-38 weeks, near term
After delivery, as a diagnostic test on placental tissue
10-13 weeks, allowing earlier diagnosis than amniocentesis
6-8 weeks, in the first few weeks of pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Chorionic villus sampling is typically performed between 10 and 13 weeks of gestation, providing earlier diagnostic genetic information than amniocentesis, which is generally performed after 15 weeks.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Rh(D) immunoglobulin is administered to Rh-negative pregnant women primarily to prevent which complication?
o: Preeclampsia in the current pregnancy
Gestational diabetes in the current pregnancy
Maternal alloimmunization against fetal Rh-positive red blood cells, preventing hemolytic disease of the newborn in future pregnancies
Preterm labor in the current pregnancy
Neural tube defects in the fetus
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitization to fetal Rh-positive red blood cells that may enter the maternal circulation, thereby preventing the development of anti-D antibodies that could cause hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Routine antenatal anomaly ultrasound scanning is typically performed at which gestational age to optimally assess fetal structural anatomy?
o: 6-8 weeks
18-22 weeks
10-12 weeks exclusively, with no later scan needed
38-40 weeks exclusively
28-30 weeks exclusively, with no earlier scan performed
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: The detailed fetal anomaly scan is typically performed at 18-22 weeks of gestation, when fetal structures are sufficiently developed and visible to allow comprehensive assessment of fetal anatomy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Iron deficiency anemia is common in pregnancy primarily due to which physiological change?
o: A decrease in total blood volume during pregnancy
Decreased iron absorption from the gastrointestinal tract during pregnancy
Increased red cell mass without any change in plasma volume
An increase in plasma volume that exceeds the increase in red cell mass, causing hemodilution, combined with increased fetal iron demand
Decreased fetal iron requirements during pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Pregnancy is characterized by a disproportionate increase in plasma volume relative to red cell mass, causing physiological hemodilution, combined with increased iron requirements for fetal growth and expanded maternal red cell mass, predisposing to iron deficiency anemia.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A high maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein level in the second trimester is most classically associated with which fetal condition?
o: Down syndrome as the classic association with elevated levels
Open neural tube defects
Gestational diabetes as the classic association
Placenta previa as the classic association
Postterm pregnancy as the classic association
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is classically associated with open neural tube defects (and other conditions such as abdominal wall defects and multiple gestation), while low levels are associated with an increased risk of Down syndrome.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Which vaccination is routinely recommended during every pregnancy, regardless of prior vaccination history, to protect the newborn against pertussis?
o: Tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
Live attenuated measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine
Live attenuated varicella vaccine
Oral polio vaccine
Live attenuated yellow fever vaccine
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: The Tdap vaccine, an inactivated (non-live) vaccine, is recommended during every pregnancy (typically in the third trimester) to boost maternal antibodies against pertussis that are passively transferred to the newborn, protecting against pertussis before the infant's own vaccination series begins.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated during pregnancy due to its live attenuated nature?
o: Inactivated influenza vaccine
Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine
Tdap vaccine
Hepatitis B vaccine (inactivated/recombinant)
COVID-19 mRNA vaccine
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Live attenuated vaccines, including MMR and varicella, are generally contraindicated during pregnancy due to theoretical risk to the fetus, whereas inactivated vaccines (such as influenza, Tdap, and hepatitis B) are considered safe and recommended.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Fundal height measurement significantly less than expected for gestational age should prompt further evaluation to exclude which condition, among others?
o: Macrosomia as the primary concern with a small fundal height
Polyhydramnios as the primary concern with a small fundal height
Fetal growth restriction
Multiple gestation as the primary concern with a small fundal height
Postterm pregnancy as the primary concern with a small fundal height
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: A fundal height measuring significantly smaller than expected for gestational age raises concern for fetal growth restriction (among other causes such as oligohydramnios or inaccurate dating), warranting further ultrasound assessment.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: The biophysical profile, used for antenatal fetal surveillance, assesses which combination of parameters?
o: Maternal blood pressure, urine protein, and reflexes only
Fetal weight, maternal weight gain, and fundal height only
Fetal breathing movements, fetal movement, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume, and non-stress test (fetal heart rate reactivity)
Maternal hemoglobin, platelet count, and liver enzymes only
Cervical length and cervical dilation only
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: The biophysical profile combines real-time ultrasound assessment of fetal breathing movements, gross body movement, fetal tone, and amniotic fluid volume with a non-stress test, each scored to give an overall assessment of fetal well-being.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A reactive non-stress test is defined by which finding on cardiotocography?
o: Persistent fetal heart rate decelerations with every contraction
Two or more fetal heart rate accelerations of adequate amplitude and duration within a 20-minute period
A completely flat fetal heart rate trace with no variability
Fetal heart rate below 100 beats per minute sustained throughout the test
Absence of any fetal movement during the recording period
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: A reactive non-stress test requires at least two fetal heart rate accelerations of sufficient amplitude (typically 15 beats per minute above baseline for 15 seconds) within a 20-minute observation period, indicating fetal well-being.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Which antenatal screening test involves ultrasound measurement of the fluid-filled space at the back of the fetal neck in the first trimester?
o: Symphysis-fundal height measurement
Amniotic fluid index measurement
Nuchal translucency measurement
Biparietal diameter measurement alone
Cervical length measurement
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Nuchal translucency measurement, performed by ultrasound in the first trimester (typically 11-14 weeks), assesses the fluid-filled space at the back of the fetal neck; increased thickness is associated with a higher risk of chromosomal abnormalities and certain structural defects.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Routine screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy is recommended primarily to prevent progression to which complication?
o: Preeclampsia as the primary complication prevented
Gestational diabetes as the primary complication prevented
Placental abruption as the primary complication prevented
Postpartum hemorrhage as the primary complication prevented
Pyelonephritis and its associated risk of preterm labor
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy carries a significant risk of progressing to acute pyelonephritis, which is associated with increased risk of preterm labor and other maternal and fetal complications, justifying routine screening and treatment.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A pregnant woman with a history of gestational diabetes in a prior pregnancy should be screened for diabetes at which time in the current pregnancy?
o: Early in the current pregnancy (first trimester), in addition to standard screening at 24-28 weeks
Only after delivery of the current pregnancy
Exclusively at 36 weeks of the current pregnancy
Screening is not necessary if the prior pregnancy's diabetes resolved after delivery
Only if the patient is symptomatic during the current pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Women with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus are at increased risk of recurrence and should be screened early in a subsequent pregnancy (in addition to the standard 24-28 week screening if the earlier test is normal), to allow early detection and management.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: The recommended total gestational weight gain range for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy body mass index carrying a singleton pregnancy is approximately which range?
o: 2 to 5 kg total for the entire pregnancy
20 to 25 kg total for the entire pregnancy
There is no recommended range, as weight gain should not be monitored during pregnancy
11.5 to 16 kg (approximately 25-35 pounds)
40 to 45 kg total for the entire pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: For women with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI carrying a singleton pregnancy, the Institute of Medicine recommends a total gestational weight gain of approximately 11.5 to 16 kg (25-35 pounds), with different ranges recommended for underweight, overweight, and obese women.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Which antenatal test directly assesses fetal karyotype and is considered diagnostic (rather than merely screening) for chromosomal abnormalities?
o: The combined first-trimester screening test
The quadruple screening test
Cell-free fetal DNA screening (non-invasive prenatal testing)
A routine anomaly ultrasound scan
Amniocentesis
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Amniocentesis, an invasive procedure sampling amniotic fluid for fetal cells, provides a definitive fetal karyotype and is diagnostic for chromosomal abnormalities, unlike screening tests (combined first-trimester screening, quadruple test, or cell-free DNA testing) which estimate risk rather than provide a definitive diagnosis.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Cell-free fetal DNA testing (non-invasive prenatal testing) analyzes which source of genetic material in maternal blood to screen for common fetal aneuploidies?
o: Fetal red blood cells isolated directly from maternal circulation
Amniotic fluid obtained via a non-invasive transabdominal aspiration
Maternal white blood cell DNA exclusively
Fetal urine collected non-invasively from the amniotic sac
Fragments of placental (trophoblastic) DNA circulating in maternal plasma
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Cell-free fetal DNA testing analyzes small fragments of placental (trophoblastic) DNA that circulate freely in maternal plasma, allowing highly sensitive screening for common aneuploidies such as trisomy 21, 18, and 13 from a maternal blood sample.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Antenatal corticosteroids (e.g., betamethasone) are administered to women at risk of preterm delivery primarily to achieve which fetal benefit?
o: Prevention of preterm labor itself
Acceleration of fetal lung maturity, reducing the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
Treatment of maternal gestational diabetes
Reduction of maternal blood pressure in preeclampsia
Prevention of neural tube defects
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by stimulating surfactant production, significantly reducing the incidence and severity of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome when given to women at risk of preterm delivery, typically between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A pregnant woman with a multiple gestation (e.g., twins) generally requires an increased daily intake of which nutrient compared to a singleton pregnancy?
o: No additional nutrients are required in multiple gestation compared to singleton pregnancy
Only additional calcium, with no change in iron or folate needs
Iron and folic acid, among other nutrients, due to increased demands
Only additional vitamin D, with no change in other nutrient needs
Reduced overall caloric intake compared to singleton pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Multiple gestation increases maternal nutritional demands, including increased requirements for iron and folic acid (among other nutrients), reflecting the needs of more than one developing fetus and an increased risk of maternal anemia.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: The linea nigra and melasma (chloasma), pigmentation changes commonly seen during pregnancy, are primarily attributed to which hormonal influence?
o: Decreased thyroid hormone levels during pregnancy
Increased insulin resistance during pregnancy
Increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone-like activity, influenced by elevated estrogen and progesterone
Decreased cortisol levels during pregnancy
Increased parathyroid hormone levels during pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Pregnancy-associated skin pigmentation changes such as linea nigra and melasma result from increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone-like activity, influenced by the elevated estrogen and progesterone levels characteristic of pregnancy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Physiological changes in maternal cardiac output during a normal singleton pregnancy typically show which overall trend?
o: A progressive decrease throughout pregnancy
A progressive increase, reaching approximately 30-50% above pre-pregnancy levels by the third trimester
No significant change from pre-pregnancy baseline
An initial decrease followed by a return to baseline by term with no net increase
A sudden, isolated increase only during labor with no antenatal change
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Maternal cardiac output progressively increases during pregnancy, reaching approximately 30-50% above pre-pregnancy levels by the third trimester, driven by increased stroke volume and heart rate to meet the metabolic demands of pregnancy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Supine hypotensive syndrome in late pregnancy results from which mechanism?
o: Compression of the abdominal aorta causing arterial hypertension
Excessive vagal stimulation from fetal movement
A direct toxic effect of pregnancy hormones on the maternal heart
Acute blood loss from placental separation
Compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus when the woman lies supine, reducing venous return
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Supine hypotensive syndrome occurs when the enlarged gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava in the supine position, reducing venous return to the heart and causing maternal hypotension, which is relieved by adopting a left lateral position.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Which trimester is generally considered the period of greatest teratogenic risk from maternal drug or toxin exposure, corresponding to the period of organogenesis?
o: The second trimester exclusively
The first trimester
The third trimester exclusively
The immediate postpartum period
Teratogenic risk is equal throughout all three trimesters
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: The first trimester, particularly weeks 3 through 8 of gestation, corresponds to the period of organogenesis and represents the period of greatest vulnerability to teratogenic effects from maternal drug, infection, or toxin exposure.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Polyhydramnios, an abnormally increased amniotic fluid volume, is associated with which maternal or fetal condition?
o: Maternal diabetes mellitus and certain fetal gastrointestinal anomalies impairing fetal swallowing
Fetal renal agenesis as the most common associated cause
Premature rupture of membranes as the most common associated cause
Severe fetal growth restriction as the most common associated cause
Postterm pregnancy as the most common associated cause
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Polyhydramnios is associated with maternal diabetes (causing fetal polyuria) and fetal conditions impairing swallowing of amniotic fluid, such as esophageal or duodenal atresia, among other causes, in contrast to oligohydramnios, which is more classically linked to renal anomalies or membrane rupture.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Oligohydramnios, an abnormally reduced amniotic fluid volume, is classically associated with which fetal condition affecting urine production?
o: Fetal gastroschisis as the classic association
Fetal diaphragmatic hernia as the classic association
Fetal renal agenesis or other severe renal anomalies
Fetal cardiac septal defects as the classic association
Fetal cleft palate as the classic association
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Since fetal urine is a major contributor to amniotic fluid volume from the second trimester onward, conditions severely impairing fetal urine production, such as bilateral renal agenesis or severe obstructive uropathy, classically cause oligohydramnios.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A pregnant woman presents with a positive antibody screen indicating Rh alloimmunization from a prior pregnancy. Which fetal complication is she at increased risk for in the current pregnancy?
o: Neural tube defects as the primary risk
Gestational trophoblastic disease as the primary risk
Ectopic pregnancy as the primary risk
Fetal hemolytic anemia and hydrops fetalis
Placenta accreta as the primary risk
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Rh alloimmunization from a prior sensitizing event places a fetus in a subsequent pregnancy (if Rh-positive) at risk for maternal antibody-mediated hemolysis of fetal red blood cells, potentially leading to severe fetal anemia and hydrops fetalis if untreated.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Group B Streptococcus screening in pregnancy is typically performed at which gestational age, with positive results guiding intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?
o: 35-37 weeks
10-12 weeks
20-22 weeks
Immediately postpartum only
Only if the woman is symptomatic with vaginal discharge
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Group B Streptococcus vaginal-rectal screening is typically performed at 35-37 weeks of gestation, with a positive result prompting intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to reduce the risk of early-onset neonatal Group B Streptococcus infection.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A pregnant woman with chronic hypertension is at increased risk of developing which pregnancy-specific complication superimposed on her underlying condition?
o: Gestational diabetes as the primary superimposed risk
Superimposed preeclampsia
Placenta previa as the primary superimposed risk
Ectopic pregnancy as the primary superimposed risk
Hyperemesis gravidarum as the primary superimposed risk
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Women with chronic hypertension are at significantly increased risk of developing superimposed preeclampsia during pregnancy, requiring closer antenatal monitoring for signs of worsening hypertension, proteinuria, or other preeclampsia features.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: The TORCH group of infections, screened for or considered in the context of adverse fetal outcomes, includes which of the following pathogens?
o: Tuberculosis, Onchocerciasis, Rabies, Chlamydia, and Hepatitis exclusively
Tetanus, Otitis, Roseola, Chickenpox, and HIV exclusively
Typhoid, Osteomyelitis, Rickettsia, Cholera, and Hookworm
Toxoplasma, Other (e.g., syphilis, varicella), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus
Trichomoniasis, Oral candidiasis, Rotavirus, Coxsackievirus, and Hantavirus
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: The TORCH acronym refers to a group of infections associated with significant congenital and perinatal morbidity: Toxoplasma gondii, Other agents (including syphilis and varicella-zoster), Rubella virus, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester carries the highest risk of which fetal outcome?
o: Neural tube defects as the primary risk of first-trimester rubella
Isolated limb reduction defects as the primary risk
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia as the primary risk
Congenital rubella syndrome, including cardiac defects, cataracts, and sensorineural deafness
Isolated fetal macrosomia as the primary risk
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester carries the highest risk of congenital rubella syndrome, a triad classically including cardiac defects (such as patent ductus arteriosus), cataracts, and sensorineural deafness, with risk and severity decreasing as gestation advances.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection in many populations and can result in which classic long-term complication in an affected infant?
o: Congenital limb deformities as the classic long-term complication
Sensorineural hearing loss
Neonatal jaundice exclusively, with no long-term sequelae
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia as the classic complication
Isolated cleft palate as the classic complication
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection is a leading cause of non-genetic sensorineural hearing loss in children, which may be present at birth or develop progressively, even in infants who appear asymptomatic at delivery.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Braxton Hicks contractions, often experienced in the later stages of pregnancy, are best distinguished from true labor contractions by which feature?
o: They occur exclusively in the first trimester
They always cause rapid, progressive cervical dilation
They are indistinguishable from true labor in every respect
They are accompanied by rupture of membranes in all cases
They are irregular, generally painless or mildly uncomfortable, and do not cause progressive cervical change
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, typically painless or mildly uncomfortable uterine contractions that do not cause progressive cervical dilation or effacement, distinguishing them from true labor contractions, which are regular and produce cervical change.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: Maternal thyroid hormone requirements typically change in which direction during a normal pregnancy, often necessitating a dose adjustment in women on thyroid replacement?
o: They increase, often requiring an increased levothyroxine dose in hypothyroid women
They decrease significantly, often requiring a reduced levothyroxine dose
They remain completely unchanged throughout pregnancy in all women
Thyroid hormone requirements become irrelevant during pregnancy
They increase only in the third trimester, with no change earlier in pregnancy
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: Maternal thyroid hormone requirements typically increase during pregnancy due to increased thyroid-binding globulin, increased metabolic demands, and placental/fetal thyroid hormone metabolism, often necessitating an increased levothyroxine dose in women with hypothyroidism.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.s: A dating ultrasound performed in the first trimester is considered the most accurate method for establishing gestational age primarily because of which feature?
o: Early fetal growth is highly consistent between individuals, making crown-rump length a reliable predictor of gestational age
It directly visualizes fetal chromosomes
It is more accurate than any method in the third trimester specifically due to larger fetal size
It replaces the need for any menstrual history in all cases
First-trimester ultrasound cannot estimate gestational age at all
obstetrics-and-gynecology/antenatal-care.e: In the first trimester, fetal growth (measured as crown-rump length) is highly consistent across pregnancies regardless of individual variation, making first-trimester ultrasound dating the most accurate method for establishing gestational age, more accurate than later scans or menstrual history alone in cases of discrepancy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Preeclampsia is defined by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation accompanied by which additional finding?
o: Fetal macrosomia as a defining diagnostic criterion
Polyhydramnios as a defining diagnostic criterion
Maternal anemia as a defining diagnostic criterion
Proteinuria or evidence of other maternal organ dysfunction
Gestational diabetes as a defining diagnostic criterion
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Preeclampsia is diagnosed by new-onset hypertension (systolic ≥140 mmHg or diastolic ≥90 mmHg) after 20 weeks of gestation, accompanied by proteinuria or, in its absence, evidence of other maternal end-organ dysfunction such as renal insufficiency, liver involvement, or thrombocytopenia.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Eclampsia is defined as the occurrence of which event in a woman with preeclampsia?
o: Isolated severe headache without any other neurological symptoms
Isolated visual disturbance without any seizure activity
A rise in blood pressure alone without any seizure
New-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures not attributable to another cause
Onset of proteinuria for the first time
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Eclampsia is defined by the occurrence of new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with preeclampsia, not attributable to other causes, representing a severe and life-threatening complication requiring urgent management.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Magnesium sulfate is administered in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia primarily for which purpose?
o: Definitive treatment and cure of hypertension
Acceleration of fetal lung maturity
Seizure prophylaxis and treatment
Induction of labor as its primary mechanism of action
Treatment of postpartum hemorrhage
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and for the treatment of eclamptic seizures, acting via mechanisms including cerebral vasodilation and reduced neuronal excitability.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: HELLP syndrome, a severe variant of preeclampsia, is characterized by which combination of laboratory and clinical findings?
o: Hyperglycemia, Elevated Leukocytes, and Low Protein
Hypertension, Edema, and Low Lymphocyte count
Hyperkalemia, Elevated Lipase, and Low Potassium
Hypoglycemia, Elevated Lactate, and Low Platelet count as an alternative but incorrect expansion
Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelet count
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: HELLP syndrome is a severe manifestation of preeclampsia characterized by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelet count, associated with significant maternal and fetal morbidity and often requiring expedited delivery.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Placenta previa refers to which abnormality of placental location?
o: The placenta implants abnormally deeply into the myometrium
The placenta separates prematurely from the uterine wall before delivery
The placenta implants in an ectopic location outside the uterus
The placenta implants over or near the internal cervical os
The umbilical cord inserts into the fetal membranes rather than the placental disc
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Placenta previa occurs when the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment, covering or lying near the internal cervical os, and classically presents with painless vaginal bleeding, typically in the third trimester.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Placental abruption, the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta before delivery, classically presents with which combination of features?
o: Painless vaginal bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus
Absence of any vaginal bleeding in the majority of cases
Isolated fetal tachycardia without any maternal symptoms
Painful vaginal bleeding with a tender, sometimes hypertonic uterus
Gradual onset of symptoms over several weeks
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Placental abruption classically presents with painful vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and often a hypertonic, contracting uterus, in contrast to the painless bleeding classically associated with placenta previa.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Placenta accreta spectrum disorders, in which the placenta abnormally adheres to or invades the myometrium, are most strongly associated with which risk factor?
o: Nulliparity without any prior uterine surgery
Multiple gestation without any prior uterine surgery
Maternal age under 20 years without any other risk factors
Prior cesarean delivery, especially with placenta previa in the current pregnancy
Low maternal body mass index
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Placenta accreta spectrum disorders are most strongly associated with prior uterine surgery (particularly cesarean delivery), especially when combined with a current placenta previa overlying the prior uterine scar.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Umbilical cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency, is most immediately dangerous because of which mechanism?
o: Direct maternal hemorrhage from the prolapsed cord
Immediate maternal cardiac arrest from vagal stimulation
Compression of the prolapsed cord between the fetal presenting part and the maternal pelvis, causing fetal hypoxia
Ascending infection of the amniotic cavity as the primary immediate danger
Uterine rupture as a direct and immediate consequence
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Umbilical cord prolapse is dangerous because the cord can become compressed between the fetal presenting part and the maternal pelvis, occluding fetal blood flow and causing acute fetal hypoxia, requiring emergency delivery, usually by cesarean section.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Shoulder dystocia, an obstetric emergency during vaginal delivery, is best described as which clinical scenario?
o: A normal variant of delivery requiring no additional intervention
Delayed delivery of the placenta after the fetus has been delivered
Failure of cervical dilation during the first stage of labor
Excessive maternal pushing effort with no fetal complication
Failure of the fetal shoulders to deliver spontaneously after delivery of the head, requiring additional obstetric maneuvers
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Shoulder dystocia occurs when the fetal anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis after delivery of the head, requiring specific obstetric maneuvers (such as McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure) to safely deliver the shoulders and avoid fetal or maternal injury.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: The McRoberts maneuver, used in the management of shoulder dystocia, involves which action?
o: Hyperflexion and abduction of the maternal hips toward the maternal abdomen
Application of fundal pressure on the uterus
Immediate cesarean section after the fetal head has already delivered
Rotation of the fetus to a breech position
Manual removal of the placenta
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: The McRoberts maneuver involves hyperflexing and abducting the maternal hips toward the abdomen, which straightens the lumbosacral angle and often frees the impacted anterior shoulder in shoulder dystocia, and is typically the first maneuver attempted.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: The first stage of labor is defined as the period from onset of true labor until which point?
o: Delivery of the fetus
Delivery of the placenta
The onset of the second stage's active pushing phase
Full cervical dilation (10 cm)
Rupture of membranes
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: The first stage of labor extends from the onset of regular, effective uterine contractions causing cervical change until full cervical dilation (10 cm), and is further divided into latent and active phases.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: The second stage of labor is defined as the period from full cervical dilation until which event?
o: Delivery of the placenta
Onset of regular contractions
Rupture of membranes
Engagement of the fetal head in the pelvis
Delivery of the fetus
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: The second stage of labor begins with full cervical dilation (10 cm) and ends with the delivery of the fetus, during which maternal pushing efforts assist descent and delivery.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: The third stage of labor is defined as the period from delivery of the fetus until which event?
o: Full involution of the uterus
The mother's discharge from the hospital
Cessation of postpartum lochia
Delivery of the placenta
Resumption of normal menstruation
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: The third stage of labor is the interval from delivery of the fetus to delivery of the placenta and membranes, typically lasting up to 30 minutes, with active management commonly used to reduce the risk of postpartum hemorrhage.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Active management of the third stage of labor, which reduces the risk of postpartum hemorrhage, typically includes administration of which class of medication?
o: Tocolytic agents to relax the uterus
Antihypertensive agents
Anticoagulant agents
Antibiotics as the primary component of active management
Uterotonic agents (e.g., oxytocin)
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Active management of the third stage of labor typically includes prophylactic administration of a uterotonic agent (most commonly oxytocin) immediately after delivery of the fetus, along with controlled cord traction, to promote uterine contraction and reduce postpartum hemorrhage risk.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Postpartum hemorrhage is most commonly caused by which etiology, remembered by the mnemonic 'the 4 T's' as the most frequent cause?
o: Uterine atony (Tone)
Retained placental tissue (Tissue) as the single most common cause overall
Genital tract trauma (Trauma) as the single most common cause overall
Coagulopathy (Thrombin) as the single most common cause overall
Amniotic fluid embolism as the single most common cause overall
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Uterine atony (failure of the uterus to contract adequately after delivery) is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage, accounting for the majority of cases, followed by retained tissue, trauma, and coagulopathy (the '4 T's').

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: A previous classical (vertical) cesarean section incision on the uterus is a contraindication to a trial of labor in a subsequent pregnancy primarily due to which risk?
o: An increased risk of placenta previa only, without any risk of rupture
An increased risk of postterm pregnancy
An increased risk of gestational diabetes
An increased risk of multiple gestation
A significantly increased risk of uterine rupture during labor
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: A classical (vertical) uterine incision carries a substantially higher risk of uterine rupture during a subsequent labor compared to a low transverse incision, and is therefore considered a contraindication to vaginal birth after cesarean.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Preterm labor is defined as regular uterine contractions with cervical change occurring at which gestational age range?
o: Before 20 weeks of gestation
After 42 weeks of gestation
Between 20 and 37 completed weeks of gestation
Only in the first trimester
Exclusively at exactly 37 weeks of gestation
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Preterm labor is defined as the onset of regular uterine contractions accompanied by cervical dilation and/or effacement occurring between 20 and 37 completed weeks of gestation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Tocolytic agents, used to temporarily delay preterm labor, are primarily administered to allow time for which intervention?
o: Permanent cessation of labor until term in all cases
Induction of fetal lung maturity directly, independent of corticosteroids
Definitive treatment of the underlying cause of preterm labor in all cases
Immediate cesarean delivery preparation only
Administration of antenatal corticosteroids and, if needed, maternal transfer to a facility with neonatal intensive care
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Tocolytic agents are used to delay delivery by 48 hours or more, primarily to allow completion of a course of antenatal corticosteroids to accelerate fetal lung maturity and, when necessary, to allow safe maternal transfer to a facility equipped for preterm neonatal care.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Premature rupture of membranes refers to which clinical scenario?
o: Rupture of membranes occurring after full cervical dilation
Rupture of membranes occurring only after 42 weeks of gestation
Artificial rupture of membranes performed by the clinician during labor
Rupture of membranes occurring during the second stage of labor
Rupture of the fetal membranes before the onset of labor
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Premature rupture of membranes refers to rupture of the amniotic sac before the onset of labor, regardless of gestational age, and is termed 'preterm premature rupture of membranes' when it occurs before 37 weeks of gestation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Chorioamnionitis, an intra-amniotic infection, is a recognized complication of prolonged rupture of membranes and classically presents with which finding?
o: Painless vaginal bleeding without any fever
Sudden severe hypertension without any fever
Isolated proteinuria without any fever or uterine tenderness
Bradycardia in both the mother and fetus
Maternal fever, uterine tenderness, and often fetal or maternal tachycardia
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Chorioamnionitis classically presents with maternal fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling amniotic fluid or discharge, and often maternal and/or fetal tachycardia, requiring prompt antibiotic treatment and consideration of expedited delivery.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: External cephalic version, a procedure to turn a fetus from breech to cephalic presentation, is typically attempted at which gestational age?
o: Around 36-37 weeks of gestation
Before 20 weeks of gestation
Only after the onset of active labor
Exclusively after 41 weeks of gestation
Immediately after delivery of a previous twin
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: External cephalic version is typically attempted around 36-37 weeks of gestation, allowing sufficient time for the fetus to remain cephalic if successful, while being late enough that spontaneous version to breech is less likely to occur afterward.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: A footling breech presentation carries a particular risk during vaginal delivery attempts due to which complication?
o: Placenta previa as a direct consequence of the presentation
Uterine rupture as the primary specific risk
Maternal seizure as a direct consequence of the presentation
Neonatal jaundice as the primary specific risk
Umbilical cord prolapse
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Footling breech presentation carries a particularly increased risk of umbilical cord prolapse during labor and attempted vaginal delivery, since the presenting part does not fill the pelvic inlet as completely as a cephalic or frank breech presentation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Vasa previa, a rare but dangerous obstetric condition, is characterized by which anatomical abnormality?
o: Fetal blood vessels traversing the fetal membranes near the internal cervical os, unprotected by placental tissue or umbilical cord
Complete placental implantation over the internal os
Abnormal invasion of placental tissue into the myometrium
An umbilical cord with only a single artery
A retained placental fragment after delivery
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Vasa previa occurs when unprotected fetal blood vessels (running through the membranes, often from a velamentous cord insertion) cross near the internal cervical os, posing a risk of fetal exsanguination if these vessels rupture, particularly with membrane rupture.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but often catastrophic obstetric emergency that classically presents with which combination of features?
o: Sudden cardiovascular collapse, respiratory distress, and disseminated intravascular coagulation, often during or shortly after labor
Gradual onset of hypertension over several days
Isolated fever without any cardiovascular or respiratory compromise
Slowly progressive anemia over several weeks
Isolated proteinuria detected on routine urinalysis
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Amniotic fluid embolism classically presents with sudden, severe cardiovascular collapse, acute respiratory distress, and disseminated intravascular coagulation, typically occurring during labor, delivery, or shortly postpartum, and carries a high mortality rate.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Uterine rupture, a rare but life-threatening complication most associated with a trial of labor after prior cesarean delivery, classically presents with which finding?
o: Gradual onset of mild abdominal discomfort over several hours with no fetal heart rate change
Painless vaginal bleeding without any abdominal pain
Isolated maternal fever without any pain or fetal distress
Sudden severe abdominal pain, fetal heart rate abnormalities, and loss of fetal station
Sudden onset of polyhydramnios
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Uterine rupture classically presents with sudden severe abdominal pain (sometimes with loss of the previously palpable presenting part), acute fetal heart rate abnormalities (often bradycardia), and can be accompanied by maternal hemodynamic instability, representing an obstetric emergency requiring immediate laparotomy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Cephalopelvic disproportion, a cause of labor dystocia, refers to which clinical situation?
o: A disparity between maternal age and gestational age
A disparity between the size of the fetal head and the dimensions of the maternal pelvis, preventing normal vaginal delivery
A disparity between fetal weight and placental weight
An abnormality of fetal cardiac rhythm during labor
A disparity between maternal blood type and fetal blood type
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Cephalopelvic disproportion refers to a mismatch between the size of the fetal head (or presenting part) and the maternal pelvis, preventing engagement or descent and resulting in labor dystocia, often necessitating cesarean delivery.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: A prolonged latent phase of the first stage of labor is generally managed by which approach in a stable mother and fetus?
o: Immediate cesarean delivery regardless of maternal or fetal status
Expectant management or rest/sedation, since it does not necessarily indicate true labor dystocia
Administration of tocolytics to stop labor entirely
Immediate operative vaginal delivery
Induction of general anesthesia for observation
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: A prolonged latent phase, while sometimes frustrating, does not necessarily indicate true labor dystocia and can often be managed expectantly or with rest/sedation, reserving intervention for confirmed active-phase abnormalities or non-reassuring fetal status.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Instrumental (operative) vaginal delivery using forceps or vacuum extraction requires which prerequisite regarding cervical dilation and fetal station?
o: Cervical dilation of only 5 cm is sufficient in all cases
Full cervical dilation and an adequately low, engaged fetal head
The fetal head must still be floating, unengaged in the pelvis
Complete absence of uterine contractions
The mother must be under general anesthesia in all cases
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Instrumental vaginal delivery requires full cervical dilation and an adequately descended, engaged fetal head, along with a clearly defined position, to ensure safe application of forceps or a vacuum device and successful delivery.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Postterm pregnancy is generally defined as pregnancy continuing beyond which gestational age?
o: 42 completed weeks of gestation
37 completed weeks of gestation
34 completed weeks of gestation
40 completed weeks of gestation, with no additional time allowed
28 completed weeks of gestation
obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.e: Postterm pregnancy is generally defined as pregnancy continuing beyond 42 completed weeks (294 days) of gestation, and is associated with increased risks including macrosomia, oligohydramnios, and placental insufficiency.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/obstetric-comp.s: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid during labor raises concern primarily for which fetal complication if aspirated at birth?
o: Neonatal jaundice as the primary concern from meconium aspiration
Congenital heart disease as a direct consequence of meconium exposure
