obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Emergency contraception with levonorgestrel is most effective when taken within which time frame after unprotected intercourse?
o: Only if taken more than one week after intercourse
As soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, though it may have some effect up to 120 hours
Only if taken exactly 30 days after intercourse
Effectiveness is identical regardless of timing within the entire menstrual cycle
Only effective if taken before intercourse occurs, not afterward
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception is most effective when taken as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse, ideally within 72 hours, though it retains some efficacy up to 120 hours, working primarily by delaying or inhibiting ovulation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Bilateral tubal ligation, a permanent method of female sterilization, prevents pregnancy through which mechanism?
o: Suppression of ovulation through hormonal feedback
Induction of permanent endometrial atrophy
Mechanical interruption of the fallopian tubes, preventing sperm from reaching the ovum
Direct removal of both ovaries
Alteration of cervical mucus consistency
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Tubal ligation achieves permanent contraception by mechanically interrupting the fallopian tubes (via cutting, clipping, or cauterization), preventing sperm from reaching and fertilizing the ovum, without altering ovarian hormone production or ovulation.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A vasectomy, a permanent method of male sterilization, prevents pregnancy through which mechanism?
o: Suppression of testosterone production
Direct removal of the testes
Blockage of the urethra
Interruption of the vas deferens, preventing sperm from being included in the ejaculate
Induction of erectile dysfunction
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Vasectomy involves surgical interruption of the vas deferens bilaterally, preventing sperm from being transported from the testes into the ejaculate, while testosterone production and other testicular functions remain unaffected.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: The lactational amenorrhea method of contraception relies on which physiological mechanism, and is effective only under specific conditions?
o: Suppression of ovulation by prolactin-mediated inhibition of gonadotropin-releasing hormone during frequent, exclusive breastfeeding
A direct spermicidal effect of breast milk hormones
Permanent sterilization achieved through breastfeeding
Complete suppression of menstruation for the woman's entire reproductive lifespan
A barrier effect created by breastfeeding-related cervical mucus changes
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: The lactational amenorrhea method relies on prolactin-mediated suppression of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (and consequently ovulation) during frequent, exclusive breastfeeding, and is effective as a temporary contraceptive method only when breastfeeding is exclusive, the infant is under 6 months old, and menstruation has not yet resumed.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Male and female condoms, unlike most other contraceptive methods, provide which additional benefit beyond pregnancy prevention?
o: Reduction in the risk of transmission of sexually transmitted infections
Permanent sterilization if used consistently over many years
Suppression of ovulation, similarly to hormonal methods
Treatment of existing pelvic inflammatory disease
Enhancement of fertility for future pregnancy attempts
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Condoms (male and female) are unique among common contraceptive methods in also providing a barrier that significantly reduces the risk of transmission of sexually transmitted infections, in addition to their contraceptive effect.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: The rhythm (calendar/fertility awareness) method of family planning relies primarily on which principle?
o: Complete abstinence from intercourse throughout the entire menstrual cycle
Use of a hormonal medication taken only during the fertile window
Surgical interruption of the fallopian tubes during the fertile window
Insertion of an intrauterine device only during the fertile window
Avoiding intercourse during the estimated fertile window around ovulation, based on menstrual cycle tracking
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: The rhythm (fertility awareness) method relies on identifying and avoiding intercourse during the estimated fertile window, calculated from menstrual cycle length, basal body temperature changes, or cervical mucus changes, without using any device or medication.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Recurrent pregnancy loss, defined as two or more consecutive pregnancy losses, warrants evaluation for which category of underlying causes, among others?
o: Uterine anatomical abnormalities, antiphospholipid syndrome, and parental chromosomal abnormalities
Only psychological factors, since recurrent loss is rarely due to any medical cause
Only environmental toxin exposure, with no role for genetic or anatomical factors
Only maternal age, with no other contributing factors considered
Only paternal age, with no maternal factors considered
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Evaluation for recurrent pregnancy loss typically includes assessment for uterine anatomical abnormalities (e.g., septate uterus), antiphospholipid syndrome and other thrombophilias, parental chromosomal abnormalities, and endocrine or other contributing factors.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A hysterosalpingogram demonstrating bilateral tubal blockage at the cornual ends most directly suggests which cause of infertility?
o: Purely ovulatory dysfunction, unrelated to any tubal pathology
Isolated male factor infertility, with normal female anatomy
Isolated cervical factor infertility, with normal tubal anatomy
Isolated uterine factor infertility, with normal tubal anatomy
Tubal factor infertility, potentially amenable to surgical or assisted reproductive management
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Bilateral tubal blockage demonstrated on hysterosalpingogram indicates tubal factor infertility, which may result from prior infection (e.g., pelvic inflammatory disease), endometriosis, or previous surgery, and may require in vitro fertilization to bypass the blocked tubes.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Unexplained infertility is diagnosed when standard investigations of which components of the reproductive process are all found to be normal?
o: Only maternal age and body mass index, without any other testing
Ovulation, tubal patency, uterine cavity, and semen analysis
Only semen analysis, without any female factor evaluation
Only ovarian reserve testing, without any other investigation
Only psychological factors, without any physical investigation
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Unexplained infertility is diagnosed after a comprehensive standard infertility evaluation, including confirmation of ovulation, tubal patency, a normal uterine cavity, and a normal semen analysis, fails to identify an underlying cause.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Varicocele, a dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus in the scrotum, is a recognized cause of male infertility primarily through which mechanism?
o: Increased scrotal/testicular temperature impairing spermatogenesis
Direct mechanical obstruction of the vas deferens
Complete testicular atrophy occurring in all affected men
Suppression of pituitary gonadotropin secretion
Direct damage to the epididymis causing obstructive azoospermia in all cases
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Varicocele is thought to impair spermatogenesis primarily by increasing scrotal and testicular temperature (impairing the normally cooler testicular environment needed for optimal sperm production), among other proposed mechanisms, and is a treatable cause of male factor infertility.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Intrauterine insemination, a less invasive assisted reproductive technique than in vitro fertilization, involves which procedure?
o: Placement of specially prepared (washed) sperm directly into the uterine cavity around the time of ovulation
Direct injection of a single sperm into a retrieved oocyte
Surgical retrieval and fertilization of oocytes outside the body
Surgical removal of an ovary for later oocyte retrieval
Transfer of a previously frozen embryo into the uterine cavity
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Intrauterine insemination involves placing specially processed (washed) sperm directly into the uterine cavity around the time of ovulation, bypassing the cervix, and is a less invasive and lower-cost option than in vitro fertilization for appropriately selected causes of infertility.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Cryopreservation of embryos or oocytes is commonly offered to which group of patients for fertility preservation?
o: Only patients who have already completed their family and desire permanent contraception
Only patients over the age of 60
Only patients with a confirmed diagnosis of infertility who do not wish to conceive
Patients about to undergo gonadotoxic treatment, such as chemotherapy for cancer
Only male patients, since female gametes cannot be cryopreserved
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Cryopreservation of oocytes or embryos is commonly offered for fertility preservation to patients facing gonadotoxic treatments (such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy for cancer) that may impair future fertility, allowing them to attempt conception later using the preserved gametes or embryos.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A basal body temperature chart, historically used to help identify ovulation, typically shows which pattern around the time of ovulation?
o: A sustained rise in basal body temperature after ovulation, due to the thermogenic effect of progesterone
A sustained fall in basal body temperature after ovulation
No change in basal body temperature throughout the entire cycle
A rise in temperature occurring several days before ovulation, followed by a fall exactly at ovulation
An unpredictable, random pattern with no relation to the menstrual cycle
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Basal body temperature typically shows a sustained rise of about 0.3-0.5°C after ovulation, attributable to the thermogenic effect of progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum, and can retrospectively help identify that ovulation has occurred.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Ovulation predictor kits, commercially available for home use, detect which hormone to help predict the timing of ovulation?
o: Luteinizing hormone surge in the urine
Follicle-stimulating hormone in the urine as the primary marker detected
Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin in the urine as the primary marker detected
Progesterone in the urine as the primary marker detected
Estradiol in the urine exclusively, without any luteinizing hormone detection
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Ovulation predictor kits detect the surge in urinary luteinizing hormone that precedes ovulation by approximately 24-36 hours, helping individuals identify the optimal window for intercourse or timed insemination.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Which of the following is a recognized indication for donor sperm use in assisted reproduction?
o: Azoospermia (absence of sperm) that is not amenable to surgical sperm retrieval
Normal semen parameters with no identified male factor infertility
Isolated female tubal factor infertility with a fertile male partner
Isolated female ovulatory dysfunction with a fertile male partner
Isolated uterine factor infertility with a fertile male partner
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Donor sperm is a recognized option for couples facing azoospermia (absence of sperm in the ejaculate) that cannot be overcome through surgical sperm retrieval techniques, or in cases of severe genetic risk from the male partner, allowing the couple to achieve pregnancy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Donor oocyte in vitro fertilization is a recognized option primarily for women with which condition?
o: Isolated male factor infertility with normal female fertility
Isolated tubal factor infertility with normal ovarian reserve
Isolated cervical factor infertility with normal ovarian reserve
Uncomplicated polycystic ovary syndrome with normal ovarian reserve
Diminished ovarian reserve or premature ovarian insufficiency
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Donor oocyte in vitro fertilization is a recognized option for women with diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, or advanced maternal age with poor oocyte quality, using oocytes from a fertility donor combined with the intended parent's or partner's sperm.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A woman using a combined hormonal contraceptive method who is a smoker over the age of 35 is at increased risk of which serious complication, influencing contraceptive choice?
o: Osteoporosis as the primary concern in this population
Endometrial cancer as the primary concern in this population
Iron deficiency anemia as the primary concern in this population
Hypothyroidism as the primary concern in this population
Cardiovascular events, including venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, and stroke
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Smoking combined with age over 35 significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular complications (venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, stroke) with combined hormonal contraceptive use, generally making progestin-only or non-hormonal methods preferable in this population.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: The subdermal contraceptive implant provides long-acting reversible contraception primarily through which mechanism?
o: Continuous release of a progestin, suppressing ovulation and thickening cervical mucus
Continuous release of estrogen only, without any progestin component
A purely mechanical barrier effect similar to an intrauterine device
Direct suppression of spermatogenesis in the male partner
Permanent sterilization achieved through tubal occlusion
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: The subdermal contraceptive implant continuously releases a progestin, which suppresses ovulation and thickens cervical mucus (impeding sperm transport), providing highly effective, long-acting reversible contraception for several years.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, in addition to providing contraception, is also used therapeutically to manage which gynecological condition?
o: Acute pelvic inflammatory disease as a primary treatment
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Ovarian torsion as a primary treatment
Acute ectopic pregnancy as a primary treatment
Primary infertility as a treatment to enhance fertility
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, beyond its contraceptive effect, is widely used therapeutically to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding by causing endometrial thinning through local progestin release, and is also used in the management of endometrial hyperplasia.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A woman desiring permanent contraception but wishing to avoid abdominal or laparoscopic surgery may be offered which alternative sterilization approach, where available?
o: Combined oral contraceptive pills, which are considered a permanent method
A copper intrauterine device, which provides permanent sterilization
The lactational amenorrhea method, which provides permanent contraception
Hysteroscopic tubal occlusion, placing an obstructive device or performing intentional scarring within the tubal ostia
Emergency contraception taken regularly, which provides permanent sterilization
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Hysteroscopic tubal occlusion techniques, which can be performed transcervically without abdominal incisions, offer an alternative approach to permanent female sterilization, though such devices are not universally available or currently in use in some regions.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: The World Health Organization's Medical Eligibility Criteria for contraceptive use provides guidance on which aspect of contraceptive prescribing?
o: The specific brand names of contraceptive products available worldwide
The safety of specific contraceptive methods in women with particular medical conditions or characteristics
The exact cost of each contraceptive method in every country
The manufacturing process of hormonal contraceptives
The marketing regulations for contraceptive advertising
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use provides evidence-based guidance on the safety of using specific contraceptive methods in women with particular medical conditions or risk factors, categorizing methods from unrestricted use to contraindicated.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A woman who has just had a first-trimester spontaneous or induced abortion can generally have an intrauterine device inserted at which time, assuming no infection is present?
o: Only after waiting a minimum of 6 months
Only after her next full menstrual cycle has completed
Immediately, at the time of the procedure
Never, since IUDs are contraindicated after any pregnancy loss
Only after a subsequent successful pregnancy has been achieved and delivered
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: In the absence of infection, an intrauterine device can generally be safely inserted immediately following a first-trimester spontaneous or induced abortion, offering convenient, timely initiation of highly effective contraception.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Postpartum contraceptive counseling should address which specific consideration for a breastfeeding woman regarding hormonal methods?
o: No difference in contraceptive choice compared to non-breastfeeding women
Preference for progestin-only methods, since estrogen-containing methods may reduce milk supply
Complete avoidance of all hormonal contraceptive methods during breastfeeding
Preference for combined estrogen-progestin methods over progestin-only methods during breastfeeding
Mandatory cessation of breastfeeding before starting any contraceptive method
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Progestin-only contraceptive methods are generally preferred in breastfeeding women, since estrogen-containing combined hormonal methods may reduce milk supply, particularly if started before lactation is well established.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: A couple practicing the standard days method of fertility awareness are advised to avoid unprotected intercourse during which portion of a regular menstrual cycle?
o: Days 1 through 7 of the cycle exclusively
Days 8 through 19 of the cycle, representing the estimated fertile window
Days 20 through 28 of the cycle exclusively
The entire cycle, with no distinction between fertile and infertile days
Only day 14 of the cycle, with all other days considered safe
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: The standard days method identifies days 8 through 19 of a regular 26-32 day menstrual cycle as the estimated fertile window, advising avoidance of unprotected intercourse (or use of a barrier method) during this period to prevent pregnancy.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Male infertility due to obstructive azoospermia (normal sperm production but blocked outflow) can sometimes be managed by which approach to achieve conception?
o: Administration of clomiphene citrate to the male partner as the definitive treatment
Administration of exogenous testosterone to the male partner to improve fertility
Increasing frequency of intercourse alone, without any medical or surgical intervention
Donor oocyte in vitro fertilization, since the female partner is unaffected
Surgical sperm retrieval directly from the testis or epididymis, combined with intracytoplasmic sperm injection
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Obstructive azoospermia, where sperm production is normal but outflow is blocked, can often be managed by surgically retrieving sperm directly from the testis or epididymis, which can then be used for intracytoplasmic sperm injection during in vitro fertilization to achieve fertilization.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), a cause of male infertility, is characterized by which combination of clinical features?
o: Normal-sized testes with completely normal fertility in all cases
Female external genitalia with normal ovarian function
Isolated color blindness with no effect on fertility
Isolated tall stature with entirely normal reproductive hormone levels and fertility
Small, firm testes, azoospermia or severe oligospermia, and gynecomastia
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) classically presents with small, firm testes, azoospermia or severe oligospermia (causing infertility), gynecomastia, and often tall stature, resulting from an extra X chromosome affecting testicular development and function.

obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.s: Age-related decline in female fertility accelerates most notably beginning around which age, reflecting progressive depletion of ovarian reserve?
o: 20 years
35 years
50 years, with no earlier decline
60 years, with no earlier decline
Fertility does not decline with age until after menopause has fully occurred
obstetrics-and-gynecology/infertility-an.e: Female fertility begins a more pronounced decline around age 35, reflecting a progressive reduction in both the quantity and quality of the remaining ovarian follicular pool, accelerating further after age 40.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: The Apgar score, used to assess a newborn's condition immediately after birth, evaluates which five parameters?
o: Heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color
Birth weight, gestational age, head circumference, length, and temperature
Blood glucose, hemoglobin, bilirubin, calcium, and sodium
Blood pressure, oxygen saturation, capillary refill, urine output, and pupil response
Feeding ability, sleep pattern, cry strength, weight gain, and stool frequency
pediatrics/neonatology.e: The Apgar score assesses heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color, each scored 0-2, at 1 and 5 minutes after birth to quickly evaluate the newborn's immediate clinical status and need for resuscitation.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, common in preterm infants, results primarily from which deficiency?
o: Pulmonary surfactant deficiency
Deficiency of maternal antibodies transferred across the placenta
Deficiency of fetal hemoglobin
Deficiency of vitamin K
Deficiency of erythropoietin
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome results from insufficient pulmonary surfactant production by immature type II pneumocytes, causing alveolar collapse (atelectasis), increased work of breathing, and hypoxemia, most common in preterm infants.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Antenatal corticosteroid administration to a mother at risk of preterm delivery reduces the incidence of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome by which mechanism?
o: Directly increasing fetal hemoglobin concentration
Accelerating fetal lung maturity and surfactant production
Directly increasing fetal birth weight
Preventing preterm labor entirely in all cases
Directly treating existing neonatal jaundice
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Antenatal corticosteroids cross the placenta and accelerate fetal lung maturation by stimulating type II pneumocyte differentiation and surfactant production, significantly reducing the incidence and severity of respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Physiological neonatal jaundice, appearing after the first 24 hours of life and resolving within about 1-2 weeks, results primarily from which mechanism?
o: A structural biliary obstruction present from birth
An ABO or Rh blood group incompatibility in every case
A hereditary deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in every case
Chronic intrauterine infection in every case
Increased bilirubin production from a higher red cell turnover combined with immature hepatic conjugation
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Physiological neonatal jaundice results from a combination of increased bilirubin production (due to higher neonatal red cell mass and shorter red cell lifespan) and transient immaturity of hepatic glucuronyl transferase enzyme activity needed for bilirubin conjugation.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is considered pathological and most urgently warrants evaluation for which cause?
o: Physiological jaundice, since this is the expected timing for a benign presentation
Breast milk jaundice, since this is the expected timing for this benign condition
Hemolytic disease (e.g., Rh or ABO incompatibility)
Normal delayed bilirubin clearance with no underlying pathology
A normal variant requiring no further evaluation
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is always considered pathological and warrants urgent evaluation, most importantly to exclude hemolytic disease of the newborn (from Rh or ABO incompatibility) which can cause rapidly rising bilirubin levels and risk of kernicterus.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Kernicterus, a severe complication of untreated hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn, results from bilirubin deposition in which tissue?
o: The basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei
The renal tubules exclusively
The hepatic parenchyma exclusively
The pulmonary alveoli exclusively
The cardiac myocardium exclusively
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Kernicterus results from deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei, causing irreversible neurological damage manifesting as choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss, and other long-term neurodevelopmental sequelae.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Phototherapy, used to treat neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, works by which mechanism?
o: Directly destroying circulating red blood cells to reduce bilirubin production
Stimulating hepatic glucuronyl transferase enzyme activity directly
Binding bilirubin in the gut to prevent its absorption
Converting unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble isomers that can be excreted without hepatic conjugation
Increasing renal excretion of unconjugated bilirubin directly
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Phototherapy uses light energy to convert unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble photoisomers, which can be excreted in bile and urine without requiring hepatic conjugation, effectively lowering serum bilirubin levels.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious gastrointestinal emergency primarily affecting preterm infants, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: Painless jaundice without any abdominal symptoms
Isolated respiratory distress without any gastrointestinal symptoms
Abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, and bloody stools
Isolated poor weight gain without any acute symptoms
A completely normal abdominal examination with systemic symptoms only
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Necrotizing enterocolitis classically presents in preterm infants with abdominal distension, feeding intolerance (with bilious or bloody residuals), and bloody stools, and can progress to intestinal perforation, sepsis, and shock if not promptly recognized and treated.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Pneumatosis intestinalis, a classic radiological finding in necrotizing enterocolitis, refers to which finding on abdominal X-ray?
o: Free air under the diaphragm exclusively, without any bowel wall gas
Calcification of the bowel wall
A double bubble sign
Air-fluid levels in the stomach exclusively
Gas within the bowel wall
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Pneumatosis intestinalis refers to the presence of gas within the bowel wall itself, a classic and diagnostic radiological finding in necrotizing enterocolitis, resulting from gas-forming bacteria invading the ischemic, damaged bowel wall.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Retinopathy of prematurity, a potentially blinding condition affecting preterm infants, is most strongly associated with which risk factor?
o: Low birth weight, prematurity, and supplemental oxygen exposure
Postterm delivery as the primary risk factor
Maternal diabetes as the primary risk factor
Congenital rubella infection as the primary risk factor
Neonatal hypoglycemia as the primary and sole risk factor
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Retinopathy of prematurity results from abnormal retinal vascular development in preterm, low-birth-weight infants, with supplemental oxygen exposure being an important additional risk factor, requiring careful oxygen titration and screening ophthalmologic examinations.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Transient tachypnea of the newborn, a relatively benign cause of neonatal respiratory distress, is thought to result from which mechanism?
o: Complete absence of pulmonary surfactant, identical to respiratory distress syndrome
Aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after birth
A congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Bacterial pneumonia acquired in utero
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Transient tachypnea of the newborn results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after birth (more common after cesarean delivery without labor), causing mild to moderate respiratory distress that typically resolves within 24-72 hours.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A newborn with bilious vomiting on the first day of life should be urgently evaluated for which surgical emergency?
o: Physiological neonatal jaundice, which does not require urgent surgical evaluation
Simple breastfeeding difficulty, which does not require urgent surgical evaluation
Transient tachypnea of the newborn, which does not require urgent surgical evaluation
Uncomplicated umbilical hernia, which does not require urgent surgical evaluation
Intestinal malrotation with volvulus
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a red flag symptom requiring urgent evaluation for intestinal malrotation with midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency that can rapidly progress to bowel ischemia and necrosis if not promptly diagnosed and treated.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Neonatal sepsis with early onset (within the first 72 hours of life) is most commonly caused by which organism, particularly in the context of maternal colonization?
o: Staphylococcus epidermidis as the most common cause of early-onset sepsis
Candida albicans as the most common cause of early-onset sepsis
Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the most common cause of early-onset sepsis
Group B Streptococcus
Herpes simplex virus as the most common cause of early-onset sepsis
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Group B Streptococcus, acquired from maternal genital tract colonization during labor and delivery, is the most common cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis, which is why universal antenatal screening and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis are recommended.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia, allowing abdominal organs to herniate into the thoracic cavity, is clinically significant primarily because of its association with which complication?
o: Isolated cosmetic abdominal wall defect with no respiratory involvement
Neonatal jaundice as the primary associated complication
Congenital heart block as the primary associated complication
Pulmonary hypoplasia and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Necrotizing enterocolitis as the primary associated complication
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia allows abdominal contents to herniate into the thoracic cavity during fetal development, compressing the developing lung and resulting in pulmonary hypoplasia and often severe persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn after birth.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula, the most common type of esophageal atresia, classically presents with which finding shortly after birth?
o: Excessive salivation/drooling and choking with the first feeding attempt
Complete absence of any symptoms until several months of age
Isolated bilious vomiting with a normal ability to feed
Isolated failure to pass meconium
Isolated jaundice without any feeding difficulty
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Esophageal atresia classically presents with excessive oral secretions/drooling and choking, coughing, or cyanosis with the first feeding attempt, as the infant is unable to swallow normally due to the blind-ending esophageal pouch, often with an associated fistula to the trachea.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A newborn with an imperforate anus (anorectal malformation) requires assessment for associated anomalies, often remembered by which mnemonic?
o: TORCH infections
The 4 T's of postpartum hemorrhage
The 5 W's of postoperative fever
The 6 P's of acute limb ischemia
VACTERL association
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Anorectal malformations are associated with other congenital anomalies summarized by the VACTERL mnemonic: Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, Tracheoesophageal, Renal, and Limb abnormalities, prompting a thorough evaluation for these associated findings.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Neonatal hypoglycemia is of particular clinical concern in infants of diabetic mothers primarily due to which mechanism?
o: Complete absence of fetal insulin production in infants of diabetic mothers
Excessive fetal glucagon production causing hypoglycemia
A direct toxic effect of maternal insulin crossing the placenta
Fetal hyperinsulinemia in response to chronic maternal hyperglycemia, causing rebound hypoglycemia after birth when the maternal glucose supply is removed
Chronic fetal malnutrition from maternal diabetes
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Chronic maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperinsulinemia (pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia in response to elevated glucose), and after birth, when the maternal glucose supply is abruptly removed, the persistently elevated fetal insulin level predisposes to significant neonatal hypoglycemia.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: The umbilical cord normally contains which combination of blood vessels?
o: One umbilical artery and two umbilical veins
Two umbilical arteries and two umbilical veins
Two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein
One umbilical artery and one umbilical vein only
Three umbilical arteries and no umbilical vein
pediatrics/neonatology.e: The normal umbilical cord contains two umbilical arteries (carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta) and one umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus); a single umbilical artery can be associated with other congenital anomalies.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Congenital hypothyroidism, if undiagnosed and untreated in the newborn period, results in which serious long-term complication?
o: Irreversible intellectual disability
Isolated short stature with entirely normal cognitive development
Isolated hearing loss with entirely normal cognitive development
Isolated cardiac defects with entirely normal cognitive development
A completely reversible condition with no long-term consequence if treatment is delayed
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Undiagnosed and untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes irreversible intellectual disability due to the critical role of thyroid hormone in early brain development, which is why universal newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism is performed to allow prompt treatment.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Vitamin K is routinely administered to newborns shortly after birth primarily to prevent which condition?
o: Neonatal jaundice as the primary target condition
Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn
Neonatal hypoglycemia as the primary target condition
Retinopathy of prematurity as the primary target condition
Necrotizing enterocolitis as the primary target condition
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Newborns have low vitamin K stores and immature gut flora (which normally contribute to vitamin K synthesis), predisposing to hemorrhagic disease of the newborn; routine intramuscular vitamin K administration at birth effectively prevents this bleeding disorder.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A cephalohematoma, a birth-related scalp finding, is distinguished from caput succedaneum by which characteristic feature?
o: It is confined within the boundaries of a single cranial bone (does not cross suture lines)
It crosses suture lines freely, unlike caput succedaneum
It is present at birth and resolves within the first 48 hours, unlike caput succedaneum
It always requires immediate surgical drainage
It is caused exclusively by forceps delivery, never by vacuum extraction
pediatrics/neonatology.e: A cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal hemorrhage confined within the boundaries of a single cranial bone (not crossing suture lines) that typically develops after birth and resolves over weeks, in contrast to caput succedaneum, which is a diffuse, poorly demarcated soft tissue swelling that crosses suture lines and is present at birth.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn is characterized by which underlying pathophysiological abnormality?
o: Failure of the normal postnatal decline in pulmonary vascular resistance, causing right-to-left shunting and hypoxemia
A structural cardiac septal defect as the sole cause in all cases
Complete absence of pulmonary vasculature
A primary disorder of the systemic (rather than pulmonary) circulation
An isolated coagulation disorder unrelated to pulmonary vascular tone
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn results from failure of the normal decline in pulmonary vascular resistance after birth, causing right-to-left shunting through the ductus arteriosus and/or foramen ovale, leading to severe hypoxemia refractory to standard oxygen therapy.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Neonatal abstinence syndrome, seen in infants born to mothers using certain substances during pregnancy, most classically results from maternal use of which class of substances?
o: Vitamin supplements taken in standard recommended doses
Folic acid supplementation
Opioids
Iron supplementation
Calcium supplementation
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Neonatal abstinence syndrome most classically results from maternal opioid use during pregnancy, causing a withdrawal syndrome in the newborn manifesting as irritability, tremors, poor feeding, and autonomic instability after birth.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A newborn who fails to breathe spontaneously and effectively at birth should first receive which initial resuscitative step, per standard neonatal resuscitation protocols?
o: Drying, warming, and stimulation, followed by positive pressure ventilation if apnea or gasping persists
Immediate chest compressions as the first step regardless of respiratory effort
Immediate intubation as the first step in every non-vigorous newborn
Immediate administration of epinephrine as the first step
Immediate umbilical vein catheterization as the first step
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Initial newborn resuscitation begins with drying, warming, and tactile stimulation; if the infant remains apneic or is gasping despite these initial steps, positive pressure ventilation is promptly initiated, following the stepwise approach of the Neonatal Resuscitation Program algorithm.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: The most important and effective initial intervention in neonatal resuscitation for a newborn with poor respiratory effort and low heart rate is which of the following?
o: Chest compressions started before any attempt at ventilation
Effective positive pressure ventilation
Immediate administration of intravenous fluids
Immediate administration of naloxone in every case
Immediate surfactant administration in every case regardless of gestational age
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Effective positive pressure ventilation is considered the single most important and effective intervention in neonatal resuscitation, as most newborns requiring resuscitation respond to adequate lung inflation and ventilation alone, without needing chest compressions or medications.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection, when symptomatic at birth, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: Isolated cataracts with entirely normal systemic examination
Petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and microcephaly
Isolated cardiac defects with entirely normal neurological examination
Bilateral parotid swelling with entirely normal systemic examination
Isolated limb reduction defects with entirely normal systemic examination
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection classically presents with a combination of findings including petechiae (from thrombocytopenia), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and microcephaly, along with the risk of long-term sensorineural hearing loss.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Meconium, the first stool passed by a newborn, is normally passed within which time frame after birth in a healthy term infant?
o: Within the first 5 minutes of life in every healthy infant
Not until 1 week of age in every healthy infant
Within the first 24-48 hours of life
Not until 1 month of age in every healthy infant
Meconium passage timing has no clinical significance
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Meconium is normally passed within the first 24-48 hours of life in a healthy term infant; delayed passage beyond this window warrants evaluation for underlying conditions such as Hirschsprung's disease, meconium plug syndrome, or cystic fibrosis.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Neonatal hypoglycemia is generally defined and managed based on which combination of factors?
o: Blood glucose level alone, regardless of any clinical symptoms
The infant's birth weight alone, regardless of blood glucose level
The mode of delivery alone, regardless of blood glucose level
Maternal blood glucose level alone, without measuring the infant's glucose
Blood glucose level combined with the presence or absence of clinical symptoms and risk factors
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Neonatal hypoglycemia management is generally guided by a combination of the measured blood glucose level, the presence or absence of clinical symptoms (jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures), and underlying risk factors (e.g., infant of a diabetic mother, prematurity, growth restriction), rather than a single glucose threshold applied uniformly.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Late-onset neonatal sepsis (occurring after 72 hours of life) is more commonly associated with which source of infection compared to early-onset sepsis?
o: Exclusively vertical transmission from maternal genital tract colonization
Exclusively transplacental viral transmission
Exclusively foodborne transmission from contaminated formula
Exclusively airborne transmission from other infants in the nursery
Nosocomial or environmental sources, including central line-associated infections in hospitalized infants
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Late-onset neonatal sepsis (after 72 hours of life) is more commonly associated with nosocomial or environmental sources of infection, including central line-associated bloodstream infections in hospitalized (particularly preterm) infants, in contrast to early-onset sepsis, which is typically acquired from maternal vertical transmission.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A preterm infant is at increased risk of intraventricular hemorrhage primarily due to which anatomical vulnerability?
o: A structurally mature and robust cerebral vasculature identical to a term infant
The fragile, immature germinal matrix vasculature adjacent to the lateral ventricles
Complete absence of any cerebral vasculature until term gestation
An overly thick, protective skull that paradoxically increases hemorrhage risk
A fully myelinated central nervous system that predisposes to bleeding
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Preterm infants have a fragile, immature germinal matrix vasculature located adjacent to the lateral ventricles that is particularly susceptible to rupture with fluctuations in cerebral blood flow or pressure, predisposing to intraventricular hemorrhage, with risk decreasing as this structure involutes with advancing gestational age.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Which screening test is universally recommended shortly after birth to detect congenital hearing loss?
o: A formal audiogram requiring active patient cooperation
Tympanometry alone, without any otoacoustic emissions or brainstem response testing
A simple clinical assessment of the infant's startle response to loud noise
Genetic testing for all known deafness-associated genes in every newborn
Otoacoustic emissions testing or automated auditory brainstem response testing
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Universal newborn hearing screening is typically performed using otoacoustic emissions testing or automated auditory brainstem response testing, both of which can be performed shortly after birth without requiring active infant cooperation, allowing early identification and intervention for congenital hearing loss.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A newborn found to have ambiguous genitalia should be urgently evaluated to exclude which potentially life-threatening endocrine condition, particularly the salt-wasting form?
o: Simple isolated hypospadias, which is not life-threatening
Physiological neonatal jaundice, which is not related to genital ambiguity
Isolated undescended testis, which is not life-threatening
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Transient tachypnea of the newborn, which is unrelated to genital findings
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn warrants urgent evaluation to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia (particularly 21-hydroxylase deficiency), as the salt-wasting form can cause a life-threatening adrenal crisis with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemic shock if not promptly recognized and treated.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Erb's palsy, a brachial plexus injury sometimes associated with difficult vaginal delivery (e.g., with shoulder dystocia), classically affects which nerve roots and produces which characteristic arm posture?
o: Lower trunk (C8-T1) injury, producing a claw hand deformity
Complete brachial plexus injury with a flail, areflexic arm
Isolated radial nerve injury with wrist drop
Isolated median nerve injury with thenar wasting
Upper trunk (C5-C6) injury, producing a 'waiter's tip' posture with the arm adducted, internally rotated, and the wrist flexed
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Erb's palsy results from injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6 nerve roots), classically producing a characteristic 'waiter's tip' posture with the arm hanging adducted and internally rotated, the elbow extended, and the wrist and fingers flexed, often associated with shoulder dystocia during delivery.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A newborn with polyhydramnios detected antenatally should be evaluated postnatally for which condition affecting normal swallowing of amniotic fluid?
o: Isolated hip dysplasia, which is unrelated to amniotic fluid volume
Isolated clubfoot, which is unrelated to amniotic fluid volume
Physiological neonatal jaundice, which is unrelated to amniotic fluid volume
Esophageal or duodenal atresia
Isolated umbilical hernia, which is unrelated to amniotic fluid volume
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Polyhydramnios can result from fetal conditions impairing normal swallowing of amniotic fluid, such as esophageal or duodenal atresia, warranting postnatal evaluation (and often a failed attempt to pass a nasogastric tube, or feeding assessment) to exclude these conditions.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: The Ballard score (or New Ballard Score) is a clinical tool used in newborns primarily to estimate which parameter?
o: The severity of neonatal jaundice
Gestational age, based on physical and neuromuscular maturity assessment
The severity of respiratory distress
The risk of neonatal sepsis
The presence of congenital heart disease
pediatrics/neonatology.e: The Ballard score (New Ballard Score) estimates gestational age based on a combination of physical maturity characteristics (e.g., skin texture, lanugo, ear cartilage) and neuromuscular maturity signs (e.g., posture, joint flexibility), particularly useful when accurate menstrual dating is unavailable.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) occurring within the first few days of life should raise particular concern for infection with which organism, given its potential for rapid, severe corneal damage?
o: Staphylococcus epidermidis, given its typically benign course in this context
Candida albicans, given its typically benign course in this context
Herpes simplex virus exclusively, with no concern for bacterial causes
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Respiratory syncytial virus, which does not classically cause conjunctivitis
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Neonatal conjunctivitis presenting very early (often within the first few days of life) should raise particular concern for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection (acquired during vaginal delivery from an infected mother), given its potential to cause rapid, severe corneal ulceration and perforation if not promptly treated.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A preterm infant is at increased risk of anemia of prematurity due to which combination of factors?
o: Excessive erythropoietin production causing polycythemia instead of anemia
A prolonged red cell lifespan compared to term infants
Complete absence of any iatrogenic blood loss in preterm infants
Reduced erythropoietin production, shortened red cell lifespan, and frequent blood sampling for laboratory testing
An entirely normal erythropoietic response identical to term infants
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Anemia of prematurity results from a combination of relatively reduced erythropoietin production in response to anemia (compared to older individuals), a shortened neonatal red cell lifespan, and iatrogenic blood loss from frequent laboratory blood sampling in the neonatal intensive care setting.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic lung disease of prematurity, is most strongly associated with which combination of risk factors?
o: Postterm delivery with entirely normal lung development
Extreme prematurity, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and oxygen toxicity
Maternal diabetes as the primary and sole risk factor
A single, brief exposure to room air oxygen at birth
Congenital heart disease as the primary and sole risk factor, unrelated to prematurity
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia results from a combination of extreme prematurity (with immature lung development), prolonged mechanical ventilation, and oxygen toxicity, causing chronic lung injury and abnormal lung development in affected preterm infants.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: A term infant with excessive lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia, and a bulging fontanelle should be urgently evaluated for which serious condition?
o: Simple physiological jaundice, which does not cause these systemic findings
Uncomplicated breastfeeding difficulty, which does not cause these systemic findings
Transient tachypnea of the newborn, which does not typically cause these findings
A benign cephalohematoma, which does not cause these systemic findings
Neonatal meningitis/sepsis
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia (or fever), and a bulging fontanelle in a neonate are concerning signs for neonatal sepsis or meningitis, requiring urgent evaluation (including blood cultures and often lumbar puncture) and empiric antibiotic treatment given the nonspecific and often subtle presentation of serious neonatal infection.

pediatrics/neonatology.s: Small for gestational age infants, particularly those with asymmetric growth restriction, are at increased risk of which metabolic complication in the immediate newborn period?
o: Hyperglycemia as the primary and most common metabolic risk
Hypercalcemia as the primary metabolic risk
Hyponatremia as the primary and most common metabolic risk
No increased metabolic risk compared to appropriately grown infants
Hypoglycemia
pediatrics/neonatology.e: Small for gestational age infants have reduced glycogen stores and impaired gluconeogenesis, placing them at increased risk of neonatal hypoglycemia, requiring close monitoring of blood glucose levels after birth.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended by the World Health Organization for approximately how long after birth?
o: The first 2 weeks of life only
The first 6 months of life
The first 24 months of life exclusively, with no other food introduced until then
The first month of life only
Exclusive breastfeeding is not recommended at any stage
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding (with no other food or liquids, aside from medically indicated supplements) for the first 6 months of life, with continued breastfeeding alongside appropriate complementary foods thereafter.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A social smile, an important developmental milestone, is typically expected to appear by which age?
o: Birth (present from the first day of life)
6-8 months
12 months
18 months
6-8 weeks
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: A social smile, in which an infant smiles responsively in reaction to social interaction (rather than a reflexive smile), typically emerges by approximately 6-8 weeks of age, serving as an important early developmental milestone.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: An infant is typically expected to achieve independent sitting without support by which age?
o: 1 month
12 months
6 months
18 months
24 months
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Independent sitting without support is typically achieved by approximately 6 months of age, reflecting adequate trunk control and postural development, and is an important gross motor milestone.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: The pincer grasp, allowing an infant to pick up small objects using the thumb and index finger, typically develops by which age?
o: 9-10 months
1-2 months
18-24 months
3 years
5 years
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The mature pincer grasp, using the thumb and index finger to pick up small objects, typically develops by around 9-10 months of age, representing an important fine motor milestone.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist even when out of sight, typically develops by which age according to Piaget's stages of cognitive development?
o: Approximately 8-9 months
Birth, as an innate ability present from day one
5 years, not developing until early childhood
12 years, not developing until adolescence
Object permanence never fully develops in typically developing children
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Object permanence, a key milestone in Piaget's sensorimotor stage of cognitive development, typically emerges around 8-9 months of age, allowing an infant to understand that an object continues to exist even when it is no longer visible.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A single word with meaning (beyond simple babbling) is typically expected to be spoken by an infant at approximately which age?
o: 3 months
6 months
12 months
24 months
4 years
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The first meaningful single word is typically spoken by approximately 12 months of age, marking an important early language milestone, followed by rapid vocabulary expansion over the subsequent months and years.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A two-word phrase (e.g., 'more milk') is typically expected to be used by a child at approximately which age?
o: 6 months
9 months
18-24 months
4 years
6 years
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The combination of two words into a simple phrase typically emerges between 18 and 24 months of age, reflecting an important stage of expressive language development.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Failure to thrive in infants and young children is generally defined by which finding on growth monitoring?
o: A single weight measurement below the 50th percentile at any one visit
Height alone falling below the 10th percentile with normal weight gain
Head circumference alone falling below the 3rd percentile with normal weight and height gain
Any weight measurement, regardless of trend, that is below the 99th percentile
Weight (or weight-for-length) persistently falling below expected percentiles or crossing down through percentile lines over time
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Failure to thrive is generally identified by weight (or weight-for-length/BMI) persistently below expected percentiles for age, or a significant downward crossing of percentile lines over serial measurements, indicating inadequate growth requiring evaluation.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Marasmus, a form of severe protein-energy malnutrition, is characterized by which clinical feature, distinguishing it from kwashiorkor?
o: Prominent bilateral pitting edema as the defining feature
A distended abdomen with fatty liver as the defining feature
Sparse, depigmented hair as the sole defining feature
Skin desquamation ('flaky paint' dermatosis) as the defining feature
Severe wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat with a general absence of edema
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Marasmus results from severe overall caloric (and protein) deficiency, causing severe wasting of muscle mass and subcutaneous fat with a generally emaciated appearance and notable absence of edema, distinguishing it from kwashiorkor, which is characterized by prominent edema despite relatively preserved fat stores.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Kwashiorkor, a form of severe malnutrition resulting predominantly from protein deficiency (with relatively preserved caloric intake), classically presents with which finding?
o: Severe generalized wasting with no edema, identical to marasmus
Bilateral pitting edema, a distended abdomen, and skin/hair changes
Isolated short stature with entirely normal body composition
Isolated vitamin C deficiency with scurvy as the primary finding
Isolated vitamin D deficiency with rickets as the primary finding
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Kwashiorkor classically presents with bilateral pitting edema (from hypoalbuminemia), a distended abdomen (from hepatomegaly with fatty infiltration), and characteristic skin and hair changes (depigmentation, thinning), resulting predominantly from severe protein deficiency.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Rickets, a disorder of defective bone mineralization in growing children, is most commonly caused by which deficiency?
o: Vitamin D deficiency
Vitamin A deficiency as the most common cause of rickets
Vitamin C deficiency as the most common cause of rickets
Vitamin B12 deficiency as the most common cause of rickets
Vitamin K deficiency as the most common cause of rickets
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Rickets most commonly results from vitamin D deficiency (or, less commonly, calcium or phosphate deficiency/abnormal metabolism), impairing normal mineralization of the growing skeleton and causing characteristic skeletal deformities.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Which clinical sign is classically associated with rickets, resulting from costochondral junction widening?
o: Koplik spots
Chvostek's sign
Harrison's groove as the sole classic sign, without any costochondral finding
Steeple sign
Rachitic rosary
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The rachitic rosary refers to palpable, beaded enlargement of the costochondral junctions along the anterior chest wall, a classic clinical sign of rickets resulting from disorganized cartilage growth at these sites due to defective mineralization.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Scurvy, resulting from vitamin C deficiency, is characterized by which clinical finding in children?
o: Gum bleeding, poor wound healing, and subperiosteal hemorrhage causing bone pain
Bilateral pitting edema as the primary finding
Night blindness as the primary and defining finding
Rachitic rosary as the primary and defining finding
Goiter as the primary and defining finding
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency impairing collagen synthesis, causing gum bleeding, poor wound healing, and subperiosteal hemorrhages that cause bone pain and tenderness, particularly in growing children.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Vitamin A deficiency, a significant cause of preventable blindness in children in some regions, classically causes which ocular finding?
o: Cataracts as the classic and defining ocular finding
Retinoblastoma as a direct consequence of the deficiency
Night blindness and xerophthalmia (including Bitot's spots)
Glaucoma as the classic and defining ocular finding
Strabismus as the classic and defining ocular finding
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Vitamin A deficiency classically causes night blindness (impaired dark adaptation) and xerophthalmia, including characteristic Bitot's spots (foamy, triangular conjunctival lesions), and can progress to corneal ulceration and permanent blindness if untreated.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: The WHO growth charts and standards for assessing childhood growth are primarily plotted against which parameter on the horizontal axis?
o: Birth weight exclusively, regardless of current age
Maternal height exclusively
Head circumference exclusively, regardless of age
Gestational age at birth exclusively, regardless of current age
Age
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Standard growth charts plot parameters such as weight, height/length, and head circumference against the child's chronological age, allowing comparison to population-based percentile curves to assess whether growth is appropriate.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by which core combination of features?
o: Isolated hyperactivity and impulsivity with normal social communication
Isolated language delay with entirely normal social interaction and behavior
Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, along with restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior or interests
Isolated motor clumsiness with entirely normal social and communication skills
Isolated academic underachievement with entirely normal social and behavioral function
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, combined with restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, with onset in the early developmental period.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is characterized by a persistent pattern of which core symptoms?
o: Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development
Isolated deficits in social communication with no attentional or behavioral component
Isolated motor tics with no attentional component
Isolated speech delay with no attentional or behavioral component
Isolated intellectual disability with no attentional or behavioral component
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that is inconsistent with developmental level and interferes significantly with social, academic, or occupational functioning.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Global developmental delay in a young child refers to which clinical presentation?
o: Delay limited exclusively to gross motor skills, with all other domains normal
Delay limited exclusively to speech and language, with all other domains normal
A term used only for delays first identified after age 10
A term reserved exclusively for children with a confirmed genetic diagnosis
Significant delay in two or more developmental domains (e.g., gross/fine motor, speech/language, cognition, social/personal)
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Global developmental delay refers to significant delay across two or more developmental domains (such as gross/fine motor skills, speech/language, cognitive skills, and social/personal skills) in a young child, warranting comprehensive evaluation for an underlying cause.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Exclusive formula feeding, as an alternative to breastfeeding, still requires supplementation with which vitamin in many recommendations, similarly to breastfed infants?
o: Vitamin D
Vitamin C, since formula is presumed deficient in this vitamin
Vitamin K administered daily throughout infancy, distinct from the single birth dose
Vitamin B12 in all formula-fed infants regardless of maternal status
Vitamin A in all formula-fed infants regardless of dietary intake
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Vitamin D supplementation is often recommended for infants, whether breastfed or formula-fed (particularly if formula intake is below a certain volume), to prevent vitamin D deficiency and rickets, since adequate sun exposure alone is often insufficient in infancy.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Introduction of complementary (solid) foods in an infant's diet is generally recommended to begin at approximately which age?
o: Immediately after birth
Not until 12 months of age at the earliest
Not until 24 months of age at the earliest
Complementary foods should never be introduced before school age
Around 6 months of age
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Complementary (solid) foods are generally recommended to be introduced at around 6 months of age, alongside continued breastfeeding or formula feeding, as breast milk or formula alone becomes insufficient to meet the growing infant's nutritional needs beyond this point.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: The Denver Developmental Screening Test is used clinically for which purpose?
o: Diagnosing specific genetic syndromes definitively
Screening for developmental delay across gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social domains
Measuring precise IQ scores in school-age children
Screening exclusively for hearing impairment
Screening exclusively for visual impairment
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The Denver Developmental Screening Test is a screening tool (not a diagnostic test) used to identify children who may have developmental delays across gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social domains, prompting further diagnostic evaluation if abnormal.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Walking independently is typically expected to be achieved by a child at approximately which age?
o: 3-4 months
6 months
3 years
5 years
12-15 months
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Independent walking is typically achieved by approximately 12-15 months of age, representing an important gross motor milestone, with a wide range of normal variation extending up to about 18 months.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A child is typically expected to be able to build a tower of 2-4 cubes at approximately which age?
o: 3 months
18 months
6 months
4 years
6 years
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Building a tower of 2-4 cubes is a fine motor milestone typically achieved by approximately 18 months of age, reflecting developing hand-eye coordination and manipulation skills.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A child is typically expected to be able to ride a tricycle at approximately which age?
o: 3 years
6 months
1 year
6 years
10 years
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Riding a tricycle is a gross motor milestone typically achieved by approximately 3 years of age, reflecting developing balance, coordination, and lower limb strength.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Stranger anxiety, a normal developmental phenomenon in infants, typically emerges at approximately which age?
o: Birth, present from the first days of life
3 years, not emerging until early childhood
6 years, not emerging until school age
6-9 months
Stranger anxiety is not a recognized normal developmental phenomenon
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Stranger anxiety, in which an infant shows wariness or distress in the presence of unfamiliar people, typically emerges at approximately 6-9 months of age, reflecting cognitive development including the ability to distinguish familiar from unfamiliar faces.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Separation anxiety in toddlers typically peaks at approximately which age before gradually diminishing?
o: At birth, with no later peak
Around 12-18 months
Around 8-10 years of age
Around 15 years of age
Separation anxiety does not have a typical age of peak intensity
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Separation anxiety, distress upon separation from a primary caregiver, typically peaks around 12-18 months of age and gradually diminishes as the child develops a more secure understanding of object permanence and caregiver constancy.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Nutritional rehabilitation in a child with severe acute malnutrition must proceed cautiously in the initial phase primarily to avoid which serious complication?
o: Refeeding syndrome
Immediate cardiac arrest from excessive fluid restriction
Acute appendicitis triggered by feeding
Immediate hepatic failure from underfeeding
Immediate renal failure from excessive protein restriction
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Nutritional rehabilitation in severely malnourished children must proceed cautiously, particularly in the initial phase, to avoid refeeding syndrome, in which reintroduction of nutrition causes dangerous intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Iron deficiency anemia in toddlers is most commonly caused by which dietary factor?
o: Excessive intake of iron-fortified infant cereal
Excessive intake of red meat
Excessive breastfeeding beyond 6 months of age
Excessive cow's milk intake displacing iron-rich foods and impairing iron absorption
Excessive intake of vitamin C-rich fruits
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Iron deficiency anemia in toddlers is commonly caused by excessive cow's milk intake, which displaces iron-rich foods from the diet and can also cause occult gastrointestinal blood loss, contributing to iron deficiency.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Which nutrient deficiency is classically associated with the neurological condition beriberi, seen in severely malnourished or alcohol-dependent populations?
o: Vitamin C deficiency, which classically causes scurvy instead
Vitamin A deficiency, which classically causes night blindness instead
Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency, which classically causes rickets instead
Vitamin K deficiency, which classically causes bleeding disorders instead
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Beriberi results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, causing either a predominantly neurological (dry beriberi, with peripheral neuropathy) or cardiovascular (wet beriberi, with high-output heart failure) presentation, seen in severely malnourished individuals.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Exclusively breastfed infants of strictly vegan mothers are at particular risk for deficiency of which vitamin, since it is found almost exclusively in animal products?
o: Vitamin C, which is abundant in many plant sources
Vitamin A, which is abundant in many plant sources (as provitamin A carotenoids)
Folate, which is abundant in many plant sources
Vitamin E, which is abundant in many plant sources
Vitamin B12
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Vitamin B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products, so exclusively breastfed infants of strictly vegan mothers (without vitamin B12 supplementation) are at particular risk of vitamin B12 deficiency, which can cause serious neurological and hematological consequences in infancy.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A 2-year-old child who is not yet speaking any words and shows limited social interaction should be evaluated for which combination of possible underlying conditions?
o: Hearing impairment, autism spectrum disorder, and global developmental delay, among other causes
Normal variation only, since language delay at this age never warrants evaluation
Isolated vitamin D deficiency as the sole cause requiring consideration
Isolated iron deficiency anemia as the sole cause requiring consideration
Isolated constipation as the sole cause requiring consideration
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Absence of any words and limited social interaction by 2 years of age warrants prompt evaluation for hearing impairment, autism spectrum disorder, global developmental delay, and other causes of language delay, since early identification allows for timely intervention.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Height velocity (growth rate) in a healthy child follows which general overall pattern from infancy through puberty?
o: A constant, unchanging growth rate from birth through the end of puberty
Rapid growth in infancy, a slower steady rate through mid-childhood, followed by a pubertal growth spurt
The fastest growth rate of the entire childhood occurring during mid-childhood (ages 6-10) rather than infancy or puberty
Growth rate that steadily declines from birth with no later increase at puberty
No predictable pattern, since growth velocity is entirely random in healthy children
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Normal childhood growth follows a characteristic pattern: rapid growth velocity in infancy, a slower and relatively steady growth rate through mid-childhood, and then an accelerated pubertal growth spurt before growth plates fuse and linear growth ceases.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Constitutional growth delay, a common cause of short stature in childhood, is characterized by which pattern?
o: A bone age that is markedly advanced compared to chronological age
Delayed bone age consistent with height age, with normal growth velocity and eventual normal adult height, often with a family history of 'late bloomers'
Growth failure with normal bone age, requiring endocrine evaluation
A permanently reduced adult height compared to genetic potential
An underlying chromosomal abnormality in the majority of cases
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Constitutional growth delay is characterized by delayed bone age consistent with the child's height age, normal growth velocity, delayed puberty, and eventual attainment of a normal adult height, often with a family history of similarly delayed growth and puberty ('late bloomers').

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Precocious puberty in girls is generally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before which age?
o: 2 years
12 years, the average age of normal onset
16 years
8 years
18 years
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Precocious puberty in girls is generally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics (e.g., breast development) before 8 years of age, warranting evaluation to distinguish central (gonadotropin-dependent) from peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) causes.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A 'red flag' developmental finding, such as persistent primitive reflexes beyond the expected age or hand preference (dominance) before 12 months, may indicate which underlying concern?
o: A normal developmental variant requiring no further evaluation in any case
A dietary deficiency that resolves entirely with vitamin supplementation alone
A normal sign of advanced intelligence requiring no further evaluation
An entirely benign finding related only to handedness with no other significance
An underlying motor or neurological abnormality requiring further evaluation
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Persistence of primitive reflexes beyond their expected age of disappearance, or early hand preference before 12 months (which may indicate weakness on the non-preferred side), are considered developmental red flags warranting further neurological evaluation.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Childhood obesity is most reliably assessed using which growth parameter, plotted against age- and sex-specific reference charts?
o: Head circumference percentile, which does not reflect body weight status
Body mass index (BMI) percentile
Mid-upper arm circumference exclusively, without any other growth parameter
Waist circumference alone, without any height or weight measurement
Skinfold thickness alone, without any BMI calculation
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Childhood obesity is most reliably assessed using body mass index (BMI) percentile, calculated from height and weight and plotted against age- and sex-specific reference charts, since normal BMI values change substantially with age during childhood.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Early introduction of potentially allergenic foods (e.g., peanut products) in infancy, based on current evidence and guidance, is now generally recommended for which reason?
o: It has been shown to have no effect whatsoever on the development of food allergy
It may help reduce the risk of developing food allergy in high-risk infants when introduced appropriately
It should always be delayed until after 3 years of age to prevent allergy
It should always be avoided entirely throughout childhood to prevent allergy
It is recommended only for infants with no risk factors for allergy, and contraindicated in high-risk infants
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Current evidence has shifted guidance toward earlier (rather than delayed) introduction of potentially allergenic foods such as peanut products in infancy, which may help reduce the risk of developing food allergy, particularly in infants at higher risk (e.g., those with eczema).

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A 2-month-old infant demonstrating good head control while briefly held in a sitting position, but with persistent head lag when pulled to sit from lying down, most likely reflects which developmental stage?
o: A definite sign of severe global developmental delay requiring immediate genetic testing
A definite sign of cerebral palsy requiring immediate intervention
A normal finding with no expected further improvement over time
Normal developmental progression, since full head control while being pulled to sit is not expected until approximately 4-6 months
An abnormal finding requiring immediate neuroimaging in all cases
