pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: At 2 months of age, some head control emerging while held upright is appropriate, but persistent significant head lag when pulled to sit from a lying position is a normal finding at this age, since full head control during this maneuver is not typically expected until approximately 4-6 months.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: Toilet training readiness in toddlers is generally assessed based on which combination of factors, rather than a fixed chronological age alone?
o: The child's physical, cognitive, and behavioral readiness signs, such as bladder awareness and ability to follow simple instructions
The child's exact chronological age alone, with training beginning precisely at 18 months for every child
The parents' preference alone, regardless of the child's developmental readiness
The child's birth weight, regardless of current developmental status
The child's head circumference percentile, regardless of behavioral readiness signs
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: Toilet training readiness is generally assessed based on a combination of physical, cognitive, and behavioral readiness signs (such as awareness of a full bladder, ability to communicate the need to void, and ability to follow simple instructions) rather than a fixed chronological age, since readiness varies among individual children.

pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.s: A child demonstrating the ability to copy a circle but not yet a square or triangle on drawing tasks is most consistent with which approximate age range?
o: Around 6 months of age
Around 10 years of age
Around 3 years of age
Around 18 months of age
Around 15 years of age
pediatrics/growth-development-and-nutrit.e: The ability to copy a circle typically emerges around 3 years of age, preceding the ability to copy more complex shapes such as a square (around 4 years) or a triangle (around 5 years), reflecting progressive fine motor and visuospatial development.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Measles (rubeola) classically presents with a prodrome of fever and the '3 C's' (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), along with which pathognomonic oral finding preceding the rash?
o: Koplik spots
Strawberry tongue as the pathognomonic finding
Oral thrush as the pathognomonic finding
Herpangina-type vesicles as the pathognomonic finding
Aphthous ulcers as the pathognomonic finding
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Koplik spots, small white/gray lesions with a red halo on the buccal mucosa, are pathognomonic for measles and classically appear 1-2 days before the onset of the characteristic maculopapular rash.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: The rash of measles classically follows which pattern of spread?
o: A caudocephalic spread, beginning on the feet and progressing upward
A rash confined exclusively to the palms and soles
A rash that appears simultaneously and uniformly over the entire body
A rash confined exclusively to the trunk with sparing of the face and extremities
A cephalocaudal spread, beginning on the face/hairline and progressing downward to the trunk and extremities
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: The measles rash classically follows a cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) pattern of spread, beginning at the hairline and face and progressively spreading downward to involve the trunk and extremities over several days.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Rubella (German measles) infection during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, is of major clinical concern primarily because of which risk?
o: Severe maternal complications, which are more concerning than any fetal risk
No fetal risk at all, since rubella is a mild childhood illness
Congenital rubella syndrome in the fetus
An increased risk of maternal malignancy later in life
An increased risk of preterm labor as the primary concern, with no fetal anomaly risk
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: While rubella is typically a mild illness in children, maternal infection during pregnancy (especially the first trimester) carries a significant risk of congenital rubella syndrome, causing serious fetal anomalies including cardiac defects, cataracts, and deafness.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Mumps classically presents with which clinical finding, resulting from viral infection of the salivary glands?
o: A generalized vesicular rash as the primary presenting feature
Bilateral (or unilateral) parotid gland swelling and tenderness
Severe pharyngeal exudate with a strawberry tongue as the primary presenting feature
Bilateral conjunctivitis as the primary presenting feature
A petechial rash as the primary presenting feature
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Mumps classically causes painful swelling and tenderness of the parotid gland(s) (parotitis), often bilateral though sometimes asymmetric, resulting from viral infection and inflammation of the salivary glands.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Varicella (chickenpox) classically presents with skin lesions described as appearing in which characteristic pattern?
o: Lesions that are all in the exact same stage of development at any given time
A rash confined exclusively to the palms and soles
Lesions in different stages of evolution simultaneously ('crops' of macules, papules, vesicles, and crusted lesions)
A single, isolated lesion without any spread
A rash appearing only after fever has completely resolved
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Varicella (chickenpox) classically presents with skin lesions in different stages of evolution simultaneously present on the body (macules, papules, vesicles, and crusted lesions all visible at once), described as a 'crops' pattern, distinguishing it from more synchronous rash presentations.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Herpes zoster (shingles) in a child or adult results from which underlying process?
o: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from a dorsal root ganglion
A new, primary varicella-zoster virus infection
Reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus
A bacterial superinfection of a healed varicella lesion
An entirely unrelated viral infection with no connection to prior varicella
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus, which persists in a dormant state within dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia after primary varicella infection, causing a characteristic dermatomal vesicular rash upon reactivation.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), caused by parvovirus B19, classically presents with which characteristic facial finding?
o: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
Bilateral parotid gland swelling
A 'slapped cheek' appearance of bright red facial erythema
Circumoral pallor with a diffuse sandpaper rash
Vesicular lesions confined to the palms and soles
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Erythema infectiosum, caused by parvovirus B19, classically presents with a bright red 'slapped cheek' facial rash, often followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the trunk and extremities.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy is of particular concern due to its association with which fetal complication?
o: Congenital cataracts as the primary fetal risk
Congenital heart block as the primary and sole fetal risk
Neural tube defects as the primary fetal risk
Congenital limb reduction defects as the primary fetal risk
Fetal anemia and hydrops fetalis
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy can cause severe fetal anemia (from viral suppression of erythroid precursors) and consequent hydrops fetalis, requiring close fetal monitoring and, in severe cases, intrauterine transfusion.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Roseola infantum (sixth disease), typically affecting infants and young children, is characterized by which classic clinical sequence?
o: Several days of high fever followed by the abrupt appearance of a rash as the fever resolves
A rash that appears before the onset of any fever
Fever and rash appearing simultaneously and persisting together for over a week
A chronic, low-grade fever lasting several weeks with no rash
A vesicular rash appearing before any fever develops
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Roseola infantum classically presents with several days of high fever in an otherwise well-appearing infant, followed by the abrupt defervescence and appearance of a diffuse maculopapular rash, typically caused by human herpesvirus 6.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Scarlet fever, caused by group A Streptococcus, classically presents with which type of rash?
o: A diffuse, finely papular ('sandpaper') erythematous rash with circumoral pallor
A vesicular rash in different stages of evolution
A rash confined exclusively to the palms and soles
A target-shaped (erythema multiforme-like) rash as the classic presentation
A petechial rash confined exclusively to the lower extremities
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Scarlet fever presents with a diffuse, finely papular erythematous rash with a characteristic 'sandpaper' texture, often accompanied by circumoral pallor and a 'strawberry tongue,' resulting from an exotoxin-producing strain of group A Streptococcus.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Hand, foot, and mouth disease, commonly caused by coxsackievirus, classically presents with vesicular lesions in which distribution?
o: Exclusively the trunk, with sparing of the extremities and mouth
Exclusively the scalp, with sparing of all other areas
Exclusively the perianal region, with sparing of all other areas
A single dermatomal distribution
The palms, soles, and oral mucosa
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Hand, foot, and mouth disease classically presents with vesicular or ulcerative lesions distributed over the palms, soles, and oral mucosa, along with mild systemic symptoms, most commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Pertussis (whooping cough) is characterized by paroxysms of severe coughing followed by which classic finding?
o: A completely silent inspiration with no sound at all
Immediate resolution of all symptoms after a single coughing episode
A high-pitched inspiratory 'whoop' as air is rapidly inhaled after a coughing fit
A vesicular rash appearing simultaneously with the cough
Bilateral parotid gland swelling accompanying the cough
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Pertussis classically causes paroxysmal coughing fits followed by a characteristic high-pitched inspiratory 'whoop' as the child rapidly inhales air after the coughing paroxysm, though this whoop may be less prominent or absent in very young infants.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: A barking, seal-like cough with inspiratory stridor, often worse at night
A high fever with drooling and inability to swallow (suggesting epiglottitis instead)
A productive cough with purulent sputum and lobar consolidation on chest X-ray
Bilateral wheeze with a prolonged expiratory phase, typical of bronchiolitis instead
Isolated hoarseness without any cough or stridor
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Croup classically presents with a distinctive barking, seal-like cough accompanied by inspiratory stridor, often worse at night, resulting from subglottic airway inflammation and narrowing, typically caused by parainfluenza virus.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Epiglottitis, a life-threatening pediatric airway emergency, classically presents with which combination of findings, in contrast to croup?
o: A gradual, barking cough developing over several days with low-grade fever
High fever, drooling, and a muffled 'hot potato' voice with rapid symptom progression
A chronic, indolent cough persisting over several weeks
Isolated conjunctivitis without any respiratory symptoms
Isolated skin rash without any respiratory symptoms
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Epiglottitis classically presents with rapid onset of high fever, drooling (due to painful swallowing), a muffled 'hot potato' voice, and significant respiratory distress, representing a life-threatening airway emergency requiring urgent, careful airway management, historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Acute otitis media in children is most commonly caused by which group of organisms?
o: Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the most common cause
Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis
Herpes simplex virus as the most common cause
Candida albicans as the most common cause
Treponema pallidum as the most common cause
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Acute otitis media in children is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, ascending from the nasopharynx via the relatively short and horizontal pediatric Eustachian tube.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Kawasaki disease, a vasculitis of childhood, is clinically significant primarily due to its potential to cause which serious cardiac complication?
o: Congenital heart block as the primary complication
Coronary artery aneurysms
Atrial septal defect as a direct complication of the disease
Rheumatic mitral stenosis as a direct complication
Patent ductus arteriosus as a direct complication
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood that, if untreated, carries a significant risk of coronary artery aneurysm formation, making prompt diagnosis and treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin important to reduce this risk.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed based on prolonged fever combined with which combination of additional clinical criteria?
o: Bilateral conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy
A single isolated skin lesion with no other associated findings
Isolated joint pain without any mucocutaneous findings
Isolated abdominal pain without any mucocutaneous findings
Isolated hearing loss without any mucocutaneous findings
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed based on fever lasting 5 or more days combined with at least four of five additional principal clinical criteria: bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes (e.g., strawberry tongue, cracked lips), a polymorphous rash, changes in the extremities (edema, erythema, later desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital toxoplasmosis, resulting from maternal infection during pregnancy, classically presents with which triad of findings in the affected infant?
o: Cataracts, deafness, and cardiac defects (the triad more classically associated with congenital rubella)
Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications
Bilateral parotid swelling, fever, and a maculopapular rash
Vesicular skin lesions, corneal scarring, and microcephaly
Jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and a purpuric rash exclusively, without any neurological findings
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Congenital toxoplasmosis classically presents with a triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications, resulting from transplacental transmission of Toxoplasma gondii, most severe when maternal infection occurs earlier in pregnancy.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: The recommended childhood immunization schedule includes the diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine primarily to prevent which combination of diseases?
o: Diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (whooping cough)
Measles, mumps, and rubella
Polio, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b
Varicella, rotavirus, and pneumococcal disease
Influenza, hepatitis A, and meningococcal disease
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: The DTaP vaccine protects against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (whooping cough), three serious bacterial diseases, and is administered as a series during infancy and early childhood with subsequent booster doses.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine typically first administered at approximately which age?
o: At birth
6 weeks of age
10 years of age
18 years of age
12-15 months
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: The MMR vaccine, a live attenuated vaccine, is typically first administered at approximately 12-15 months of age (after maternal antibody levels have sufficiently declined), with a second dose usually given before school entry.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: The oral rotavirus vaccine is administered in infancy primarily to prevent which clinical syndrome?
o: Bacterial meningitis as the primary target disease
Pertussis as the primary target disease
Congenital rubella syndrome as the primary target disease
Severe rotavirus gastroenteritis with dehydration
Neonatal tetanus as the primary target disease
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: The oral rotavirus vaccine protects against rotavirus, a leading cause of severe gastroenteritis and dehydration in infants and young children worldwide, and is administered as an oral series in early infancy.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Diarrheal illness in children, particularly in resource-limited settings, is most effectively and inexpensively managed for mild to moderate dehydration using which intervention?
o: Oral rehydration solution
Intravenous antibiotics as the first-line intervention for all diarrheal illness
Immediate hospitalization for intravenous fluids in every case regardless of severity
Complete fasting until diarrhea resolves completely
Antimotility agents as the first-line intervention in young children
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Oral rehydration solution, a carefully formulated mixture of glucose and electrolytes, is the cornerstone of management for mild to moderate dehydration from diarrheal illness in children, being effective, inexpensive, and avoiding the need for intravenous access in most cases.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Acute bacterial meningitis in infants beyond the neonatal period is most commonly caused by which group of organisms, given widespread vaccination against some historical causes?
o: Group B Streptococcus as the predominant cause beyond the neonatal period
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis
Escherichia coli as the predominant cause beyond the neonatal period
Listeria monocytogenes as the predominant cause beyond the neonatal period
Haemophilus influenzae type b as the predominant cause, given continued high rates despite vaccination
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Beyond the neonatal period, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are now the most common causes of bacterial meningitis in children in regions with widespread Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination, which has dramatically reduced the incidence of Hib meningitis.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: A lumbar puncture in a child with suspected bacterial meningitis typically reveals which combination of cerebrospinal fluid findings?
o: Elevated white cell count (predominantly neutrophils), elevated protein, and low glucose
A completely normal cerebrospinal fluid profile in the majority of bacterial meningitis cases
Low white cell count with elevated glucose, typical of bacterial infection
Elevated glucose and low protein, typical of bacterial infection
Predominantly eosinophils with normal glucose and protein
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Bacterial meningitis classically produces cerebrospinal fluid findings of an elevated white cell count (predominantly neutrophils), elevated protein, and low glucose (reflecting bacterial glucose consumption), distinguishing it from the typically lymphocyte-predominant, normal glucose profile seen in viral meningitis.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: A child presenting with fever, headache, and a non-blanching purpuric rash should be urgently evaluated and treated for which serious condition?
o: Simple viral upper respiratory infection, which does not cause a non-blanching rash
Meningococcemia (invasive Neisseria meningitidis infection)
Contact dermatitis, which does not typically present with fever and headache
Uncomplicated scarlet fever, which classically produces a blanching sandpaper rash
Roseola infantum, which classically produces a rash after fever resolution, not a purpuric rash
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Fever, headache, and a non-blanching (petechial or purpuric) rash in a child are classic warning signs of meningococcemia, a life-threatening infection requiring immediate empiric antibiotic treatment and urgent medical evaluation, as it can rapidly progress to septic shock.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital rubella syndrome, resulting from maternal rubella infection in early pregnancy, classically includes which triad of findings in the affected infant?
o: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications (more classically associated with congenital toxoplasmosis)
Ambiguous genitalia, salt-wasting, and hyperkalemia
Cardiac defects (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus), cataracts, and sensorineural deafness
Bilateral parotid swelling, fever, and a maculopapular rash
Vesicular skin lesions, corneal scarring, and microcephaly
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Congenital rubella syndrome classically presents with a triad of cardiac defects (particularly patent ductus arteriosus and pulmonary artery stenosis), cataracts, and sensorineural deafness, resulting from disruption of organogenesis by maternal rubella infection, especially in the first trimester.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital varicella syndrome, resulting from maternal varicella infection in early pregnancy, is characterized by which combination of findings?
o: Cardiac defects, cataracts, and deafness (more classically associated with congenital rubella)
Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications (more classically associated with congenital toxoplasmosis)
Limb hypoplasia, cutaneous scarring in a dermatomal distribution, and ocular/neurological abnormalities
Ambiguous genitalia and salt-wasting adrenal crisis
Isolated hepatosplenomegaly with no limb or neurological involvement
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Congenital varicella syndrome, resulting from maternal varicella infection (typically in the first or early second trimester), classically presents with limb hypoplasia, characteristic cutaneous scarring in a dermatomal distribution, and ocular and neurological abnormalities.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital Zika virus infection, transmitted from an infected mother to her fetus, is most classically associated with which severe fetal finding?
o: Macrocephaly with normal brain structure
Isolated cardiac defects with entirely normal brain structure
Isolated limb reduction defects with entirely normal brain structure
Isolated deafness with entirely normal brain structure
Microcephaly with associated brain malformations
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Congenital Zika virus infection is most classically associated with severe microcephaly and associated structural brain malformations, resulting from the virus's neurotropic effects on the developing fetal brain.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Diagnosis of pediatric HIV infection in an infant born to an HIV-positive mother requires which type of test, rather than standard antibody testing, due to passive transfer of maternal antibodies?
o: Standard HIV antibody testing, which remains reliable in infants of HIV-positive mothers
HIV DNA or RNA polymerase chain reaction (virologic) testing
A rapid antigen test identical to that used for streptococcal pharyngitis
A simple clinical diagnosis based on symptoms alone, without any laboratory testing
Tuberculin skin testing, which is used for tuberculosis rather than HIV
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Because maternal HIV antibodies passively cross the placenta and can persist in an infant's circulation for up to 18 months, diagnosis of HIV infection in infants born to HIV-positive mothers requires virologic testing (HIV DNA or RNA polymerase chain reaction) rather than standard antibody-based testing.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital syphilis, if it presents with clinical findings in the newborn period, can include which classic finding among others?
o: Isolated cataracts with entirely normal systemic examination
Isolated cardiac defects with entirely normal systemic examination
Hepatosplenomegaly, skin rash, and 'snuffles' (nasal discharge)
Bilateral parotid gland swelling as the classic finding
Isolated limb hypoplasia with entirely normal systemic examination
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Symptomatic congenital syphilis can present with hepatosplenomegaly, a characteristic skin rash (including on the palms and soles), and 'snuffles' (persistent nasal discharge), among other findings, resulting from transplacental transmission of Treponema pallidum.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Impetigo, a common superficial bacterial skin infection in children, classically presents with which finding?
o: Deep, painful abscesses with systemic toxicity as the primary presentation
A single, large bullous lesion exclusively, with no crusting
Honey-colored crusted lesions, typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes
A purely vesicular eruption identical in appearance to varicella
A completely painless, non-erythematous macule
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Impetigo classically presents with honey-colored crusted skin lesions, typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, most commonly affecting exposed areas of skin such as the face and extremities in young children.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Head lice (Pediculosis capitis) infestation in school-age children is primarily transmitted by which mechanism?
o: Direct head-to-head contact or, less commonly, sharing of personal items such as combs and hats
Airborne respiratory droplet transmission
Fecal-oral transmission through contaminated food or water
Vector-borne transmission through mosquito bites
Bloodborne transmission through shared needles
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Head lice are most commonly transmitted through direct head-to-head contact, and less commonly through sharing of personal items such as combs, hats, or hair accessories, and are not related to poor hygiene.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Scabies, caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, classically presents with which symptom, often worse at night?
o: A completely painless, non-pruritic rash
Intense pruritus, often with burrows visible between the fingers or in other characteristic locations
High fever as the dominant and defining symptom
Isolated joint pain without any skin findings
A purely vesicular eruption identical to varicella
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Scabies classically causes intense pruritus, often worse at night, with characteristic burrows visible in the web spaces of the fingers, wrists, and other typical locations, resulting from the mite burrowing into the epidermis and an associated hypersensitivity reaction.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Tuberculosis in children commonly presents differently than in adults, often with which distinguishing feature?
o: An exclusively cavitary pulmonary presentation identical to typical adult reactivation tuberculosis
Complete absence of any risk for disseminated disease in children
A universally asymptomatic presentation in all infected children
An exclusively latent presentation with no possibility of active disease in childhood
A higher likelihood of extrapulmonary and disseminated disease, particularly in young children
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Children, particularly young children, are more likely than adults to develop extrapulmonary and disseminated forms of tuberculosis (including miliary tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis), reflecting less mature cell-mediated immunity, in contrast to the more typical cavitary pulmonary reactivation pattern seen in adults.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test result should be interpreted in the context of which factor, since the same induration size may be interpreted differently?
o: The individual's blood type, which directly determines the interpretation cutoff
The individual's specific risk factors for tuberculosis exposure and progression to active disease
The individual's exact age in months, with no other risk factor considered
The time of year the test was performed, with no other factor considered
The individual's vaccination history against varicella, which directly determines the interpretation cutoff
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Interpretation of the Mantoux tuberculin skin test result (the size of induration considered positive) depends on the individual's specific risk factors for tuberculosis exposure and progression to active disease, with lower thresholds used for higher-risk individuals (e.g., close contacts of active cases, immunocompromised individuals).

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital hepatitis B infection, acquired perinatally, is effectively prevented through which combined intervention shortly after birth?
o: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine administered to the infant shortly after birth
Maternal antiviral treatment alone during the third trimester, without any infant intervention
Cesarean delivery alone, without any infant vaccination or immunoglobulin
Avoidance of breastfeeding alone, without any infant vaccination or immunoglobulin
No effective preventive intervention currently exists for perinatal hepatitis B transmission
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Perinatal hepatitis B transmission is effectively prevented through a combination of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (providing immediate passive immunity) and the hepatitis B vaccine (providing active immunity) administered to the infant shortly after birth, particularly important when the mother is hepatitis B surface antigen-positive.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Osteomyelitis in children most commonly affects which anatomical location, related to the vascular anatomy of growing bone?
o: The epiphysis of long bones as the most common site, rather than the metaphysis
The diaphysis (shaft) of long bones as the most common site
The articular cartilage exclusively, sparing the underlying bone
The metaphysis of long bones
The flat bones of the skull as the most common site in children
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Pediatric osteomyelitis most commonly affects the metaphysis of long bones, reflecting the relatively sluggish blood flow through the metaphyseal vascular loops in this region, which predisposes to bacterial seeding during hematogenous spread.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Septic arthritis in children is considered an orthopedic emergency primarily because delayed treatment can result in which serious complication?
o: Complete, spontaneous resolution without any need for treatment
A benign, self-limited condition with no risk of joint damage
Isolated skin discoloration with no joint involvement
Isolated fever with no risk to the joint itself
Irreversible cartilage destruction and joint damage
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Septic arthritis is a pediatric orthopedic emergency because bacterial infection within the joint space can rapidly cause irreversible destruction of articular cartilage and joint damage if not promptly diagnosed and treated with joint drainage and antibiotics.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Congenital tuberculosis, though rare, can result from transplacental or intrapartum transmission and should be considered in an infant with which combination of findings?
o: Isolated cataracts with no systemic findings
Isolated cardiac defects with no systemic findings
Hepatosplenomegaly, respiratory distress, and failure to thrive in the setting of maternal tuberculosis exposure
A completely normal examination with no clinical suspicion warranted
Isolated limb reduction defects with no systemic findings
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Congenital tuberculosis should be considered in an infant presenting with hepatosplenomegaly, respiratory distress, and failure to thrive, particularly when there is a history of maternal tuberculosis, though it remains a rare cause of neonatal illness.

pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.s: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection, acquired most commonly during vaginal delivery from a mother with active genital herpes lesions, can present with which pattern of disease?
o: A single, uniform presentation identical in every affected infant
Localized skin/eye/mouth disease, central nervous system disease, or disseminated disease
Exclusively asymptomatic infection with no clinical disease in any case
Exclusively a chronic, slowly progressive skin rash with no other organ involvement
Exclusively isolated conjunctivitis with no risk of systemic involvement
pediatrics/pediatric-infectious-diseases.e: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection can present in one of three patterns: localized skin/eye/mouth disease, central nervous system disease (encephalitis), or disseminated disease involving multiple organs, with the disseminated and central nervous system forms carrying significant morbidity and mortality if not promptly treated with antiviral therapy.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Bronchiolitis, most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus, primarily affects which age group?
o: Infants under 2 years of age, most commonly under 6 months
School-age children between 6 and 12 years
Adolescents between 13 and 18 years
Exclusively neonates within the first week of life
Exclusively adults, with rare occurrence in children
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Bronchiolitis, most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus, primarily affects infants under 2 years of age (with peak incidence under 6 months), causing inflammation and obstruction of the small airways (bronchioles).

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Bronchiolitis classically presents with which combination of clinical findings?
o: A barking cough with inspiratory stridor as the dominant feature
Wheezing, tachypnea, and increased work of breathing following a viral upper respiratory prodrome
Drooling and inability to swallow as the dominant feature
Bilateral parotid gland swelling as the dominant feature
A petechial rash as the dominant feature
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Bronchiolitis classically presents with wheezing, tachypnea, and increased work of breathing (retractions, nasal flaring) following a 1-2 day viral upper respiratory prodrome (rhinorrhea, mild fever), reflecting small airway inflammation and obstruction.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Childhood asthma is characterized by which combination of underlying pathophysiological features?
o: Irreversible, fixed airway obstruction with no inflammatory component
A purely structural airway abnormality present from birth with no inflammatory component
Reversible airway obstruction, airway inflammation, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness
Isolated upper airway obstruction with entirely normal lower airway function
A condition caused exclusively by bacterial infection with no allergic component
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Asthma is characterized by chronic airway inflammation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness to various triggers, and reversible airway obstruction (distinguishing it from fixed obstructive diseases), typically presenting with recurrent wheezing, cough, and dyspnea.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol) are used in acute asthma exacerbations primarily for which effect?
o: Long-term reduction of airway inflammation as their primary mechanism
Direct antihistamine effect blocking allergic mediators
Direct antiviral effect against the triggering respiratory virus
Rapid bronchodilation through relaxation of airway smooth muscle
Direct antibiotic effect against bacterial superinfection
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Short-acting beta-2 agonists provide rapid bronchodilation by relaxing airway smooth muscle through beta-2 adrenergic receptor stimulation, making them the first-line rescue treatment for acute asthma exacerbations, though they do not address the underlying airway inflammation.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Inhaled corticosteroids are used as controller (maintenance) therapy in persistent asthma primarily to achieve which effect?
o: Long-term reduction of airway inflammation, decreasing exacerbation frequency and severity
Immediate bronchodilation during an acute exacerbation
Direct antihistamine effect as their primary mechanism
Permanent cure of the underlying asthma
Direct antiviral effect against respiratory viral triggers
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred controller therapy for persistent asthma, reducing chronic airway inflammation over time, thereby decreasing the frequency and severity of exacerbations and improving overall asthma control, though they do not provide immediate symptom relief.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive genetic disorder, results from mutations affecting which protein?
o: The dystrophin protein, as in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Hemoglobin beta-globin chains, as in sickle cell disease
The LDL receptor, as in familial hypercholesterolemia
Factor VIII, as in hemophilia A
The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) chloride channel
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Cystic fibrosis results from mutations in the CFTR gene, encoding a chloride channel protein, causing abnormal chloride and water transport across epithelial cells and leading to thick, viscous secretions affecting the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and other organ systems.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Cystic fibrosis classically affects the respiratory system by causing which pathological process?
o: Complete absence of mucus production, causing dry, friable airways
Isolated laryngeal edema with no lower airway involvement
A purely restrictive lung pattern with no infective component
Thick, viscous mucus obstructing airways, leading to recurrent infections and progressive bronchiectasis
An isolated pleural effusion with no airway involvement
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Cystic fibrosis causes production of thick, viscous mucus that obstructs the airways, impairing mucociliary clearance and predisposing to recurrent bacterial infections (classically including Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and progressive bronchiectasis over time.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: The sweat chloride test, a key diagnostic investigation for cystic fibrosis, evaluates which parameter?
o: The pH of sweat, which is decreased in affected individuals
The glucose concentration in sweat
The protein content of sweat
The concentration of chloride ions in sweat, which is elevated in affected individuals
The bacterial culture of sweat
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: The sweat chloride test measures the concentration of chloride ions in sweat, which is characteristically elevated in individuals with cystic fibrosis due to defective CFTR-mediated chloride reabsorption in sweat gland ducts, forming the basis of this key diagnostic test.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A ventricular septal defect, the most common congenital heart defect, typically causes which type of shunt?
o: A right-to-left shunt in the vast majority of uncomplicated cases
A left-to-right shunt, due to higher pressure in the left ventricle compared to the right
No shunting at all, since blood flow is unaffected
A shunt that reverses direction spontaneously every few minutes
An exclusively bidirectional shunt with no dominant direction
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: A ventricular septal defect typically causes a left-to-right shunt, since left ventricular pressure normally exceeds right ventricular pressure, allowing oxygenated blood to flow from the left to the right ventricle through the defect, potentially causing pulmonary overcirculation.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Tetralogy of Fallot, a cyanotic congenital heart defect, consists of which four anatomical components?
o: Atrial septal defect, mitral stenosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, and a bicuspid aortic valve
Patent ductus arteriosus, coarctation of the aorta, aortic stenosis, and a single ventricle
Complete atrioventricular septal defect, tricuspid atresia, transposition of the great arteries, and truncus arteriosus
Ventricular septal defect, pulmonary (right ventricular outflow tract) stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return, hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis, and a single ventricle
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of four classic anatomical features: a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary (right ventricular outflow tract) stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy (secondary to the stenosis), and an overriding aorta positioned above the ventricular septal defect.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A 'tet spell' (hypercyanotic spell) in an infant with Tetralogy of Fallot is classically managed acutely by which simple maneuver?
o: Immediate administration of a diuretic as the first-line acute intervention
Placing the infant in a knee-to-chest position
Immediate administration of a beta-agonist bronchodilator as the first-line intervention
Placing the infant flat with legs elevated above the heart
Immediate administration of intravenous insulin
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: A 'tet spell' is classically managed acutely by placing the infant in a knee-to-chest position, which increases systemic vascular resistance and reduces the right-to-left shunt across the ventricular septal defect, improving pulmonary blood flow and oxygenation.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Coarctation of the aorta, a congenital narrowing of the aorta, classically presents with which finding on physical examination?
o: Bounding pulses in all four extremities equally
Complete absence of any peripheral pulse in all four extremities
Bounding femoral pulses with diminished brachial pulses (opposite to the classic pattern)
Identical, normal pulses in all four extremities with no blood pressure discrepancy
Diminished or delayed femoral pulses compared to the upper extremity (brachial) pulses, with associated upper extremity hypertension
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Coarctation of the aorta classically presents with diminished or delayed femoral pulses compared to brachial pulses (radiofemoral delay), along with upper extremity hypertension relative to the lower extremities, reflecting the aortic narrowing typically located near the ductus arteriosus.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Patent ductus arteriosus, a persistent connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery after birth, classically produces which finding on auscultation?
o: A mid-systolic ejection click with no murmur
An early diastolic decrescendo murmur exclusively
A late systolic murmur with a mid-systolic click, typical of mitral valve prolapse instead
A continuous, 'machinery-like' murmur
Complete absence of any audible murmur in all cases
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Patent ductus arteriosus classically produces a continuous, 'machinery-like' murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border/infraclavicular area, resulting from continuous blood flow from the higher-pressure aorta to the lower-pressure pulmonary artery throughout both systole and diastole.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Transposition of the great arteries, a cyanotic congenital heart defect presenting in the immediate newborn period, results from which anatomical abnormality?
o: A simple ventricular septal defect with normally connected great arteries
An isolated atrial septal defect with normally connected great arteries
A bicuspid aortic valve with normally connected great arteries
An isolated patent ductus arteriosus with normally connected great arteries
The aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle, creating two parallel, non-communicating circulations
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Transposition of the great arteries occurs when the aorta arises from the morphologic right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the morphologic left ventricle, creating two parallel circulations that are incompatible with survival unless there is mixing of blood through an associated shunt (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus, atrial or ventricular septal defect).

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Rheumatic fever, a delayed complication of untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis, is diagnosed using which set of clinical criteria?
o: The Bishop score
The Ranson criteria
The Rotterdam criteria
The Jones criteria
The Wells score
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: The Jones criteria are used to diagnose acute rheumatic fever, incorporating major criteria (carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) and minor criteria, combined with evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Acute rheumatic fever most commonly leads to chronic damage of which cardiac valve, if carditis occurs during the acute illness?
o: The tricuspid valve, as the most commonly and severely affected valve
The pulmonary valve, as the most commonly and severely affected valve
The aortic valve exclusively, with sparing of the mitral valve in all cases
No valve is typically affected, since carditis resolves completely in all cases
The mitral valve
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Acute rheumatic fever most commonly causes chronic damage to the mitral valve (classically progressive mitral stenosis over years), though the aortic valve can also be affected, resulting from an autoimmune response triggered by prior group A streptococcal infection.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A functional (innocent) heart murmur in a child is distinguished from a pathological murmur by which characteristic feature?
o: It is always diastolic in timing, unlike pathological murmurs
It is always associated with cyanosis
It is always accompanied by failure to thrive
It is typically soft, systolic, varies with position, and occurs in a child with normal growth and no other cardiac symptoms
It is always louder than any pathological murmur
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Innocent (functional) heart murmurs in children are typically soft, systolic in timing, vary with patient position or respiration, and occur in an otherwise well child with normal growth, no cyanosis, and no other symptoms, distinguishing them from pathological murmurs which often have additional concerning features.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A child presenting with sudden onset of unilateral wheeze and decreased breath sounds, with a history of playing with small toys, should be evaluated for which condition?
o: Simple viral bronchiolitis, which classically causes bilateral rather than unilateral findings
Foreign body aspiration
Asthma exacerbation, which classically causes bilateral rather than unilateral findings
Pneumothorax as the most likely cause given this specific history
Congenital lobar emphysema as the most likely cause given this specific history
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Sudden onset of unilateral wheeze and decreased breath sounds, particularly with a history of a choking episode or access to small objects, is highly suggestive of foreign body aspiration, requiring prompt evaluation (often with bronchoscopy) for removal.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Community-acquired pneumonia in children is most commonly caused by which organism in school-age children and adolescents, distinct from the typical bacterial causes in younger children?
o: Group B Streptococcus as the most common cause in school-age children
Respiratory syncytial virus as the most common cause in school-age children
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Listeria monocytogenes as the most common cause in school-age children
Escherichia coli as the most common cause in school-age children
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, causing 'atypical' pneumonia, is a particularly common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in school-age children and adolescents, often presenting with a more gradual onset and extrapulmonary symptoms compared to typical bacterial pneumonia.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A chest X-ray in a child with lobar consolidation and a productive cough is more suggestive of which type of pneumonia, compared to a diffuse interstitial pattern?
o: Atypical (e.g., viral or mycoplasma) pneumonia, which more classically causes lobar consolidation
Tuberculosis exclusively, with no other cause producing lobar consolidation
Typical bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae)
Pulmonary edema exclusively, unrelated to any infectious process
A normal finding requiring no further clinical correlation
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Lobar consolidation on chest X-ray, combined with a productive cough and often high fever, is more suggestive of typical bacterial pneumonia (classically Streptococcus pneumoniae), in contrast to the more diffuse, interstitial pattern often seen with atypical or viral pneumonia.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Cyanotic congenital heart disease in a newborn is generally distinguished from a primary respiratory cause of cyanosis by which bedside test?
o: A chest X-ray alone, which reliably distinguishes cardiac from respiratory causes in all cases
Auscultation of a heart murmur alone, since murmurs are always present in cyanotic heart disease and always absent in respiratory disease
The hyperoxia test, in which oxygen saturation fails to significantly improve with 100% supplemental oxygen in cardiac disease
Measurement of blood glucose alone, since hypoglycemia is specific to cyanotic heart disease
A capillary refill time measurement alone, since it reliably distinguishes the two causes
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: The hyperoxia test helps distinguish cyanotic congenital heart disease from primary respiratory or pulmonary causes of cyanosis: in cardiac disease with a fixed right-to-left shunt, oxygen saturation typically fails to rise significantly with 100% supplemental oxygen, whereas respiratory causes usually show a more significant improvement.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: An atrial septal defect, if left untreated into adulthood, can eventually lead to which long-term complication from chronic pulmonary overcirculation?
o: Immediate neonatal cyanosis in all cases, requiring urgent intervention at birth
Pulmonary hypertension and, in severe cases, Eisenmenger syndrome with shunt reversal
Complete spontaneous resolution without any long-term risk in all cases
Isolated systemic hypertension unrelated to any pulmonary vascular change
Immediate complete heart block in all untreated cases
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: An untreated atrial septal defect can, over years to decades, lead to chronic pulmonary overcirculation and progressive pulmonary vascular disease, potentially resulting in pulmonary hypertension and, in severe cases, Eisenmenger syndrome, where the shunt direction reverses to right-to-left, causing cyanosis.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a severe cyanotic congenital heart defect, is characterized by which anatomical abnormality?
o: Underdevelopment of the left ventricle, mitral valve, and aortic valve/arch, rendering the left heart unable to support systemic circulation
Underdevelopment of the right ventricle only, with a normally functioning left heart
A simple, isolated small ventricular septal defect with otherwise normal cardiac anatomy
An isolated bicuspid aortic valve with normal ventricular development
An isolated atrial septal defect with normal ventricular development
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome involves severe underdevelopment of the left ventricle, mitral valve, and aortic valve and arch, rendering the left heart unable to support systemic circulation, requiring the ductus arteriosus to remain patent for survival until surgical palliation.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin E1 infusion is a critical initial management step for which category of congenital heart disease?
o: All forms of congenital heart disease equally, regardless of ductal dependence
Only acyanotic lesions with a small ventricular septal defect
Only lesions causing pulmonary overcirculation without any duct dependence
Duct-dependent congenital heart lesions, where systemic or pulmonary blood flow relies on a patent ductus arteriosus
Isolated atrial septal defects, which are never duct-dependent
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Prostaglandin E1 infusion, which maintains ductus arteriosus patency, is a critical initial management step for duct-dependent congenital heart lesions (such as hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical coarctation, or severe pulmonary/tricuspid atresia), where closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth would be catastrophic.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A continuous murmur in a newborn that persists beyond the first few days of life, when a patent ductus arteriosus would normally be expected to functionally close, may indicate which clinical scenario?
o: A completely normal finding requiring no further evaluation in any newborn
A persistent patent ductus arteriosus, more common in preterm infants
Definitive evidence of tetralogy of Fallot, since this lesion always produces a continuous murmur
Definitive evidence of transposition of the great arteries, which classically produces a continuous murmur
A finding exclusively associated with maternal diabetes, unrelated to any specific cardiac lesion
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: A continuous murmur persisting beyond the first few days of life, when functional ductal closure would normally be expected, may indicate a persistent patent ductus arteriosus, which is more common in preterm infants due to reduced sensitivity of the immature ductal tissue to the normal postnatal closure stimuli.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Chronic hypoxemia in children with uncorrected cyanotic congenital heart disease can lead to which compensatory hematological change?
o: Chronic anemia as the primary hematological consequence
Secondary polycythemia (increased red blood cell production)
Isolated thrombocytopenia as the primary hematological consequence
Isolated leukopenia as the primary hematological consequence
No hematological changes occur in chronic cyanotic heart disease
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Chronic hypoxemia in uncorrected cyanotic congenital heart disease stimulates increased erythropoietin production, leading to secondary polycythemia as a compensatory mechanism to improve tissue oxygen delivery, though this can also increase blood viscosity and thrombotic risk.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Clubbing of the fingers and toes, when seen in a child, is classically associated with which category of underlying disease?
o: Acute viral upper respiratory infection as the most common associated cause
Simple iron deficiency anemia as the most common associated cause
Uncomplicated asthma with good control as the most common associated cause
Chronic hypoxemia from cyanotic congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease
Normal variation with no underlying pathology in any child
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Digital clubbing in children is classically associated with chronic hypoxemia, such as from cyanotic congenital heart disease, or chronic suppurative lung disease (e.g., cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis), reflecting long-standing tissue hypoxia and its effects on the nail bed and distal digit.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A pneumothorax in a newborn, sometimes occurring spontaneously or associated with mechanical ventilation, classically presents with which clinical finding?
o: A completely asymptomatic presentation with entirely normal breath sounds
Bilateral, symmetric decreased breath sounds without any respiratory distress
Isolated jaundice without any respiratory finding
Isolated bradycardia without any respiratory distress
Sudden respiratory distress with asymmetric breath sounds and possible tracheal deviation
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Neonatal pneumothorax classically presents with sudden respiratory distress, asymmetric breath sounds (decreased on the affected side), and in tension pneumothorax, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, requiring prompt recognition and, if significant, needle decompression or chest tube placement.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Chronic tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea in children is most definitively treated by which intervention when conservative measures fail?
o: Long-term oral antibiotic therapy as the definitive treatment
Long-term inhaled corticosteroid therapy as the definitive treatment
Continuous positive airway pressure as the only available treatment, with surgery never indicated in children
Weight loss alone in all cases, regardless of tonsillar size
Adenotonsillectomy
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Adenotonsillectomy is the most common and generally definitive treatment for obstructive sleep apnea in children caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy, typically resulting in significant improvement or resolution of symptoms.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A child with recurrent episodes of wheeze that respond well to bronchodilator therapy, with symptom-free intervals between episodes, is most consistent with which diagnosis?
o: Foreign body aspiration, which typically causes persistent rather than episodic symptoms
Asthma
Bronchiolitis, which typically presents as a single acute illness rather than recurrent episodes
Congenital lobar emphysema, which typically causes persistent rather than episodic symptoms
Cystic fibrosis, which typically causes chronic rather than purely episodic symptoms
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Recurrent, episodic wheeze that responds well to bronchodilator therapy, with symptom-free intervals between episodes, is the classic clinical pattern of childhood asthma, reflecting its underlying reversible airway obstruction.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Peak expiratory flow rate measurement, used in the assessment and monitoring of asthma, primarily reflects which aspect of lung function?
o: The degree of large airway obstruction
Total lung capacity, independent of airway obstruction
Diffusion capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide
Alveolar gas exchange efficiency directly
Pulmonary vascular resistance directly
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Peak expiratory flow rate primarily reflects the degree of large airway obstruction and is a simple, effort-dependent measurement that can be used by patients at home to monitor asthma control and detect early signs of an impending exacerbation.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Nasal cannula oxygen delivery in infants with bronchiolitis is generally used to maintain oxygen saturation above which general threshold, guiding the need for supplemental oxygen?
o: Approximately 90-92%, according to commonly used clinical guidelines
Exactly 100% at all times, with any lower value considered unacceptable
Below 70%, since lower saturations are considered acceptable in bronchiolitis
Oxygen saturation is not monitored or used to guide management in bronchiolitis
Above 99% at all times, with no tolerance for any lower reading
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Clinical guidelines for bronchiolitis management generally use an oxygen saturation threshold around 90-92% to guide the initiation of supplemental oxygen therapy, avoiding both undertreatment of significant hypoxemia and overuse of oxygen and prolonged hospitalization for borderline saturations.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A newborn with a large, isolated ventricular septal defect and evidence of pulmonary overcirculation may develop which symptom pattern in early infancy?
o: Immediate cyanosis at birth as the dominant and defining symptom
Poor feeding, faltering growth, tachypnea, and diaphoresis with feeds, reflecting early heart failure
Complete absence of any symptoms throughout infancy in all cases
Isolated clubbing without any feeding or growth difficulty
Isolated polycythemia without any feeding or growth difficulty
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: A large ventricular septal defect causing significant left-to-right shunting and pulmonary overcirculation can lead to symptoms of heart failure in early infancy, including poor feeding, faltering growth, tachypnea, and diaphoresis (sweating) with feeding, reflecting the increased work of breathing and metabolic demand.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return, a cyanotic congenital heart defect, is characterized by which anatomical abnormality?
o: The pulmonary veins drain normally into the left atrium, with an isolated ventricular septal defect as the only abnormality
A single pulmonary vein draining abnormally, with the remaining three draining normally into the left atrium
All four pulmonary veins drain into the systemic venous circulation or right atrium rather than the left atrium
Complete absence of any pulmonary venous connections
Normal pulmonary venous return with an isolated abnormality of the pulmonary arteries instead
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return occurs when all four pulmonary veins fail to connect normally to the left atrium, instead draining into the systemic venous circulation or directly into the right atrium, requiring an associated shunt (such as a patent foramen ovale) for survival and typically presenting with cyanosis.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Pulmonary function testing showing a reduced forced expiratory volume in one second relative to forced vital capacity (reduced FEV1/FVC ratio) that improves significantly with bronchodilator administration is characteristic of which pattern?
o: A purely restrictive lung disease pattern, such as pulmonary fibrosis
A normal lung function pattern requiring no further evaluation
An isolated diffusion abnormality unrelated to airway caliber
Reversible obstructive lung disease, such as asthma
A fixed, irreversible obstructive pattern with no bronchodilator response, such as advanced bronchiectasis
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio indicating airway obstruction that shows significant improvement (reversibility) after bronchodilator administration is characteristic of asthma, distinguishing it from fixed obstructive patterns seen in some other chronic lung diseases.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Pulmonary hypertension in a child with a large, uncorrected left-to-right shunt lesion can eventually lead to shunt reversal and cyanosis, a phenomenon known by which eponym?
o: Trousseau's syndrome, which refers to a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state rather than shunt reversal
Klinefelter syndrome, which refers to a chromosomal disorder rather than shunt reversal
Eisenmenger syndrome
Ebstein's anomaly, which refers to a specific tricuspid valve malformation rather than shunt reversal
DiGeorge syndrome, which refers to a genetic immunodeficiency and cardiac anomaly syndrome rather than shunt reversal
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Eisenmenger syndrome refers to the reversal of a previously left-to-right shunt to a right-to-left shunt, occurring when chronic pulmonary overcirculation from an uncorrected shunt lesion leads to progressive, irreversible pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension exceeding systemic pressures.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A child with cystic fibrosis often requires supplementation with which category of substances due to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency?
o: Water-soluble vitamins exclusively, with no need for pancreatic enzyme supplementation
Iron supplementation exclusively, with no need for pancreatic enzymes or fat-soluble vitamins
Calcium supplementation exclusively, with no need for pancreatic enzymes
Pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
No supplementation is needed in cystic fibrosis, since pancreatic function is typically preserved
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, common in cystic fibrosis, impairs digestion and absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins, necessitating pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy with meals and supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: Ebstein's anomaly, a congenital cardiac malformation, involves which structural abnormality?
o: Apical displacement of an abnormal tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, causing 'atrialization' of part of the right ventricle
Complete absence of the mitral valve
Isolated stenosis of the pulmonary valve with a structurally normal tricuspid valve
Isolated coarctation of the aorta with a structurally normal tricuspid valve
Complete transposition of the great arteries with a structurally normal tricuspid valve
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Ebstein's anomaly is characterized by apical displacement of an abnormally formed tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, resulting in 'atrialization' of the proximal right ventricle and a variably functioning, often regurgitant tricuspid valve, which can cause right heart failure and, in some cases, cyanosis.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A child with suspected foreign body aspiration and complete airway obstruction with an ineffective cough should be managed with which immediate first-aid maneuver?
o: Immediate needle cricothyroidotomy as the first response in every case
Observation alone, without any physical intervention
Immediate administration of a bronchodilator inhaler
Positioning the child flat on their back with no other intervention
Back blows and/or abdominal thrusts (or chest thrusts in infants), depending on age
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Complete airway obstruction from a foreign body with an ineffective cough is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate first-aid maneuvers: back blows and chest thrusts in infants under 1 year, or abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) in older children, to attempt to dislodge the obstructing object.

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.s: A single ventricle physiology (e.g., hypoplastic left heart syndrome) is ultimately palliated through a series of staged surgical procedures, culminating in which final procedure that separates the systemic and pulmonary circulations?
o: The Kasai portoenterostomy, which is used for biliary atresia rather than cardiac palliation
The Ponseti method, which is used for clubfoot rather than cardiac palliation
The Whipple procedure, which is used for pancreatic surgery rather than cardiac palliation
The McRoberts maneuver, which is used in obstetric emergencies rather than cardiac palliation
The Fontan procedure
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.e: Staged single-ventricle palliation (for conditions such as hypoplastic left heart syndrome) typically culminates in the Fontan procedure, which directs systemic venous return directly to the pulmonary arteries, allowing the single functional ventricle to support only the systemic circulation.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Gastroesophageal reflux in infants, common and usually physiological, is generally distinguished from gastroesophageal reflux disease by which feature?
o: The complete absence of any regurgitation, which defines simple reflux
Occurrence exclusively in infants over 2 years of age
Occurrence exclusively during sleep, with no daytime symptoms
The presence of complications such as poor weight gain, feeding refusal, or respiratory symptoms
A requirement for surgical intervention in all affected infants
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Physiological gastroesophageal reflux (frequent 'spitting up') is common and self-limited in infants, while gastroesophageal reflux disease is diagnosed when reflux causes complications such as poor weight gain, feeding refusal, esophagitis, or respiratory symptoms, warranting further evaluation and management.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Celiac disease, an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion, is characterized by which histological finding on small bowel biopsy?
o: Normal villous architecture with isolated eosinophilic infiltration
Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis
Granuloma formation with transmural inflammation, typical of Crohn's disease instead
Continuous mucosal inflammation limited to the colon, typical of ulcerative colitis instead
Complete absence of any small bowel abnormality
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Celiac disease classically causes villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes on small bowel biopsy, resulting from an autoimmune response to gluten (specifically gliadin) in genetically susceptible individuals.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Which serological test is commonly used for screening for celiac disease, given its high sensitivity and specificity?
o: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody
Anti-nuclear antibody as the primary screening test for celiac disease
Rheumatoid factor as the primary screening test for celiac disease
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibody as the primary screening test for celiac disease
Anti-mitochondrial antibody as the primary screening test for celiac disease
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody testing is the preferred initial serological screening test for celiac disease due to its high sensitivity and specificity, with total IgA level also checked to exclude selective IgA deficiency, which can cause a false-negative result.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Congenital pyloric stenosis and Hirschsprung's disease are both surgical causes of vomiting/obstruction in infants; which of the following best distinguishes their typical presentations?
o: Both conditions present identically with bilious vomiting starting on day one of life
Pyloric stenosis classically causes failure to pass meconium, while Hirschsprung's disease causes projectile vomiting at 2-8 weeks
Both conditions are managed identically with observation alone, without any surgical intervention
Neither condition is associated with any vomiting or bowel symptoms
Pyloric stenosis classically causes non-bilious projectile vomiting around 2-8 weeks of age, while Hirschsprung's disease classically causes failure to pass meconium in the newborn period
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Pyloric stenosis classically presents with non-bilious, projectile vomiting emerging around 2-8 weeks of age in a previously well infant, while Hirschsprung's disease classically presents with delayed passage of meconium and abdominal distension in the newborn period, reflecting their distinct underlying pathologies and typical timing.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Nephrotic syndrome in children is characterized by which combination of clinical and laboratory findings?
o: Hematuria, hypertension, and mild proteinuria, typical of nephritic syndrome instead
Isolated hematuria without any proteinuria or edema
Isolated hypertension without any proteinuria or edema
Isolated hyperkalemia without any proteinuria or edema
Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (leading to hypoalbuminemia and consequent edema) and hyperlipidemia, resulting from increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins, most commonly due to minimal change disease in children.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Minimal change disease, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, is characterized by which finding on light microscopy of a renal biopsy?
o: Essentially normal-appearing glomeruli, with abnormalities visible only on electron microscopy (podocyte foot process effacement)
Diffuse crescentic glomerulonephritis visible on light microscopy
Extensive glomerular scarring and sclerosis visible on light microscopy
Membranous thickening of the glomerular basement membrane visible on light microscopy
Mesangial IgA deposition visible on light microscopy
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Minimal change disease is characterized by essentially normal-appearing glomeruli on light microscopy, with the diagnostic abnormality (effacement of podocyte foot processes) visible only on electron microscopy, and typically shows an excellent response to corticosteroid therapy.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, a form of acute nephritic syndrome in children, classically follows infection with which organism at which typical site?
o: Group A Streptococcus, following pharyngitis or impetigo (skin infection)
Staphylococcus aureus, following a urinary tract infection
Escherichia coli, following a gastrointestinal infection
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, following a pulmonary infection
Candida albicans, following an oral infection
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis classically follows infection with nephritogenic strains of group A Streptococcus, typically pharyngitis or impetigo (skin infection), with a latent period of 1-3 weeks before the onset of nephritic symptoms (hematuria, hypertension, edema, and often reduced urine output).

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Hemolytic uremic syndrome in children is classically triggered by infection with which organism?
o: Streptococcus pneumoniae as the classic triggering organism
Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (e.g., O157:H7)
Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the classic triggering organism
Herpes simplex virus as the classic triggering organism
Candida albicans as the classic triggering organism
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Hemolytic uremic syndrome in children is classically triggered by infection with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (particularly serotype O157:H7), often following a diarrheal illness, leading to the characteristic triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Vesicoureteral reflux in children is a significant risk factor for which recurrent complication?
o: Recurrent respiratory tract infections as the primary associated complication
Recurrent gastrointestinal infections as the primary associated complication
Recurrent skin infections as the primary associated complication
Recurrent urinary tract infections with risk of renal scarring
Recurrent bone infections as the primary associated complication
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Vesicoureteral reflux predisposes to recurrent urinary tract infections by allowing retrograde flow of urine (and potentially bacteria) from the bladder toward the kidneys, increasing the risk of pyelonephritis and subsequent renal scarring if recurrent infections are not identified and managed.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) results from which chromosomal abnormality in the majority of cases?
o: A deletion of part of chromosome 21
An extra copy of chromosome 18
An extra copy of chromosome 21, most commonly from meiotic nondisjunction
An extra copy of chromosome 13
A balanced translocation with no extra genetic material in all cases
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Down syndrome most commonly results from trisomy 21, an extra full copy of chromosome 21, typically arising from meiotic nondisjunction (most often during maternal meiosis, with increasing risk with advanced maternal age), though rarer causes include translocation and mosaicism.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Down syndrome is associated with an increased risk of which congenital cardiac defect in particular?
o: Tetralogy of Fallot as the most specifically associated cardiac defect
Atrioventricular septal defect (endocardial cushion defect)
Transposition of the great arteries as the most specifically associated cardiac defect
Coarctation of the aorta as the most specifically associated cardiac defect
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome as the most specifically associated cardiac defect
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Down syndrome is particularly associated with an increased risk of atrioventricular septal defect (endocardial cushion defect), among other congenital heart defects, warranting routine echocardiographic screening in affected infants.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is generally associated with which overall prognosis compared to Down syndrome?
o: An identical, generally favorable prognosis to Down syndrome
A better long-term prognosis than Down syndrome, with normal life expectancy
A significantly more severe prognosis, with most affected infants not surviving beyond the first year of life
No associated increase in mortality compared to the general population
A prognosis that improves progressively with age, becoming normal by adulthood
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.e: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) carries a significantly more severe prognosis than Down syndrome, with multiple severe congenital anomalies (including cardiac defects) and most affected infants not surviving beyond the first year of life.

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.s: Turner syndrome, resulting from complete or partial absence of one X chromosome in a phenotypic female (45,X), classically presents with which combination of features?
o: Tall stature with normal ovarian function and normal fertility
