ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A patient presenting with unilateral facial pain, numbness, and recurrent epistaxis, found on examination to have a nasal mass with bony erosion on imaging, should be managed with which priority approach?
o: Urgent biopsy and staging workup to evaluate for sinonasal malignancy, with multidisciplinary oncologic management as indicated
Simple observation with reassurance, since bony erosion is a benign and expected finding in most nasal masses
Immediate high-dose oral antihistamine therapy as the sole management
Immediate, aggressive nasal irrigation alone, without any further diagnostic workup
Reassurance that this presentation is typical of simple allergic rhinitis
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: The combination of facial pain, numbness, recurrent epistaxis, a nasal mass, and bony erosion on imaging is highly concerning for sinonasal malignancy, warranting urgent biopsy for histological diagnosis and appropriate staging workup to guide multidisciplinary oncologic management.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Loss of smell (anosmia) accompanying an upper respiratory viral infection is generally managed with which approach, given the typical clinical course?
o: Immediate surgical intervention as the standard first-line treatment
Supportive care and observation, since a substantial proportion of cases improve spontaneously over weeks to months
Immediate, permanent reassurance that recovery is impossible in any case
Long-term systemic antibiotic therapy as the standard treatment
Immediate radiotherapy as the standard treatment
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Post-viral anosmia is generally managed with supportive care, olfactory training, and observation, since a substantial proportion of affected individuals experience at least partial spontaneous improvement over subsequent weeks to months, though some cases can result in more prolonged or permanent olfactory dysfunction.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Nasal valve collapse, a cause of nasal obstruction related to weakness or narrowing of the internal or external nasal valve area, can be clinically assessed using which simple bedside maneuver?
o: The Rinne test, which is used to assess hearing rather than nasal airflow
The Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which is used to assess vertigo rather than nasal airflow
The Weber test, which is used to assess hearing rather than nasal airflow
The swinging flashlight test, which is used to assess pupillary function rather than nasal airflow
The Cottle maneuver, in which gently lifting the cheek to widen the nasal valve area improves airflow if valve collapse is contributing to obstruction
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: The Cottle maneuver involves gently pulling the cheek laterally to widen the internal nasal valve area; improvement in airflow with this maneuver supports a diagnosis of nasal valve collapse as a contributing cause of nasal obstruction, helping guide consideration of surgical correction if conservative measures fail.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: The sphenoid sinus, the most posteriorly located paranasal sinus, is clinically significant due to its close anatomical relationship with which structures?
o: The mandible and temporomandibular joint exclusively
The external ear canal exclusively, with no relationship to any intracranial structure
The optic nerve, internal carotid artery, and pituitary gland
The parotid gland exclusively, with no relationship to any intracranial structure
The thyroid gland exclusively, with no relationship to any intracranial structure
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: The sphenoid sinus lies in close anatomical proximity to critical structures including the optic nerve, internal carotid artery, and pituitary gland, making sphenoid sinusitis or masses in this region clinically significant due to the risk of involvement of these adjacent structures.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Acute tonsillitis caused by group A Streptococcus classically presents with which combination of findings, distinguishing it from a typical viral pharyngitis?
o: Prominent cough and rhinorrhea with mild throat discomfort, typical of viral infection instead
Exudative tonsils, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and absence of cough
Conjunctivitis and diarrhea as the dominant associated symptoms
A vesicular rash on the palms and soles as the dominant associated finding
Isolated hoarseness without any exudate or lymphadenopathy
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Streptococcal tonsillitis (as reflected in clinical scoring systems like the Centor criteria) classically presents with exudative tonsils, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and notably the absence of cough, helping distinguish it from typical viral pharyngitis, which often features cough and rhinorrhea.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), a complication of acute tonsillitis, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: Bilateral, symmetric mild sore throat without any trismus
A painless neck mass without any throat symptoms
Severe unilateral throat pain, trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), and a muffled 'hot potato' voice with uvular deviation
Isolated ear pain without any throat or mouth findings
A vesicular rash on the soft palate as the dominant finding
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Peritonsillar abscess classically presents with severe, often unilateral throat pain, trismus, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, and deviation of the uvula away from the affected side, resulting from a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and the pharyngeal muscles.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Infectious mononucleosis, caused by Epstein-Barr virus, classically presents with which triad of findings in adolescents and young adults?
o: Isolated fever without any pharyngitis or lymphadenopathy
A vesicular oral rash with no fever or lymphadenopathy
Isolated hepatosplenomegaly without any pharyngitis
Bilateral parotid swelling without any pharyngitis or lymphadenopathy
Fever, pharyngitis (often exudative), and lymphadenopathy
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Infectious mononucleosis classically presents with a triad of fever, pharyngitis (often exudative, resembling streptococcal tonsillitis), and lymphadenopathy (often posterior cervical), and is frequently accompanied by fatigue, splenomegaly, and sometimes hepatomegaly.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Administration of amoxicillin to a patient with infectious mononucleosis (mistakenly treated for suspected streptococcal pharyngitis) classically produces which reaction?
o: A diffuse maculopapular rash
Immediate anaphylaxis in the vast majority of cases
No reaction whatsoever, since amoxicillin is entirely safe in this setting
Acute renal failure as the classic reaction
Acute hepatic failure as the classic and most common reaction
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Administration of amoxicillin (or ampicillin) to a patient with infectious mononucleosis classically produces a diffuse, often widespread maculopapular rash, thought to result from a transient, virus-related alteration in immune reactivity rather than a true drug allergy.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Laryngeal carcinoma, most commonly squamous cell carcinoma, is most strongly associated with which risk factors?
o: A diet high in fiber and low in red meat
Chronic allergic rhinitis as the predominant risk factor
Frequent, high-volume voice use alone, without any tobacco or alcohol exposure
A sedentary lifestyle as the predominant risk factor
Tobacco use and heavy alcohol consumption
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is most strongly associated with tobacco use and heavy alcohol consumption, which act synergistically to significantly increase risk, with persistent hoarseness being a key early warning symptom warranting further evaluation.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Persistent hoarseness lasting more than several weeks in an adult, particularly a smoker, should prompt evaluation to exclude which serious diagnosis?
o: Simple viral laryngitis, which typically resolves within days to a couple of weeks
Allergic rhinitis, which does not typically cause isolated persistent hoarseness
Laryngeal carcinoma
Gastroesophageal reflux disease as the only possible cause, requiring no further evaluation
A benign vocal cord nodule as the only possible cause, requiring no further evaluation
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Persistent hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks, particularly in a smoker or in the presence of other risk factors, warrants laryngoscopic evaluation to exclude laryngeal carcinoma, since early detection significantly improves treatment outcomes.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Vocal cord nodules, a benign cause of chronic hoarseness, most commonly result from which underlying cause?
o: A viral infection of the vocal cords, similarly to acute laryngitis
Malignant transformation of laryngeal epithelium
A congenital abnormality present from birth in the majority of cases
Gastroesophageal reflux disease as the primary and sole cause in all cases
Chronic vocal abuse or misuse (e.g., in singers or teachers)
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Vocal cord nodules typically result from chronic vocal abuse or misuse (repetitive vocal trauma), commonly seen in individuals with high vocal demands such as singers, teachers, and public speakers, causing bilateral, symmetric, callus-like lesions on the vocal cords.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A branchial cleft cyst, a congenital lateral neck mass, most commonly arises from persistence of remnants of which branchial arch/cleft?
o: The fourth branchial cleft as the most common site of origin
The first branchial cleft as the most common site of origin
The third branchial cleft as the most common site of origin
The fifth branchial cleft, which does not exist in normal human embryology
The second branchial cleft
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: The second branchial cleft is the most common site of origin for branchial cleft cysts, typically presenting as a lateral neck mass along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, usually becoming apparent in older children or young adults.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A thyroglossal duct cyst, unlike a branchial cleft cyst, is characteristically located in which region of the neck?
o: The lateral neck, along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
The posterior triangle of the neck exclusively
The submandibular region exclusively, with no midline component
The supraclavicular fossa exclusively
The midline, often near or at the level of the hyoid bone
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: A thyroglossal duct cyst is characteristically located in the midline of the neck, often at or near the level of the hyoid bone, reflecting its origin from remnants of the thyroglossal duct along the path of thyroid gland descent during embryological development.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Ludwig's angina, a serious, rapidly progressive infection of the floor of the mouth, is most commonly caused by which source?
o: A viral upper respiratory infection as the most common cause
A congenital branchial cleft cyst becoming infected
An insect bite to the floor of the mouth
Dental infection, particularly of the lower molars
A thyroglossal duct cyst becoming infected
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Ludwig's angina most commonly arises from dental infection, particularly involving the second or third lower molars, and represents a rapidly progressive, potentially airway-threatening cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces requiring urgent management.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma shows a notably higher incidence in certain populations (e.g., Southern China) and is strongly associated with which infectious agent?
o: Human papillomavirus, which is more classically linked to oropharyngeal carcinoma
Hepatitis B virus, which is more classically linked to hepatocellular carcinoma
Helicobacter pylori, which is more classically linked to gastric malignancy
Herpes simplex virus, which is not strongly linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Epstein-Barr virus
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection, along with genetic and dietary factors (such as consumption of salted preserved foods), contributing to its notably higher incidence in certain populations, including Southern China and parts of North Africa.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A patient presenting with a painless, slowly enlarging neck mass that moves with swallowing is most likely to have a mass arising from which structure?
o: The parotid gland, which does not typically move with swallowing
A lymph node, which does not typically move with swallowing
The thyroid gland
The submandibular gland, which does not typically move with swallowing
A branchial cleft cyst, which does not typically move with swallowing
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: A neck mass that moves upward with swallowing is characteristic of a thyroid gland mass, since the thyroid is enclosed within the pretracheal fascia, which is attached to the larynx and moves with it during swallowing.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Obstructive sleep apnea in adults is most commonly associated with which risk factor?
o: Low body mass index as the predominant risk factor
Young age, with the highest incidence in adolescents rather than middle-aged or older adults
Female sex, with a substantially higher incidence than in males
Obesity, particularly with increased neck circumference
Regular aerobic exercise as a risk-increasing factor
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Obesity, particularly with increased neck circumference (reflecting soft tissue deposition around the upper airway), is the most significant and common risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea in adults, along with other factors such as male sex, older age, and anatomical airway narrowing.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A tracheostomy, a surgical airway created through the anterior neck into the trachea, is generally indicated in which clinical scenario, among others?
o: Simple, uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection with no airway compromise
Mild, well-controlled asthma with no acute exacerbation
Uncomplicated allergic rhinitis with no airway obstruction
A normal, healthy individual as a purely elective, non-medically indicated procedure
Prolonged mechanical ventilation requirement, or upper airway obstruction that cannot be managed by less invasive means
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Tracheostomy is generally indicated for patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation (to reduce complications associated with prolonged translaryngeal intubation) or those with upper airway obstruction that cannot be adequately managed by less invasive means, providing a secure, long-term airway.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Retropharyngeal abscess, a serious deep neck space infection most common in young children, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: A completely painless neck mass with entirely normal swallowing and breathing
Isolated mild sore throat with no fever or neck stiffness
A condition confined exclusively to adults, never occurring in young children
Isolated ear pain with entirely normal neck examination
Fever, neck stiffness/torticollis, odynophagia, and sometimes respiratory distress
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Retropharyngeal abscess classically presents with fever, neck stiffness or torticollis (often held in an extended position), odynophagia (painful swallowing), and in more severe cases, respiratory distress, representing a potentially airway- and life-threatening deep neck space infection requiring prompt imaging and treatment.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Deep neck space infections, including retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal abscesses, are of particular concern due to their potential to spread into which life-threatening space?
o: The peritoneal cavity, via a direct anatomical connection
The pleural cavity exclusively, with no risk of mediastinal spread
The pericardial sac exclusively, with no risk via the mediastinum itself
A risk limited exclusively to the contralateral neck, with no thoracic extension possible
The mediastinum, via the danger space or direct extension along fascial planes
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Deep neck space infections can spread inferiorly along fascial planes (including the 'danger space') into the mediastinum, causing descending necrotizing mediastinitis, a life-threatening complication requiring urgent surgical drainage and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Acute epiglottitis in adults, though less common than in the historical pediatric presentation, classically presents with which combination of symptoms?
o: Severe sore throat disproportionate to physical examination findings, odynophagia, and muffled voice
A gradual, mild sore throat developing over several weeks
A completely painless throat examination with no associated symptoms
Isolated hoarseness with no sore throat or odynophagia
A condition that never causes any airway compromise in adults
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Adult epiglottitis classically presents with severe sore throat that appears disproportionate to relatively unremarkable oropharyngeal examination findings, along with odynophagia and a muffled voice, reflecting the supraglottic location of the inflammation, and requires careful airway assessment given the risk of rapid deterioration.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Recurrent tonsillitis in a child is generally considered for tonsillectomy when episodes meet certain frequency criteria, such as which commonly cited threshold?
o: A single episode of tonsillitis in a lifetime
Two episodes in a 10-year period
Seven or more episodes in one year, or a similarly defined frequency over 2-3 years, per commonly used clinical criteria
Any episode of mild, self-limited viral pharyngitis
A frequency threshold is never used, since tonsillectomy is never based on episode frequency
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Commonly used criteria (such as the Paradise criteria) for considering tonsillectomy in recurrent tonsillitis include seven or more well-documented episodes in the preceding year, or a similarly defined frequency sustained over 2-3 years, reflecting a significant symptom burden justifying surgical intervention.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Obstructive sleep apnea in children is most commonly caused by which anatomical factor, distinct from the more common adult risk factors?
o: Obesity as the predominant and most common cause in children, similarly to adults
Advanced age as the predominant risk factor in children
Male sex as the predominant and most significant risk factor in children
Adenotonsillar hypertrophy
Alcohol use as a common contributing factor in children
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Obstructive sleep apnea in children is most commonly caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy, in contrast to adults, where obesity and other factors are more prominent, and adenotonsillectomy is often curative in affected children.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A parotid gland tumor causing facial nerve weakness should raise particular concern for which underlying pathology?
o: A benign pleomorphic adenoma, which classically and commonly causes facial nerve weakness
A simple parotid cyst, which classically and commonly causes facial nerve weakness
Malignancy, since facial nerve involvement is uncommon with benign parotid tumors
Sialolithiasis (a salivary gland stone), which classically causes facial nerve weakness
Acute viral parotitis, which classically causes facial nerve weakness
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Facial nerve weakness in association with a parotid gland mass raises significant concern for malignancy, since benign parotid tumors (such as the common pleomorphic adenoma) typically do not cause facial nerve dysfunction, reflecting the nerve's vulnerability to invasion by malignant rather than benign processes.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor, most frequently arises in which gland?
o: The sublingual gland, which is the least common site for this tumor type
The parotid gland
The minor salivary glands exclusively, with no involvement of major salivary glands
The submandibular gland as the single most common site, more so than the parotid
The thyroid gland, which is not a salivary gland at all
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor overall, most frequently arises in the parotid gland, typically presenting as a slow-growing, painless, mobile mass.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Sialolithiasis (salivary gland stones) most commonly affects which salivary gland, related to the characteristics of its secretions and duct anatomy?
o: The submandibular gland
The parotid gland, which is affected less frequently than the submandibular gland
The sublingual gland, which is affected less frequently than the submandibular gland
The minor salivary glands, which are affected far less frequently than the submandibular gland
The lacrimal gland, which is not a salivary gland
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: The submandibular gland is most commonly affected by sialolithiasis, related to its more viscous, mucous-rich secretions and the longer, more tortuous course of its duct (Wharton's duct) that ascends against gravity, predisposing to stone formation and impaction.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A patient with a salivary gland stone classically presents with which symptom pattern, related to eating?
o: Symptoms that occur exclusively during sleep, with no relationship to eating
Symptoms that are completely unrelated to any meal or salivary stimulation
Postprandial (after eating) pain and swelling of the affected gland
Continuous, unchanging pain and swelling throughout the day regardless of eating
Symptoms that occur exclusively before eating, resolving immediately upon food intake
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Salivary gland stones classically cause postprandial pain and swelling of the affected gland, as eating stimulates salivary flow that becomes obstructed by the stone, causing painful glandular distension that typically subsides gradually between meals.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Oral leukoplakia, a white patch on the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off, is clinically significant primarily because it represents which type of lesion?
o: A potentially premalignant lesion requiring biopsy to exclude dysplasia or malignancy
A universally benign, entirely reactive lesion requiring no further evaluation in any case
An exclusively infectious (candidal) lesion that always resolves with antifungal treatment
A lesion that always represents invasive squamous cell carcinoma at the time of initial presentation
A lesion exclusively associated with viral infection, with no association with tobacco use
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Oral leukoplakia is considered a potentially premalignant lesion, and biopsy is generally recommended to assess for dysplasia or early malignant change, particularly given its association with risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol use.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Oral candidiasis (thrush), presenting with white plaques on the oral mucosa that CAN be scraped off (unlike leukoplakia), is particularly common in which patient populations?
o: Healthy young adults with no risk factors, as the population most commonly affected
Elderly patients with well-fitted dentures and excellent oral hygiene exclusively
Infants, denture wearers, and immunocompromised individuals (including those on inhaled corticosteroids)
A condition exclusively affecting the esophagus, never the oral cavity
A condition with no recognized association with any medication use
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Oral candidiasis commonly affects infants (with immature immune systems), denture wearers (due to altered oral flora and moisture retention under dentures), and immunocompromised individuals, including those using inhaled corticosteroids without proper mouth rinsing after use.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A patient presenting with trismus, drooling, and a muffled voice following a dental infection should be evaluated for which serious complication, in addition to peritonsillar abscess?
o: A simple, uncomplicated dental caries requiring only routine dental filling
A benign salivary gland stone with no associated infection
A condition requiring no further evaluation beyond simple oral antibiotics
A deep neck space infection, such as a parapharyngeal or submandibular space abscess
An isolated, uncomplicated case of oral thrush
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Trismus, drooling, and a muffled voice following a dental infection raise concern for a deep neck space infection (such as parapharyngeal or submandibular space involvement, including Ludwig's angina), warranting prompt imaging and, often, surgical drainage in addition to antibiotic therapy.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: The 'safety pin' sign or radiopaque object visible on a lateral neck or chest X-ray in a child with sudden onset of coughing and choking should raise suspicion for which diagnosis?
o: A congenital vascular ring compressing the airway, which does not classically appear as a discrete radiopaque object
Foreign body aspiration or ingestion
Acute epiglottitis, which does not classically produce a discrete radiopaque foreign body appearance
Croup, which does not classically produce a discrete radiopaque foreign body appearance
A retropharyngeal abscess, which does not classically produce a discrete radiopaque foreign body appearance
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: A radiopaque object visible on imaging in a child with sudden onset of coughing, choking, or respiratory distress is classic for foreign body aspiration or ingestion, prompting further evaluation (often bronchoscopy or endoscopy) for confirmation and removal.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Reinke's edema, a benign condition affecting the vocal cords, is most strongly associated with which risk factor?
o: Viral upper respiratory infection as the primary and most common cause
Chronic smoking
A single episode of vocal strain, unrelated to any chronic exposure
A congenital condition present from birth in the majority of cases
Chronic allergic rhinitis as the primary and most common cause
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Reinke's edema, characterized by fluid accumulation within the superficial layer of the vocal cord lamina propria, is most strongly associated with chronic smoking, and often also occurs in individuals with voice overuse, causing a characteristically low-pitched, hoarse voice.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Vocal cord paralysis, whether unilateral or bilateral, most commonly results from injury to which nerve?
o: The hypoglossal nerve, which controls tongue movement rather than the vocal cords
The recurrent laryngeal nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve, which is not the primary motor nerve to the vocal cords
The spinal accessory nerve, which controls the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid rather than the vocal cords
The facial nerve, which controls facial expression rather than the vocal cords
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Vocal cord paralysis most commonly results from injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (a branch of the vagus nerve), which can occur from surgical injury (particularly thyroid or neck surgery), malignant invasion, or other causes along the nerve's course.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis, unlike unilateral paralysis, is of particular clinical concern primarily due to which risk?
o: A risk limited exclusively to voice change with no airway concern whatsoever
A condition that never requires any intervention regardless of severity
A risk limited exclusively to swallowing difficulty with no airway concern
A condition that always resolves spontaneously without any risk of complication
Airway obstruction, since both cords may lie close to the midline, significantly narrowing the glottic airway
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis is of particular concern because both paralyzed cords may lie close to the midline, significantly narrowing the glottic airway and creating a risk of airway obstruction, sometimes requiring tracheostomy, in contrast to unilateral paralysis, which more typically causes voice and aspiration issues with less airway compromise.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Laryngomalacia, the most common cause of congenital stridor in infants, is characterized by which underlying abnormality?
o: Excessive floppiness and collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration
A fixed, rigid subglottic stenosis present from birth
A vascular ring compressing the trachea externally
A congenital vocal cord paralysis affecting both cords
A completely normal laryngeal structure with no anatomical explanation for the stridor
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Laryngomalacia results from excessive floppiness of the supraglottic structures (particularly the epiglottis and arytenoid cartilages), which collapse inward during inspiration, causing the characteristic inspiratory stridor that typically worsens with feeding, crying, or supine positioning, and generally improves spontaneously as the child grows.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A branchial cleft fistula, unlike a simple branchial cleft cyst, is characterized by which anatomical feature?
o: A completely closed, isolated cystic cavity with no external or internal communication
A tumor arising from thyroid tissue with no connection to any branchial remnant
An abnormal communication (tract) connecting the skin surface to the pharynx or a deeper structure
A condition confined exclusively to the parotid gland with no external opening
A lesion that is always malignant, unlike the benign branchial cleft cyst
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: A branchial cleft fistula (or sinus) is characterized by an abnormal epithelial-lined tract that provides a communication between the skin surface and the pharynx or another internal structure, in contrast to a branchial cleft cyst, which is a closed cystic cavity without such an external or internal opening.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Cervical lymphadenopathy in a child that is persistent, non-tender, firm, and associated with systemic symptoms such as fever and weight loss should raise concern for which category of underlying causes?
o: A simple, self-limited reactive lymphadenopathy from a recent minor viral illness, which does not require further evaluation regardless of these features
Malignancy (such as lymphoma) or a chronic granulomatous infection (such as tuberculosis)
A benign branchial cleft cyst, which does not classically present with systemic symptoms
A simple dental abscess, which typically resolves quickly with antibiotics and does not cause prolonged systemic symptoms
A condition that never warrants any further diagnostic evaluation in a child
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Persistent, non-tender, firm cervical lymphadenopathy associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats in a child raises concern for malignancy (such as lymphoma) or a chronic granulomatous infection (such as tuberculosis or atypical mycobacterial infection), warranting further diagnostic evaluation including possible biopsy.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A carotid body tumor (paraganglioma), a rare neck mass arising at the carotid bifurcation, classically demonstrates which characteristic finding on examination and imaging?
o: Complete immobility in all directions, unlike the classic Fontaine sign
A cystic, fluid-filled appearance on imaging with no vascular characteristics
A location exclusively within the parotid gland, unrelated to the carotid bifurcation
Lateral but not vertical mobility (the 'Fontaine sign'), and splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries on imaging
A tumor that is always malignant with a very poor prognosis in the majority of cases
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: A carotid body tumor classically demonstrates lateral but not vertical mobility on palpation (the Fontaine sign), reflecting its attachment at the carotid bifurcation, and characteristically splays apart the internal and external carotid arteries on imaging, reflecting its origin from paraganglion cells at this location.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A patient presenting with a hoarse voice, dysphagia, and a neck mass, with a history of significant smoking and alcohol use, should be urgently evaluated for which possibility?
o: A simple, benign vocal cord nodule from voice overuse, which typically does not present with a neck mass or dysphagia
A benign thyroglossal duct cyst, which is a congenital rather than acquired lesion
A head and neck malignancy, such as laryngeal or hypopharyngeal carcinoma
Reinke's edema alone, which does not classically cause dysphagia or a distinct neck mass
A simple viral laryngitis, which typically resolves within days to weeks without dysphagia or a mass
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: The combination of hoarseness, dysphagia, and a neck mass in a patient with significant smoking and alcohol use history is a red flag presentation requiring urgent evaluation for head and neck malignancy, such as laryngeal or hypopharyngeal carcinoma, given the strong epidemiological association of these risk factors with such cancers.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Zenker's diverticulum, an outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa, classically arises through a weak area known as which anatomical landmark?
o: The cricothyroid membrane, which is unrelated to Zenker's diverticulum formation
The thyrohyoid membrane, which is unrelated to Zenker's diverticulum formation
The foramen cecum, which is related to thyroglossal duct remnants rather than Zenker's diverticulum
The pyriform sinus in its entirety, rather than a specific weak point within the pharyngeal wall
Killian's triangle, located between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and cricopharyngeus muscles
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Zenker's diverticulum classically arises through Killian's triangle, an area of relative muscular weakness between the oblique fibers of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the transverse fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle, allowing mucosal herniation with increased intraluminal pressure during swallowing.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: A globus sensation, the persistent feeling of a lump in the throat without an identifiable structural cause, is often associated with which underlying condition, among other possibilities?
o: Acute bacterial epiglottitis, which causes an acute rather than chronic sensation with significant additional findings
A large, obstructing laryngeal carcinoma, which is generally excluded as part of the workup for globus sensation
A retropharyngeal abscess, which causes an acute rather than chronic presentation with additional systemic findings
A condition that always indicates an underlying malignancy requiring immediate aggressive treatment
Laryngopharyngeal reflux
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Globus sensation is often associated with laryngopharyngeal reflux (acid or non-acid reflux affecting the pharynx and larynx), among other possible contributing factors, though a thorough evaluation is still generally recommended to exclude structural or other pathology before attributing symptoms to reflux.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Direct laryngoscopy, allowing detailed examination of the larynx, is generally indicated for a patient with persistent hoarseness lasting longer than which approximate duration?
o: 24 hours
Three years
One hour
Ten years
Two to three weeks
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Direct or indirect laryngoscopic examination of the larynx is generally recommended for patients with hoarseness persisting beyond approximately two to three weeks (particularly in adults, and especially those with risk factors such as smoking), to evaluate for underlying structural, inflammatory, or neoplastic causes.

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Angioedema involving the tongue, lips, and airway, whether allergic or hereditary (C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency) in origin, is a medical emergency primarily due to which risk?
o: A risk limited exclusively to cosmetic disfigurement with no airway concern
A condition that always resolves within minutes without any treatment or monitoring
A risk limited exclusively to gastrointestinal symptoms with no airway involvement
Rapid airway compromise from soft tissue swelling
A condition confined exclusively to the skin with no mucosal or airway involvement possible
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Angioedema involving the tongue, lips, or airway structures is a medical emergency because rapidly progressive soft tissue swelling can cause airway compromise and obstruction, requiring prompt recognition and, in severe cases, urgent airway management alongside treatment directed at the underlying cause (allergic versus hereditary).

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.s: Sialadenitis, acute inflammation/infection of a salivary gland, is more likely to occur in dehydrated or postoperative patients primarily due to which contributing factor?
o: Reduced salivary flow, predisposing to retrograde bacterial contamination of the gland via its duct
Excessive salivary flow overwhelming the gland's normal defenses
A condition entirely unrelated to hydration status or salivary flow
An exclusively viral etiology unrelated to any flow-related mechanism
A condition that occurs exclusively in well-hydrated, ambulatory outpatients
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.e: Reduced salivary flow, as seen in dehydrated or postoperative patients, predisposes to retrograde bacterial contamination ascending the salivary duct into the gland, increasing the risk of acute suppurative sialadenitis, classically involving the parotid gland.
